summary: Pedro de Leme instituted the Leme entailed estate before 1550.
The British Factory in Madeira was established before 1774.
Joaquim Melchior Gonçalves emigrated to Brazil before 1834.
A newspaper, O Realista, may have been published before 1834, though its existence is doubtful.
All collegiate chapters in Madeira had been abolished by 1834.
The Praça de São João in Funchal was demolished before 1860.
Francisco de Freitas Correia had the chapel of Nossa Senhora do Perpétuo Socorro built at Queimada, Água de Pena; the printed year 1244 is presumably a misprint.
Members of the Deniz family were using the surname in the fourteenth century.
Filipe Perestrelo came to Portugal from Lombardy in the late fourteenth century.
Maria de Bourbon granted Vostitza and Corinth to Reniero Acciaiuoli.
Guilherme Arnau accompanied Philippa of Lancaster to Portugal.
At Alenquer, King Fernando granted houses in Lisbon to Machico, master of his barge.

mentions.as_written: 12 dias dabril de mjl e iiij xbij anos (1379)

summary: João Gonçalves Zarco was probably born shortly after 1390.
Prince Henry the Navigator was born.
Filippone Palestrello proved his family's nobility.
Porto Santo and Madeira were discovered in the first quarter of the fifteenth century.
Simão Acciaioly arrived in Madeira from Florence.
Joana Tavares lived in Madeira in the mid-fifteenth century.
Valentim Fernandes settled in Lisbon as a printer and publisher.
Gil Anes founded the chapel of Nosso Senhor Jesus Cristo in Santa Cruz.
Manuel Afonso Sanha and Mécia de Carvalhal founded an entail at Ponta Delgada.
The first entailed estates in Madeira date from the late fifteenth century, after which sesmeiros held land as absolute owners.
The Corpo Santo chapel was built by Funchal seafarers.
Álvaro de Ornelas founded the entailed estate of Consolação in Caniço.
Caniço was made one of about ten 'lugares' when the towns of Funchal and Machico were created.
By the mid-fifteenth century communications between Madeira and Europe were no longer very rare.
The parish of Machico was created with its seat in Tristão Vaz's chapel.
Gomes Eanes de Azurara wrote his chronicle covering the discovery of Madeira.
João Esmeraldo reportedly built a Santo Amaro chapel at Lombada dos Esmeraldos.
Madeira was the first of the fifteenth-century Portuguese discoveries.
Canarian islanders came to Madeira, probably introducing the word gofio.
André Gonçalves de França arrived and received sesmaria lands at Estreito da Calheta.
A small settled population existed in the Curral das Freiras by the late fifteenth century.
Braz Gonçalves de Gaias lived in Machico.
Corregedores were present in Madeira to curb abuses of jurisdiction by donataries and their ouvidores.
Machico and Porto Santo became the archipelago's first towns.
Florentines including the Salviati rose against the Medici and were defeated, some fleeing into exile.
The Madeiran sugar industry reached great development in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, giving rise to confectionery-making.
João Gonçalves da Câmara was probably born about 1414.
Portugal conquered Ceuta, its first African conquest, with members of the Order of Christ taking part.
According to Cordeiro, the Canaries were discovered for the third time by the Béthencourts.
Before 1418 the archipelago was already known to Portuguese navigators.
Zarco and Tristão Vaz probably reconnoitred the archipelago between 1418 and 1425.
Porto Santo was discovered, traditionally in 1418 (or 1419); Bartolomeu Perestrelo was falsely said to have taken part.
The Provedoria register spanned from 1419 until the office was extinguished in 1775.
Passing Ponta de São Lourenço, the caravel São Lourenço approached Machico bay.
Zarco made the first landing on Madeira at Machico on the feast of the Visitation, where accompanying Franciscans reportedly celebrated the first Mass; next day he reached Porto do Seixo.

mentions.as_written: domingo 2 de Julho do mesmo ano

summary: Madeira was discovered by João Gonçalves Zarco and Tristão Vaz under Prince Henry, most commonly dated 1419, by some 1420.
Bartolomeu Perestrelo became donatary of Porto Santo.
According to a family document, João Escorcio Drumond moved to Madeira.
Constança Rodrigues de Almeida founded the chapel and almshouse of Santa Catarina in Funchal, reputedly the first church and first charity on Madeira; the date 1425 is carved on its portal.
Sugar cane was introduced into Madeira, reportedly from Sicily.
Tristão Vaz settled at Machico with his wife and children.
Santa Cruz was probably created as an autonomous parish.
Settlement of Madeira began under the first donatary captains, with settlers from mainland Portugal, some first sheltering at the Ilhéus of Funchal.
The date inscribed over its outer door marks the first construction of the São Paulo chapel.
The parish of Câmara de Lobos, apparently the first outside Funchal, was created with its seat in the Espírito Santo chapel.
The parish of Calheta was created, first seated at the Estrela chapel.
Frei Rogério arrived and apparently formed the first regular Franciscan community on Madeira.
King João I granted Bartolomeu Perestrelo and Margarida Martins houses in Rua Nova.
The Franciscans began building the hospice and hermitage of São João in Funchal.
Death of King João I, closing the first period of Madeiran history in Azevedo's scheme.
King Duarte granted the archipelago to Prince Henry, requiring the kingdom's coin to circulate, and its spiritual jurisdiction to the Order of Christ.
Portuguese discoverers landed two horses on the African coast, naming Angra dos Cavalos.
Frei Pedro da Guarda was born in Guarda.
The Porto Santo captaincy was restored to the second Bartolomeu Perestrelo, per the Elucidário's date.
The church of Nossa Senhora do Calhau was built and became seat of Santa Maria Maior, Funchal's first parish.
The dowry deed for the marriage of Isabel Gonçalves da Câmara, Zarco's daughter, to Diogo Afonso de Aguiar was drawn up.
A charter issued in Lisbon granted the spirituality of the islands to the Order of Christ.
Charters of 1440, 1446 and 1450 granted the captaincies of Machico, Porto Santo and Funchal to their first captains.
The parishes of Ribeira Brava and Caniço were reportedly created.
Manuscripts claim the parish of São Vicente was founded, a date the Elucidário rejects.
Prince Henry granted the captaincy of Machico to Tristão Vaz.
Colonisation of Ponta do Sol began.
Nuno Tristão discovered the island of Arguim.
Battle of Varna, after which Henrique Alemão reputedly vowed to go on pilgrimage.
Cadamosto anchored at Porto Santo, according to his narrative.
Cadamosto anchored in the bay of Machico.
Malvasia vines were reportedly imported from Crete; Cadamosto found newly planted vines on Madeira.
Funchal already had a meat market.
Prince Henry granted the captaincy of Porto Santo to Bartolomeu Perestrelo by charter.
A document spells the donatary's surname 'Zargo'.
Pestana Júnior dates Cadamosto's voyages to 1449 and 1450.
A royal letter of Afonso V wrote Zarco's name as Zarquo.
Afonso V confirmed the grant of the islands to Prince Henry.
The parish of Machico was created, with Frei João Garcia sent as its first vicar.
Chapters from Prince Henry and the Order of Christ on alcaides and taxes were registered in the Funchal council archive.
A diploma required the alcaide's assistants in Funchal to be of good conduct.
The Funchal municipality already existed, the donatary being ordered to propose candidates for alcaide to its senate.
João Gonçalves Zargo founded the entail later held by the counts of Calheta.
Prince Henry granted João Gonçalves Zarco the captaincy of Funchal.
Cadamosto's voyage account, which spelt the name Zarco, recorded wine and vine growing in Madeira.
Construction of the Portuguese fortress on Arguim began.
Antão Pacheco and Gomes Pacheco came to Madeira.
João Afonso Escudeiro came to Madeira.
Rodrigo Enes is conjectured to have settled at Ponta do Sol.
Infante D. Fernando ordered two officials appointed to share out irrigation water.
Royal confirmation of Zargo's grant of the Funchal captaincy.
D. Afonso V raised Funchal to the status of town, with Machico and Baleira (Porto Santo) probably made towns and municipalities about the same time.
Diogo de Teive contracted with Prince Henry to build Madeira's first water-powered sugar mill, giving the Infante a third of its sugar.
D. Afonso V granted Funchal a charter exempting islanders from siza, tolls and levies.
Azurara wrote his chronicle around this year.
Zargo donated land beside the São Paulo chapel for Funchal's first hospital.
Cadamosto's voyage to Madeira, in which he described its prized timber including cedar and yew.
The Acciaiuoli principality was destroyed by Mehmed II.
António Correia was born in Madeira.
Infante D. Henrique confirmed Henrique Alemão's land grant at Madalena do Mar.
King Afonso V confirmed Henrique Alemão's land grant at Madalena do Mar.
Bartolomeu Perestrelo died at Vila Baleira, aged a little over fifty.
The first Franciscan friars left the São João hospice in Funchal for Xabregas near Lisbon.
Gonçalo Eanes de Velosa died, according to his epitaph dated era 1497.
Afonso V again confirmed the donation of the islands to Prince Henry.
Death of the earlier holder of the Valença title.
Garcia Homem de Sousa founded the chapel of Santo Amaro.
The Genoese navigator António da Nola called at Madeira on a voyage with Diogo Gomes.
The Portuguese discovered Santiago island in Cape Verde on the feast of St James the Less.

mentions.as_written: um de Maio do ano de 1460

summary: By charter of Afonso V, Zarco was ennobled as João Gonçalves de Câmara de Lobos and granted a coat of arms bearing a tower and wolves.
Prince Henry issued a donation charter granting the islands' spirituality to the Order of Christ, referring to the start of settlement.
Prince Henry granted the University of Coimbra twelve marks of silver yearly from the Order of Christ's Madeiran tithes for the chief chair of theology.
Prince Henry the Navigator, lord of Madeira, died.
Afonso V granted the archipelago to Prince Fernando, who thus inherited the lordship of Madeira from Prince Henry.
Rui Mendes Pereira, called o Tacão, came to Madeira.
João de Braga settled in Madeira and received a land grant at Laranjal.
Infante D. Fernando issued the oldest known levada law, appointing two sworn men to share out irrigation water.
Infante D. Fernando ordered municipal offices to be filled by annual election.
The Elucidário considers 1461 the most probable year of Zargo's death, though 1471 is also possible.
Infante D. Fernando answered a Funchal petition asking that Jews and Genoese be barred from trading in Madeira.
Municipal records mention the first flag of Funchal, sent by Infante D. Fernando.
Afonso V confirmed the donation of Madeira and Zargo's captaincy grant.
Oldest recorded appointment of a corregedor in Madeira, Denis Anes de Aragão.
João Gonçalves Zargo died around 1467 and his son succeeded to the captaincy of Funchal.
Inhabitants of Câmara de Lobos were ordered to join the Corpus Christi procession with their crafts.
Funchal's first hospital was built at public expense near the chapel of São Paulo.
Manuel Afonso de Sanha received a land grant from Ponta Delgada to Ribeira das Vacas.
Afonso V confirmed the grant of Madeira's black soap works to Rui Gonçalves da Câmara.
Pope Paul II issued a brief alluding to the great forest fire of Madeira.
The first surviving book of Funchal council proceedings dates from this year.
Infante D. Fernando asked the donatary João Gonçalves da Câmara to build a council house and municipal pound in Funchal, granting land by the church.
São Vicente was constituted as a parish in the late fifteenth century.
D. Afonso de Aragão, a Neapolitan knight, reached Madeira.
Gonçalo Diniz da Silva founded an Almas Pobres chapel in Santa Maria Maior.
Pedro de Brito Oliveira Pestana and João Mendes de Brito came to Madeira.
Adão Gonçalves Ferreira built the chapel that became Nossa Senhora do Monte.
Tristão Vaz Teixeira, first donatary of Machico, died.
Diogo and Francisco Pires were resident in Madeira.
A letter from the infanta required everyone to serve in municipal offices regardless of exemptions.
Lopo Vaz was working as a goldsmith in Funchal.
Estêvão do Azinhal sat on the governing body of the town of Funchal.
Afonso V granted António Leme letters of nobility and a coat of arms (another entry dates it 12 November).
Frutuoso dates the Funchal charter (foral) to 1472, a date Azevedo considered erroneous.
Luís Álvares da Costa, with his son, founded the Franciscan convent of São Francisco in Funchal.
Rui Gonçalves da Câmara leased the Lombada da Ponta do Sol to João Esmeraldo for 600$000 réis plus an annual rent.
The infante ordered that no slave might keep a house of his own.
Rui Gonçalves da Câmara moved to São Miguel in the Azores as its captain-donatary.
Infanta D. Beatriz reportedly ordered the chapel of Nossa Senhora dos Anjos built.
The Água de Mel entail was instituted in the last quarter of the fifteenth century.
The corregedor Álvaro Fernandes came to Madeira with jurisdiction over the whole island.
João Batista settled in Madeira.
Frei Nuno Cão came to Madeira on behalf of the Order of Christ to superintend religious services.
João Afonso was buried in the Espírito Santo chapel.
João Alvares was living in Ribeira Brava.
Álvaro de Ornelas founded the entailed estate at Quinta, Caniço.
Pedro de Brito de Oliveira Pestana and his brother settled in Madeira.

mentions.as_written: fins do terceiro quartel do século XV

summary: The Genoese brothers João Baptista and Urbano Lomelino arrived in Madeira.
Franciscans under Frei Rodrigo de Arruda reached Funchal, a papal brief authorised the community, and the friars moved from São João into the convent of São Francisco.
A royal charter created the customs houses of Funchal, Santa Cruz and Machico, the Funchal customs being the archipelago's oldest public office.
The first war contribution was imposed on Madeira and was resisted by the nobles.
The Florentine João Salviati, implicated in a conspiracy against the Medici, took refuge in Madeira.
A document cited by Azevedo shows Madeira already sending representatives to the Cortes.
The chapel of Nossa Senhora da Estrela was reportedly built.
The French settler Rui Vaz Uzel (Urzel) came to Madeira and settled at Tábua.
Rui Teixeira and Branca Ferreira sold the Curral estate to captain-donatary João Gonçalves da Câmara; it was later given to the Convent of Santa Clara.
João Esmeraldo, from Picardy, arrived in Funchal.
Henrique Aragão settled in Funchal.
Antão Álvares de Sousa settled in Santa Cruz.
Lopo Franco de Monção came to Madeira.
Fernão Álvaro de Agrela settled in Madeira.
Funchal residents were exempted from a duty on certain goods.
D. Diogo, Duke of Viseu and lord of Madeira, was killed by King João II, and the lordship passed to his brother D. Manuel.
A decree allowed captured runaway slaves to be sold if unclaimed within four months, and an inquiry into slaves' lives was ordered.
A regulation fixed the order of the trades in the Funchal Corpus Christi procession.
Álvaro Afonso donated land for the Misericórdia building.
D. Fernando, Duke of Bragança, was executed for conspiracy against João II.
Martim de Leme came to Madeira with recommendations from the infante D. Fernando.
The Funchal hospital moved to Santa Maria Maior.
A letter ordered irrigation water released on Sundays to all water-rights holders (heréus), the first official use of the term in its modern sense.
A levy on wine was authorised to meet the island's municipal expenses.
D. Manuel, Duke of Beja, ceded land in the Campo do Duque, Funchal, for the church (later cathedral) and town hall; sources give 5 June or 5 November 1485.
King João II granted arms to João Fernandes de Andrade.
Frei Pedro da Guarda came to Madeira to live in the convent of São Bernardino.
The Funchal council ordered foreigners, including sugar growers, to leave the island by September, but the Duke, lord of Madeira, blocked the expulsion by letter of 7 August.
Duke D. Manuel ordered a square, council house, notaries' office and pillory built on the Campo do Duque in Funchal.
Afonso Sanches reportedly sailed from Portugal, was carried to America and later landed in Madeira.
The Machico customs house was again ordered to operate.
João do Porto was appointed Judge of Residues, the earliest known holder of the office.
Rodrigo Enes made testamentary provisions ordering a chapel of the Holy Spirit in the church of Ponta do Sol.
Diogo Cabral, Zarco's son-in-law and founder of the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Estrela at Calheta, died and was buried in it.
Council records place Funchal's meat market near Santa Catarina.
D. Manuel wrote to the Madeirans urging the foundation of a nunnery.
D. Manuel assigned half of the island's fines to building the Funchal church.
The captain-donatary allowed merchants and householders to carry sword and dagger until curfew.
João Gonçalves da Câmara was born in Funchal.
Vasco Martins Moniz founded by will an entailed estate at Caniçal for his son Garcia Moniz.
Natives of Gran Canaria, La Palma, Tenerife and La Gomera were forbidden to reside in Madeira.
João Afonso Correia founded the first of the Torre Bela entails.
Gonçalo Alves de Araújo came to Madeira in the late fifteenth century.
Teresa de Lira, wife of D. Afonso de Aragão, lived at this time; according to some genealogies their son introduced the Lira surname to Madeira.
Diogo de Arvelos settled in Machico.
D. Nuno de Aguiar, bishop of Tangier, died in mainland Portugal.
The captain-donatary founded the Convent of Santa Clara in Funchal, whose construction began in 1492; the first nuns entered in 1497.
João Gonçalves da Câmara gave the Curral to the Santa Clara convent as dowry for his daughters, the place becoming known as Curral das Freiras.
A war levy was imposed but never paid.
The wine levy was applied to building Funchal Cathedral, whose construction began shortly afterwards.
The Funchal council requested a 'Tronco' to detain the insane.
Brás Ferreira made his will naming himself founder of the chapel of São Brás at Arco da Calheta.
Period covered by the archival list of judges of residues and chapels.
King João II issued charters regulating irrigation water and denying private rights over springs, and reserving ash and cedar wood to the Crown, the oldest such laws known in Madeira.

mentions.as_written: 7 de Março e de 7 de Maio de 1493

summary: A letter of João II ordered the captains to restore obstructed levadas, fining obstructors 500 cruzados, and referred to their 'terradas & trastes'.
Duke Manuel ordered walls built round the town of Funchal.
Date inscribed on a window of the so-called house of Columbus, marking its Renaissance restoration.
A royal letter revoked the order to wall Funchal, allowing only bastions.
Francisco Álvares was appointed first judge of the Funchal customs house.
D. Manuel ascended the throne and asked the Funchal council to acclaim him and hold João II's funeral rites.
The council ordered butchers to slaughter cattle at Cabo do Calhau.
Death of the poet João Gomes da Ilha, the Troubadour.
A petition to the Funchal council asked that the brothel quarter be moved away from the seafront.
Sugar of one and two boilings was priced at 350 and 600 reais per arroba.
A regimento denied foreigners permanent residence in Madeira.
D. Manuel published the decree expelling the Jews from Portugal.
Gonçalo Anes de Velosa founded the Albergaria de São Bartolomeu for poor clergy in Funchal, and died that year, being buried in the church he founded.
The levy of gibonetes was established.
Rui Gonçalves da Câmara made his will naming his natural son as successor.
A charter shows that an armoury already existed in Madeira.
D. Manuel's charter made Madeira permanently and inalienably Crown land, together with the mastership of the Order of Christ, dealing a major blow to the donataries' privileges.
Madeira produced over 120,000 arrobas of sugar.
Zarco's children reportedly gave the organ to the Santa Clara convent.
Francisco da Silveira wrote verses mocking a Madeiran nobleman in Castile.
Vasco Martins Moniz de Meneses founded an entail by an approved will.
Terra Negra's pamphlet refers to Madeira as it was in 1498, the time of the voyage recounted in the Lusíadas.
João Esmeraldo acquired the Lombada da Ponta do Sol from Rui Gonçalves da Câmara.
D. Manuel ordered that sentences in Madeira not confirmed by him should not be executed.
By a charter (alvará), King Manuel allowed foreigners to reside permanently and trade freely in Madeira.
Álvaro de Ornelas instituted an entailed estate in Caniço.
King Manuel I granted Machico its arms and ordered bronze standard weights, which bear this date.
An old manuscript dates the building of the present parish church of Machico to this year.
King Manuel gave an organ to the parish church of Machico.
Death of Lopo Fernandes Pinto, one of the first sesmaria land-grant holders in the Santana and São Jorge area.
João Martins de Aldromar is recorded as living in Câmara de Lobos.
Pedro Giraldes lived in Calheta.
Madeira and Porto Santo had about 16,000 inhabitants.
D. Manuel issued the first royal diploma ordering Madeira's nobles and vassals to serve with him in an African expedition; the demand was later revoked for Madeira.
Probable foundation of the Misericórdia of Machico.
Bartolomeu Nunes lived in Porto Santo.
The Acciaioli family came from Florence to Madeira and founded the morgado of Nossa Senhora da Natividade.
António and Leonardo Espínola came from Genoa to Madeira.
The Misericórdia of Santa Cruz was founded.
Bartolomeu Malheiro gave land for a new hospital in Funchal.
Lourenço Vaz Pereira da Gama came to Madeira as provedor of the deceased and absent.
D. Isabel de Abreu had the first chapel of Nossa Senhora da Conceição built at Amoreiras, Arco da Calheta.
João Escórcio Drumond built the chapel of São Pedro on the Lombada de São Pedro, Santa Cruz.
João Rodrigues Madureira fought in Africa.
The chapel of Nossa Senhora do Loreto was built at Lombada do Loreto, Arco da Calheta.
João Afonso Escudeiro founded a chapel of São Lázaro in Santa Cruz.
Martim and Isabel Afonso founded the Anjos chapel in Canhas.
Damião de Góis lived and wrote his chronicles.
The João Diniz springs flowed directly onto the Funchal beach.
The chapel of Santo António at Achada de Santo António, Santana, was founded around the mid-16th century.
Permanent settlers were already living on the slopes of the Ribeira da Janela.
The Piedade chapel on Monte Gordo, Caniçal, is said to have been founded by Garcia Moniz.
Manuel de Faria Azeredo was shipwrecked in Madeira and settled there.
Madeira's sugar output exceeded 300,000 arrobas around the mid-16th century.
Pedro Lopes de Figueiredo resided in Machico and Santa Cruz.
The parish of Campanário was created and the Vera Cruz chapel passed to it.
António de Almada married Isabel Rodrigues Leal of Porto da Cruz.
The Manueline Madre de Deus chapel at Caniço was built, reputedly by the Salvago family.
According to Dr Azevedo, the colonia contract emerged from the sesmaria held under entailment.
Pedro Bogalho settled in Madeira.
João de Barros wrote of the lasting timber shortage caused by the first fire on Madeira.
Soft stone was widely used in Madeiran building before hard basalt became general.
Fr. Pedro de Bettencourt was born in Madeira around the mid-16th century.
Lopo Rebelo lived and died in Funchal.
In the late 16th century Madeiran customs began to change through wider contacts, trade, overseas service and Spanish rule.
The chapel of Nossa Senhora das Neves was built.
Manuel Camilo de Melo e Alvino arrived in Madeira, bringing the Alvino surname.
António de Aragão e Teive settled in Madeira.
Pedro Ribeiro and Mécia de Carvalhal lived around this time.
João Rodrigues Mondragão settled in Madeira.
Pedro Figueira settled in Madeira.
Gonçalo Pinto Alcoforado came to Madeira and settled in Machico.
André Gonçalves Alvarenga settled with his family in Funchal.
Afonso de Viana settled in Caniço, founding the Viana family in Madeira.
João Gonçalves da Câmara, Zarco's eldest son, second captain-donatary of Funchal and founder of the Convent of Santa Clara, died in Funchal aged 87 (sources give 25 or 26 March).
By royal charter of D. Manuel I, Ponta do Sol was raised to the status of town and municipality.
A petition by Funchal residents to abolish the customs houses of Santa Cruz and Machico was refused.
A royal letter extended the wine levy of Ponta do Sol and Calheta to the works of the Funchal church.
It was ordered that in the towns the Corpus Christi procession be held on the Sunday after the feast.
King Manuel confirmed the earlier water laws of Madeira and eased the building of aqueducts (levadas).
A royal charter added a moio of wheat to the stipend of the priest of Seixal.
By royal charter Calheta was raised to a town and made a municipality, reducing the area of Ponta do Sol.
A royal reply to the Funchal council already referred to Vila Nova da Calheta.
A royal letter to the Funchal council recommended using ash against the sugar-cane borer.
João de França founded at Estreito da Calheta one of Madeira's oldest entails.
On Deserta Grande shepherds repelled about 80 Englishmen led by the corsair Penteado by rolling stones down on them.
An alvará ended the restrictions on Madeiran sugar exports.
Lopo de Abreu sailed to India with Lopo Soares's fleet.
The donataries obtained a royal alvará allowing them to have slaves' ears cut off as punishment for certain crimes.
Rodrigo Enes founded the chapel of Santa Catarina in Calheta.
A charter of King Manuel confirmed and extended Madeira's water regulations; the main common levadas were built in this period.
A regulation fixed the officers of the Funchal council.
Frei Pedro da Guarda died at the convent of São Bernardino, Câmara de Lobos.
João Gomes de Abreu sailed as a ship's captain in the fleet to India.
Cadamosto's Navegações, describing Madeira and Porto Santo, were first published in Italian.
Death of Sanha, founder of a chapel at Ponta Delgada.
D. Manuel ordered the construction of a new hospital in Funchal.
Bishop D. João Lobo blessed the unfinished Igreja Grande of Funchal, later the cathedral, and the parish seat moved there.
The Order of Christ sent Bishop D. João Lobo to Madeira, the first bishop to visit the island, before the diocese was created.
Martim Afonso and Isabel Afonso reportedly founded the chapel of Nossa Senhora dos Anjos at Canhas, with an entail.
Baltazar de Teive was born in Madeira.
Sebastião de Morais, o Velho, proved his nobility.
A charter of D. Manuel ordered the Funchal council to be governed like Lisbon's, with only noblemen as councillors and triennial elections confirmed by the king.
A regulation first set the municipality's place behind the canopy in the Corpus Christi procession.
By royal charter D. Manuel raised Funchal to city status, the first city in Portugal's overseas domains.
D. João Lobo, Bishop of Tangier, consecrated the chapel of Espírito Santo at the Lombada dos Esmeraldos, Ponta do Sol, the first consecrated church in Madeira.
The parish of Estreito de Câmara de Lobos was created, according to the annotator of the Saudades.
D. Manuel granted concessions by royal letter to Simão Gonçalves da Câmara.
The king ordered the people of Funchal to provide themselves with arms and horses.
A royal letter announced Fernão Rodrigues's mission to Madeira to combat the sugar-cane borer.
The chapel of Nossa Senhora do Loreto in Arco da Calheta was reportedly built.
Vasco Martins Moniz died at Torrão.
Madalena, Canhas and Tabua are supposed to have been separated from Ponta do Sol as parishes around this time.
João de França died and was buried in the church he had founded at Estreito da Calheta.
João Esmeraldo founded the Santo Espírito entail at the Lombada da Ponta do Sol.
Nuno Fernandes Cardoso and Leonor Dias founded by will the entail of São João de Latrão at Gaula.
António de Abreu went to India.
Foreigners were permitted to load Madeiran sugar for export.
King Manuel confirmed João Esmeraldo's noble privileges.
Rui Pires held the oldest recorded appointment as juiz de fora in Funchal.
Gaspar do Casal was born in Santarém.
João Esmeraldo founded the Lombada dos Esmeraldos entail.
Clearance of sugar exports was restricted to the Funchal customs house.
By his will João Afonso Escudeiro founded the Bemposta and São Lázaro entails; he died that year.
The transfer of the Funchal leper house to Santa Catarina was permitted.
Simão Gonçalves da Câmara was born in Funchal.
Arms were granted to the Espínola de Adorno branch.
Pedro da Luz was clerk of the Funchal Misericórdia.
A royal letter ordered protection for João de Carceres, builder of Funchal's first bastion and defensive walls.
João de Abreu arrived at the bar of Goa.
The Misericórdia of Funchal was founded and King Manuel gave the hospital and the chapel of the Holy Kings to it.
João Gonçalves da Câmara returned to Africa with several hundred men to fight the Moors.

Pope Leo X's bull Pro excellenti praeeminentia created the diocese of Funchal, ending the Order of Christ's spiritual supremacy; the church became a cathedral, D. Diogo Pinheiro was named first bishop and Frei Nuno Cão first dean.
Simão Acciaiuoli, the first of the family known in Madeira, came to the island.
Lopo Dias de Lira Varela became moço fidalgo of the royal household.
The 1490 ban was revoked for Canarians working in Madeira as sugar masters.
Lopo Franco became the first judge of the Santa Cruz council.
Bombardiers in Madeira were granted privileges.
The Funchal Câmara ordered all lepers confined at São Lázaro.
The Regimento das Madeiras, Madeira's first forest code, was issued, ordering pine and chestnut planting and banning felling without council licence.
D. Manuel issued a charter at Almeirim forbidding changes to the Santa Luzia levada in Funchal, which already existed.
D. Manuel assigned the wine tax to finish the Misericórdia hospital in Funchal.
King Manuel raised Santa Cruz to a town and municipality, created from Machico territory (dated 20 or 26 June 1515).
The royal letter creating Santa Cruz was presented at Machico, where some councillors objected.
King Manuel granted a common foral to Funchal, Ponta do Sol and Calheta, fixing tithes, the fifth of sugars, alcaidaria revenues, soap prices and other dues.
António de Abreu sailed from Malacca with three ships to explore the Moluccas.
Machico and Santa Cruz jointly received a foral with privileges, providing for a customs house.
António de Teive was born at Ribeira Brava.
Bishop D. Duarte, visiting Madeira to perform episcopal functions, consecrated Funchal Cathedral on St Luke's day.
The parish of São Jorge, including the Arco, was created, probably with a chaplain appointed.
Father Luís Gonçalves da Câmara was born in Madeira.
Urbano Lomelino died, entailing his estate to complete and maintain the Santa Cruz convent of Nossa Senhora da Piedade.
D. Manuel gave the processional cross to Funchal Cathedral.
The Misericórdia's hospital building in Santa Cruz was erected.
António da Gama was born in Funchal.
Pedro Álvares de Almada erected the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Graça in Santa Cruz.
The will of João Rodrigues de Freitas's son claimed the founding of the Madalena chapel.
João Esmeraldo was granted arms and made a nobleman of the royal household.
Plague afflicted Funchal from before 1521, with the sick isolated outside the city, until it ceased in 1538.

mentions.as_written: 1521, aos dezassete dias do mes de Março

summary: King Manuel I died.
João Rodrigues de Noronha was captain of Ormuz under governor Duarte de Menezes.
Amid plague and famine, Funchal council chose St James the Less as the city's patron by lot.

mentions.as_written: onze dias do mês de Junho do ano de quinhentos e vinte e um

summary: Construction of the chapel of St James in Funchal began with a solemn procession.

mentions.as_written: aos vinte e um de Julho

summary: Gaspar Frutuoso, the chronicler, was born in Ponta Delgada.
João Esmeraldo divided his Santo Espírito entail into the entails of Santo Espírito and Vale da Bica.
A royal charter allowed the wife and daughters-in-law of the Porto Santo donatary Bartolomeu Perestrelo to be styled 'dom'.
King João III confirmed the division of the Esmeraldo entails.
Funchal resolved to paint St James the Less on the city's banner and seal.
João Rodrigues de Freitas died at Madalena and was buried in the church founded by Henrique Alemão.
Pedro Álvares was juiz of the Funchal municipal council.
Amid plague and famine, the captain, council and cathedral chapter of Funchal made a solemn perpetual vow to St James, with a feast on 1 May.

mentions.as_written: Sábado vinte e quatro dias do mês de Janeiro

summary: The first stone of the São Tiago church in Funchal was laid in a solemn procession.
João Mendes de Brito and Isabel Fernandes Tavares founded the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Apresentação at Ribeira Brava as seat of an entail.
António Espínola donated land at the edge of Funchal on which the chapel of São Tiago was built.
A royal grant of arms was issued to Pedro Berenguer or a successor.
A document attesting the Drumond family's Scottish origin was issued in Scotland.
The first book of resolutions of the Funchal cathedral chapter begins.
The Saint Anthony chapel of Santana was first built.
Gil de Carvalho built a small hermitage, probably dedicated to Saint Anthony, at Alcoforado.
Jean Gossart painted «Nossa Senhora do Amparo», now in the Sacred Art Museum.
Probable birth year of Padre Manuel Álvares.
António de Abreu returned to India as appointed captain-major of Malacca.
Bishop D. Diogo Pinheiro died at Tomar after governing the diocese of Funchal for 12 years.
The cathedral dean's salary was raised to 25,000 réis a year.
João Fernandes de Andrade (do Arco) died and was buried in his chapel at Arco da Calheta.
Simão Gonçalves da Câmara renounced the captaincy of Funchal and his son João Gonçalves da Câmara took over its administration.
King João III confirmed the Andrade arms to Fernão Dias de Andrade.
Porto Santo had some 820 inhabitants, the earliest recorded population figure for the island.
Simão Acciaioly received a grant of arms and confirmation of nobility.
Bartolomeu Perestrelo (III) succeeded as donatary of Porto Santo.
A royal charter fixed the annual stipend of the Porto Santo parish priest.
Francisco Homem de Gouveia and his wife Isabel Afonso founded the Reis Magos entail at Estreito da Calheta, with the chapel of the Reis Magos at Lombo dos Reis as its seat.
Simão Gonçalves da Câmara, captain of Funchal, died nearly destitute at Matosinhos, and his son João Gonçalves da Câmara assumed personal government of the captaincy.
Date of a map showing a 'Great Java' that Major linked to António de Abreu's voyages.
João Rodrigues Neto Calassa died in the Rua dos Netos, Funchal.
Padre João Soares became chaplain of the Faial hermitage.
Pedro Frazão was living in Madeira.
An anadel-mór of musketeers was appointed for Madeira.
Fernão Nunes and Filipa Nunes posed as prophets on Porto Santo, gaining wide credence and inciting disorders; the corregedor's inquiry ended on 10 March 1533.
Simão Gonçalves da Câmara led a Madeiran expedition that relieved Santa Cruz do Cabo de Gué from a Moorish siege.
The parish church of Santa Cruz was built under João de Freitas, granted its chancel on 29 September.
Funchal was raised by papal bull to an archdiocese with suffragans Angra, Cape Verde, São Tomé and Goa, its cathedral becoming an archiepiscopal see.
D. Martinho de Portugal was appointed Archbishop of Funchal, the only holder of that title, governing until 1547.
Death of Francisco Moniz, founder of the Porto do Moniz settlement.
A fine of 20 cruzados was set for soliciting votes or bribing electors.
D. Sebastião de Morais was born in Funchal.
The Misericórdia of Calheta was founded by royal charter, its founder being Pedro Giraldes.
Pedro Pacheco justified his nobility.
António Teixeira founded the Penha de Águia entail.
João Bettencourt de Vasconcelos was born.
Arms were granted to the Espínola de la Rosa branch.
António de Leme built the chapel of São Filipe at the Quinta do Leme, dated 1535 by Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo and 1536 elsewhere.
The fourth donatary of Funchal died aged 47, apparently of the plague then raging in Madeira.
Leonor Ribeiro died.
Two half-prebend canonries were added to the Funchal cathedral chapter.
Ameixoeira, near Lisbon, then called Funchal, became a parish independent of Lumiar.
The Fleming João Esmeraldo died and was buried in his church at the Lombada.
António da Gama went to study law at Coimbra.
Jordão de Freitas received Amboina from the king of Ternate.
The parish of Santa Maria Maior in Funchal was created by division, with António Mourão as first vicar.
A royal alvará granted the blind Baltazar Dias a privilege to print and sell his works (dated '29 February', an impossible date in 1537).
After a lawsuit lasting until 1536, King João III removed Diogo Teixeira from the captaincy of Machico.
Bishop Ambrósio Brandão came to Madeira and exercised episcopal functions on behalf of Archbishop D. Martinho de Portugal, conferring minor orders among others on Manuel Alvares.
A provision required the council clerk to be a nobleman entitled to ride a saddled mule.
Frei António Pires Cabral signed as vicar of the churches of Caniço.
Chapel chaplains at Madalena do Mar were allowed to administer sacraments.
King João III granted a coat of arms to Amador de Almeida.
Fr. Hercules da Cunha was already vicar of Santa Cruz.
A strong earthquake struck Funchal and a severe plague followed until May, ending, according to Frutuoso, after a procession to St James's chapel; the vow is commemorated by the 1 May procession.
Father Sebastião Vaz is recorded as vicar of Estreito de Câmara de Lobos.
Permission was granted to build a baptismal font at Madalena do Mar.
A papal bull transferred Funchal's four suffragan sees to Lisbon, ending the archbishopric of Funchal.
Gonçalo Fernandes died and was buried in his chapel at Arco da Calheta (one entry gives 15 June 1539).
The Society of Jesus was founded.
Diogo Teixeira, deposed captain of Machico, died in Funchal without legitimate heir, and the captaincy reverted to the Crown.
D. Diogo de Teive was baptised at Ribeira Brava.
Fernão Tavares de Vasconcelos settled in Santa Cruz.
A collegiate church with four beneficiaries was established at Ribeira Brava.
King João III granted the captaincy of Machico to António da Silveira (one entry gives 1542).
João Gonçalves da Câmara, later donatary of Funchal, was born in Lisbon.
Francisco de Couto Cardoso, founder of an entailed estate in Paul do Mar, died.
A royal alvará ordered the works on the São Lourenço bastion in Funchal to continue.
António da Gama took his bachelor's degree.
João III confirmed Jordão de Freitas's lordship of Amboina granted by the king of Ternate.
Frei Afonso da Ilha published Tesouro da Virtude.
Tristão Gomes de Castro was born in Madeira.
Jerónimo Barreto, later bishop of Funchal, was born in the archdiocese of Braga.
New Christians presented judicial evidence of false accusations in Rome.
Simão Acciaioly, founder of the entail on whose lands the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Natividade was built, died.
Luís de Figueiredo de Lemos, later bishop of Funchal, was born on Santa Maria in the Azores.
The Order of Christ's grain commandery of Porto Santo was valued at 64,000 réis.
Diogo Soares Perestrelo inherited the captaincy of Porto Santo.
Fernão Favela died, according to Henriques de Noronha (Rodrigues de Azevedo gives 1537).
António Favila died and was buried in the Chapel of Nossa Senhora da Ajuda.
Luís Doria Velosa, builder of the Piornais levada, died.
Fr. António da Visitação was born in Madeira.
Dr. António da Gama competed for a chair at Coimbra University.
Padre Luís Gonçalves da Câmara made his profession in the Society of Jesus at Coimbra.
Padre Manuel Alvares entered the Society of Jesus.
Padre Luís Gonçalves da Câmara was appointed rector of the College of Coimbra.
The Inquisition was definitively established in Portugal.
D. Manuel de Noronha was appointed bishop of Lamego.
D. Martinho de Portugal, Archbishop of Funchal, died in Lisbon.
Jorge Lomelino died and was buried in the church of the Convento de Nossa Senhora da Piedade at Santa Cruz.
António da Silveira sold the captaincy of Machico, with royal authorisation, to D. Afonso de Portugal, Count of Vimioso.
The office of factor was created at the Santa Cruz customs house, with Domingos Fernandes appointed.
A royal decree added a moio of wheat to the stipend of the vicar of Ribeira Brava.
António Galvão wrote his treatise on ancient and modern discoveries, including the discovery of Madeira.
The office of doorkeeper already existed at the Santa Cruz customs house.
D. Sebastião de Morais entered the Society of Jesus.
The posts of almoxarife and alcaide de mar were created at the Machico customs house.
A royal charter increased the salary of the treasurer of Caniço church.
A royal charter created the parish of Faial.
The ordenanças militia were established in Madeira.
Fr. João Pinto da Vitória was born in Madeira.
Most of Madeira's collegiate chapters were created.
The archdiocese of Funchal was abolished by the bull Super universis.
The office of clerk already existed at the Santa Cruz customs house.
The king granted a son of João Rodrigues Cavaleiro the office of notary of the Holy Office.
D. Fr. Gaspar do Casal was appointed third bishop of Funchal.
Cardinal Infante D. Henrique issued the first index of condemned autos.
Irvão (Hirão) Teixeira died and was buried in Machico.
Cristóvão Pires, having built and endowed the original chapel of São Roque at Faial, asked the chapter of Funchal Cathedral for licence to hold services there.
Confession rolls recorded 2,700 slaves in Funchal, rising to 3,000 after four ships brought 300 more.
Possession of the see of Funchal was taken for Bishop Gaspar do Casal by proxy through Dr. António da Costa.
The English traveller Nichols recorded banana cultivation in Madeira.
Thomas Nichols lived in the Canary Islands.
A royal charter increased the curate's stipend at Ponta Delgada, the oldest record of the parish name.
Pedro Nunes Cardoso died in Gaula.
A royal charter raised the São Jorge parish priest's stipend and created a curacy at Santana served jointly with São Jorge.
D. Inês Moniz was born.
A royal charter increased the stipend of the Fajã da Ovelha curate, the oldest known document naming the parish.
A royal charter erected Seixal into a parish.
The post of organist at Funchal Cathedral already existed.
Duarte Mendes de Vasconcelos built the Chapel of the Magi at Quinta dos Reis, Monte.
Bishop D. Sancho Truxillo, visiting Madeira, consecrated the rebuilt church of the São Francisco convent in Funchal (one entry dates his visit to 1548).
Isabel Afonso died.
The Order of Christ's commandery of the Machico and Porto Santo fish tithes was valued at 35,000 réis.
Festivities with the game of canes marked António Gonçalves da Câmara's return to Madeira.
Simão Gonçalves da Câmara left for the kingdom, leaving his uncle Francisco Gonçalves da Câmara as interim captain-donatary of Funchal.
João Gavião died in Caniço.
French privateers raided Porto Santo and sacked its parish church.
Pope Paul IV confirmed Jorge de Lemos as bishop of Funchal.
A royal charter appointed Gaspar Calaça almoxarife of the Porto Santo customs post.
A royal decree fixed the stipend of the vicar of Ribeira Brava in money, silver, wheat and wine.
A royal charter increased the stipend of the vicar of Campanário, showing the parish already existed.
Cristóvão de Leme died in prison in Lisbon, shortly after his father Pedro.
A levy of 7,000 cruzados was imposed to pay for the fortifications of Funchal.
The oldest parish registers of Santo António date from this year, taken as the creation of an autonomous curacy.
António Alves Uzadamar became the first judge of the Machico customs house.
The post of preacher was created in Santa Cruz parish.
A royal charter divided Funchal's single parish into the Sé and Santa Maria Maior (Calhau) parishes and created a collegiate body for the church.
D. Fr. Jorge de Lemos governed the diocese of Funchal as its first resident bishop, reorganising the cathedral chapel music.
Gaula was separated from Santa Cruz and made a parish.
A royal charter raised the stipend of the vicar of Caniço to 8$300 réis a year.
A charter set the annual stipend of the vicar of Santa Maria Maior.
Jorge Pinto founded the entail of Ilha at São Jorge.
A royal charter further increased the pay of the priest of Fajã da Ovelha.
A royal charter fixed the stipend of the parish priest of Ponta do Sol.
Mendo d'Ornelas e Vasconcelos married Helena Gomes at Machico.
Rui de Sousa rebuilt the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Estrela.
Queen Catarina granted arms to the Spaniard Diogo Martins.
The stipend of the vicar of Machico was fixed at 12,300 réis plus wheat and wine.
A royal charter increased the stipend of the priest of Ponta do Pargo, showing the parish existed by then.
An order was given to build the enclosure behind the Blessed Sacrament chapel of Funchal Cathedral.
Canon Manuel Ferreira Teixeira gave the Selvagens islands to his niece Filipa Cabral de Vasconcelos.
The parish of Água de Pena began to function under Padre Tomé Gomes.
Saint-Sulpice arrived in Lisbon as French ambassador.
The parish of Caniçal was created, the oldest of Madeira's small parishes.
Filipe Gentil de Limoges founded the chapel of São Filipe in Funchal and instituted his entail.
A royal charter raised the priest's stipend at Estreito da Calheta, proving the parish already existed.
King Sebastião created by charter the post of jailer of the Funchal Aljube.
A royal charter created two curacies at the Sé, relieving the dean of parish duties.

Queen-regent Catarina promulgated the Regimento das Madeiras, Madeira's forest code, requiring licences for felling, ordering chestnut and pine planting and entrusting forest protection to local officials.
Queen Catarina ordered the Socorridos, Piornais and Castelejo levadas to be cleaned at the owners' expense.
An alvará of Queen-regent Catarina extended the cleaning duty to all levadas, placing them under the captain-donataries with priority for cane fields and mills.
Cardinal D. Henrique issued three charters on stream and levada cleaning and water pricing favouring sugar cane.
António Galvão's Tratado dos Descobrimentos first published the legend of Machim.
Bishop Jorge de Lemos left Madeira for Portugal, where he became chief almoner to King Sebastião.
The salary of the dean of Funchal chapter was raised to 45,000 réis a year.
The flag of the city of Funchal bore the image of St James the Apostle.
A royal charter further regulated irrigation water.
The office of judge of the Santa Cruz customs house was created and Tomé Alves appointed.
A royal charter further regulated irrigation water.
The stipend of the Sé curates was raised to 17,450 réis.
A royal decree fixed the stipend of the priest of Caniçal at 14,300 réis.
A royal warrant raised the salary of the clerk of the ecclesiastical chamber from three to eight thousand réis.
Santana received its own chaplain, Father Sebastião de Moraes.
A royal decree banned profane acts and masks in churches and processions.
A royal charter created the parish of Monte, making the chapel of Nossa Senhora do Monte a parish church.
Gonçalo Pires lived in Funchal as clerk of accounts.
A customs register records Madeira wine exports valued at 3,200 réis a pipe.
Santo António probably became a parish, separated from the Sé.
The post of chapel master of Funchal cathedral was officially created.
The Jesuits settled in the São Bartolomeu hospice in Funchal.
Manuel Vieira and Favila Vieira were living in Funchal.
Period covered by the 24 register volumes of the Provedoria index in the Torre do Tombo.
A charter of King Sebastião created the parish of São Pedro in Funchal, seated in the São Paulo chapel, ending Franciscan service there (20 July according to the Provedoria index).
A charter appointed Gonçalo Fernandes first constable of the fortress of São Lourenço.
A royal charter raised the stipend of the vicar of Ponta do Sol to 13$300 réis.
Montluc's fleet sailed from Bordeaux early in September.
King Sebastião created the Funchal Seminary by royal charter.
French pirates sacked Porto Santo, its earliest recorded raid, before attacking Funchal the next day.
French corsairs sacked Funchal and the nuns of Santa Clara fled to the Curral das Freiras.

French Huguenot corsairs under Montluc, guided by Gaspar Caldeira, landed at Praia Formosa and sacked Funchal, storming the fortress of São Lourenço, profaning the cathedral and the Santa Clara convent, whose nuns fled to the Curral; Gaspar de Braga died resisting them. The attack, during the captaincy of Francisco Gonçalves da Câmara, prompted new coastal fortifications.
The Portuguese ambassador in France protested to Charles IX over the sack of Funchal, demanding punishment.
Cardinal Henrique wrote to the French ambassador about the sack of Funchal.
The French ambassador Forquevaux wrote to his government from Madrid about the sack.
King Sebastião issued regulations for the coastal lookout posts (vigias) of the archipelago.
Pompeu Arditti wrote his account describing Madeira's dense forests.
João Enes Rocha was almoxarife in Funchal.
Fr. António da Visitação took the Carmelite habit.
The Calheta Misericórdia was empowered to collect its rents and debts by enforcement, like the royal treasury.
A royal charter of King Sebastião ruled that no one was exempt from lookout service.
D. Pantaleão de Teive died in Madrid.
King Sebastião founded the Jesuit college of Funchal by royal charter.
D. Manuel de Noronha died and was buried in the chapel of São Nicolau at Lamego.
Nominated by King Sebastião, Fernando de Távora was appointed bishop of Funchal by the pope, who accepted the resignation of Jorge de Lemos.
Pedro Gonçalves de Arvelos served as judge in Santa Cruz.
Francisco de Sousa wrote his Tratado das Ilhas Novas.
Period for which the names of twelve parish priests of Câmara de Lobos are known.
The Jesuits were established in Madeira from 1570 until their expulsion in 1760.
The founding Jesuit community left Lisbon for Madeira.
The founding Jesuit community arrived in Madeira and lodged at the São Bartolomeu church and hospice.
Solemn opening of the Jesuit classes in Funchal.
The fleet carrying Inácio de Azevedo and forty Jesuits anchored at Funchal, stayed there, and left for Brazil on 30 June.
Huguenot corsairs attacked the fleet off La Palma in the Canaries and killed the forty Jesuits, led by Inácio de Azevedo, who had passed through Madeira.
A stone commemorates the martyrdom of Inácio de Azevedo and 39 Jesuits off La Palma, which it dates to 15 July 1579 (the martyrdom occurred in 1570).
Pope Pius V confirmed Fernando de Távora as fifth bishop of Funchal.
A regulation organised the ordenanças into companies and capitanias-mores.
D. Sebastiana de Albuquerque married Jacinto de Freitas, establishing the Albuquerque name in Madeira.
Gaspar de Teive contracted a silk manufacturer to produce silk in Madeira.
Jerónimo Dias Leite took possession of a half-prebend canonry at Funchal Cathedral.
Padre Nuno Vaz, the first known vicar of Porto Santo, apparently began serving the parish.
Funchal's defence plan was revised to a three-bastion fortress and city walls with five gates.
António Correia died, according to several genealogists.
The stipend of the priest of Água de Pena was raised to 9$000 réis.
Os Lusíadas, containing Camões's reference to Madeira, was published.
D. Jerónimo Barreto was appointed bishop of Madeira.
A charter increased the stipend of Gonçalo de Aguiar, parish priest of Estreito de Câmara de Lobos.
A royal charter raised vicars' stipends in Ponta do Sol and Ribeira Brava.
King Sebastião's charter raised the Gaula priest's stipend to 20$000 réis.
A royal charter authorised the curacy that created the parish of Arco da Calheta.
A charter increased the pay of beneficiaries of the Machico and Santa Cruz collegiate churches.
The vicar's stipend of São Pedro was raised to 25,000 réis.
A royal charter increased the stipend of Belchior Mourato, vicar of Caniço.
A royal decree set the São Jorge priest's salary at 25,000 réis, when the parish had 106 households.
Fernando de Távora resigned the see of Funchal and became royal almoner.
Bishop Jerónimo Barreto received episcopal consecration.
The stipend of the vicar of the newly independent parish of Fajã da Ovelha was fixed at 20,000 réis.
D. Aleixo de Teive was found dead with 24 wounds.
The Funchal seminary actually began operating at some point in this period.
D. Jerónimo Barreto was Bishop of Funchal and had lodgings on Rua Direita.
Giulio Landi's description of Madeira was published in Latin and Italian at Piacenza.
Simão Gonçalves da Câmara accompanied King Sebastião on his first African expedition.
D. Sebastião confirmed Gonçalo de Freitas da Silva's Asian lordships.
Oldest cited royal letter concerning the parish of Porto do Moniz.
A royal letter names the Porto do Moniz parish Nossa Senhora da Conceição da Ponta do Tristão.
King Sebastião raised the Santo António priest's stipend as the parish reached 120 households.
Bishop Jerónimo Barreto arrived in Funchal to govern the diocese.
A pay increase granted to Funchal's sargento-mor shows the ordenanças existed.
Padre Luís Gonçalves da Câmara died in Lisbon aged 57.
Pedro Gonçalves da Câmara sold Zarco's house to Francisco Gonçalves da Câmara.
A royal charter fixed the São Vicente parish priest's stipend at 25$000 réis.
The Seixal priest's stipend was raised to 20$000 réis a year.
Pedro Berenguer de Lemilhana came to Madeira in the last quarter of the sixteenth century.
A 100,000-cruzado levy was imposed for Funchal's fortifications.
Diogo Soares Perestrelo succeeded as donatary of Porto Santo.
King Sebastião confirmed the donataries' revenues, including rights over water and wind.
A royal charter of King Sebastião created Simão Gonçalves da Câmara, fifth captain-donatary of Funchal, Count of Calheta, the first known noble title in Madeira.
King Sebastião authorised Bishop Jerónimo Barreto to create a curacy in the Câmara de Lobos parish church.
A royal charter created a curacy in Machico.
A document recorded the chapel of the Reis Magos at Ponta Delgada as already in poor repair.
Bishop Jerónimo Barreto abolished the curacy of Vera Cruz.
Two further half-prebend canonries were added to the cathedral chapter of Funchal.
The Alecrins entail was instituted.
Earliest record of the Senhor Jesus pilgrimage at Ponta Delgada.
Death of D. Fernando de Távora, who was buried in the convent of São Domingos, Lisbon.
By alvará the curacy of Câmara de Lobos was made removable.
Ponta Delgada became a full parish with a vicar's stipend.

Royal charters of 1 March 1577 raised the stipends of the priests of several Madeiran parishes, including Tábua, Monte (then 58 households), Ponta do Pargo (20$000 réis) and Porto do Moniz, the last being the first document to use that name.
The number of beneficiaries of the Ribeira Brava church was reduced to three.
A royal charter empowered Bishop Jerónimo Barreto to erect the parish of Porto da Cruz.
The parish of Canhas was created and installed in the chapel of São Tiago.
Period covered by the list of Madeiran and Azorean students at the University of Coimbra.
The Franciscan convent of Funchal underwent major repairs and enlargements under its guardian Fr. Diogo Nabo.
The sugar masters and residents of Ponta do Sol were obliged to join the Corpus Christi procession with torches and canes.
The chapel of São Cristóvão at Ponta Delgada was recorded in poor repair.
D. Sebastião de Morais's life of Princess Maria of Portugal was published in Bologna.
D. Gaspar de Teive was killed at the battle of Alcácer Quibir.

Madeira's first diocesan synod, held in Funchal Cathedral under Bishop Jerónimo Barreto, drew up and promulgated the Diocesan Constitutions, which among other things forbade plays in churches without the bishop's licence.
The Cardinal-King D. Henrique made judicial offices royal appointments, curtailing the powers of the donataries.
The chapel of São Roque served as the parish church of São Roque.
King D. Henrique reduced the notaries and judicial clerks of Funchal from 35 to 17.
Jerónimo Dias Leite wrote his manuscript on the discovery of Madeira.
Bishop Luís Figueiredo de Lemos promulgated the Constituições Extravagantes.
A royal charter of the Cardinal-King abolished the Funchal parish of São Pedro and authorised Bishop Jerónimo Barreto to create the parishes of São Roque and São Martinho.
Bishop Jerónimo Barreto approved the diocesan constitutions by alvará and ordered their enforcement, including rules regulating teaching.
A royal charter on irrigation water in Madeira was issued.
Bernardo Tavares de Sousa settled in Madeira after 1580.
With the start of Philippine rule the captain-donataries ceased residing in Madeira and were succeeded by governors-general.
A bronze standard weight bearing Funchal's original arms was made.
João Bettencourt de Vasconcelos sailed to India as captain of the nau São Gregório.
The Duke of Alba's army, including António Herédia, entered Portugal.
Guiomar Lomelino donated land for the new parish church of Porto da Cruz.
The fort of São Filipe in Funchal was apparently built during Philippine rule.
The fifth captain-donatary of Funchal, Simão Gonçalves da Câmara, died in Funchal after a stroke suffered in 1578.
João Gonçalves da Câmara, sixth and last effective captain-donatary of Funchal, died at Almeirim.
Philip II was proclaimed king of Portugal, the proclamation being made in Funchal.
A royal charter set the annual stipend of the vicar of Santa Cruz.
Luís Fernandes de Matos Coutinho settled in Madeira and set up a trading house in Funchal.
João Cahus of Rouen settled in Funchal as a merchant.
Francisca Frazão married Diogo de Ornelas e Vasconcelos.
The combined customs revenue of Madeira and Porto Santo was recorded for the seven years 1581 to 1587.

Under Philippine (Spanish) rule Madeira was governed by governors-general, beginning with João Leitão, who took over the administration of the whole archipelago; the captains-donatary were reduced to honorary status.
Bishop Jerónimo Barreto published the diocesan Constitutions.
Belchior de Teive was already a law professor at Salamanca.
The stipend of the vicar of Ponta Delgada was raised to 25$000 réis.
A royal charter raised the stipends of the vicars of several parishes, including Monte, Ponta do Pargo, Campanário and Seixal, to 25$000 réis a year.
A charter raised the stipend of the parish priest of São Martinho.
Fearing a landing by the French fleet of D. António, Prior of Crato, António do Carvalhal brought 300 men to Funchal.
João Bettencourt de Vasconcelos was beheaded on Terceira for supporting Philip II.
Tristão Vaz da Veiga, governor-general of the archipelago, kept twelve Indian slaves.
Fr. João do Espírito Santo was hanged in Funchal for supporting the cause of the Prior of Crato.
Zenobio Acciaioli founded the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Natividade at Faial.
A provision of Philip II appointed João Leitão treasury provedor and dispatched him to Madeira.
Madalena do Mar was made an independent parish by Bishop Jerónimo Barreto.
Philip II granted the captaincy of Machico to Tristão Vaz da Veiga.
At the naval battle off Vila Franca do Campo, D. Francisco de Portugal, Count of Vimioso, died fighting for the Prior of Crato.
Agostinho Herrera was sent to Madeira as general of arms and governor-general to prepare its defences against the French fleet of the Prior of Crato.
Administration of foundlings was entrusted to the bishop.
Padre Manuel Álvares died at the College of Évora.
Agostinho Herrera left Madeira and João Leitão resumed full civil and military jurisdiction.
D. Fr. Gaspar do Casal died in Coimbra.
Pedro Gonçalves de Azevedo proved his nobility.
Manuel Tomás was born in Guimarães.
D. Luís Figueiredo de Lemos was presented as bishop of Funchal in 1585 and, after papal confirmation, arrived in Madeira on 4 August 1586.
The Constituições Synodaes do Bispado do Funchal of Bishop Jerónimo Barreto's 1578 synod were printed in Lisbon, and Barreto was transferred to Silves.
A provision still styled Simão Gonçalves da Câmara captain-donatary of Funchal.
João Leitão's government ended and Tristão Vaz da Veiga was appointed governor-general of Madeira on 19 October 1585, taking office on 22 November.
Manuel Dias de Andrade was born around this year.
D. Luís Figueiredo de Lemos governed the diocese and built the first episcopal palace in Funchal.
The annotator of the Saudades gives this year for the creation of the parish of Tábua.
Two ships seized by a corsair in Funchal bay were recovered.
A diocesan synod under Bishop Luís Figueiredo de Lemos promulgated new diocesan constitutions.
Bishop Luís Figueiredo de Lemos found the chapel at Achadas da Cruz in poor condition.
Pope Sixtus V confirmed D. Sebastião de Morais as bishop of Funai, the first diocese in Japan.
A royal charter on irrigation water was issued.
The parish of São Pedro in Funchal was restored by Filipe I.
A royal charter fixed the stipend of the priest of Madalena do Mar at 20,000 réis.
An English ship raiding shipping off Funchal was sunk.
D. Sebastião de Morais died in Mozambique while travelling to his diocese.
A royal charter named the priest of Santana vicar, marking roughly when it became an independent parish.
The vicar's stipend at Ponta Delgada was fixed at 16$000 réis plus wheat and wine.
A royal charter raised the stipend of the priest of Tábua.
The parish of São Pedro in Funchal was restored.
Death of D. Inês Moniz.
D. Jerónimo Barreto died in Silves aged 45.
A royal charter raised the São Roque priest's stipend to 19,000 réis, half a moio of wheat and a quarter of wine.
A royal charter increased the stipend of the vicar of Campanário.
A further charter added money, wheat and wine to parish priests' stipends, including São Roque and São Martinho.
Padre Leão Henriques died in Lisbon.
A royal charter increased the priests' stipends at São Jorge and São Vicente with wheat and wine.
A collegiate with two beneficiaries was created in the parish of São Pedro.
A royal charter created the curacy of Ponta do Sol.
Royal charters created curacies in several parishes, including Porto Santo (20,000 réis a year), Calheta, Santa Cruz, Santa Maria Maior and São Pedro.
The Seixal priest's stipend was increased by half a moio of wheat and a quarter of wine.
Gaspar Frutuoso wrote the Saudades da Terra in São Miguel, a key source for Madeira's history; the same year Jerónimo Dias Leite was named full-prebend canon.
Gaspar Frutuoso described Rua Direita as the largest street in Funchal, and described the parish of Tábua.
Gaspar Frutuoso described Santana as rich farmland.
Frutuoso recorded the reduced number of notaries then serving in Funchal.
Gaspar Frutuoso described the south-west coast localities, including Paul do Mar.
Gaspar Frutuoso recorded household counts for parishes such as Caniço (200), Faial (about 100) and Porto do Moniz (thirty).
Gaspar Frutuoso wrote that the parish of Porto Santo was dedicated to the Salvador.
According to Frutuoso, Porto Santo had about 400 households, some 1,600 inhabitants.
Gaspar Frutuoso already called the springs by the name of João Diniz.
Gaspar Frutuoso described the Pico do Castelo on Porto Santo as naturally defensible.
Gaspar Frutuoso recorded that the landing place at Machico was called the Desembarcadouro, and recorded the name Ponta Delgada.
Antonia Jaime Cuibém and her husband Roberto Vizovi came to Madeira.
Gaspar Frutuoso described Malvasia as the best wine in the world, exported to India.
The captaincy of Machico yielded about 900,000 réis a year to its donatary, per Frutuoso.
Gaspar Frutuoso described Seixal as a parish of about twenty households with a church of São Brás.
An eight-volume register of chapels was begun by the Juiz dos Resíduos e Capelas.
A charter raised the stipends of the vicar and beneficiaries of Santa Cruz.
A post of preacher was created in Machico church.
António Pereira de Barredo was appointed governor-general of Madeira.
Madeira declined as its sugar and timber trades were overtaken by America and Africa.
Simão Darja owned a sugar-cane mill in Funchal.
The English colony began to gain importance in Madeira.
Funchal extended as far as the Cabo do Calhau.
Porto Santo's decline became marked.
Madeira's Malvasia wine began to gain great renown.
Aires de Ornelas de Vasconcelos founded the morgado and chapel of Nossa Senhora da Consolação at the Quinta, Caniço.
The Monte priest's stipend was fixed at 16,000 réis, a moio of wheat and a pipe of wine.
A royal alvará reset parish stipends: the Ribeira Brava vicar's at 27,000 réis plus wheat and wine, and the Câmara de Lobos priest's money stipend at 11$000 réis.
António Pereira de Barredo took office as governor-general of Madeira.
Gaspar Frutuoso, author of the Saudades da Terra, died at Ribeira Grande aged 69.
A royal charter raised or fixed the stipends of the priests of Tábua and Porto da Cruz in money, wine and wheat.
Philip II created the Conselho de Fazenda.
The bishop D. Luís de Figueiredo transferred the inhabitants of Achadas da Cruz to the parish of Porto Moniz.
A royal charter raised the Água de Pena priest's stipend to 19$000 réis plus grain and wine.
A charter fixed the Gaula priest's stipend at 16$000 réis plus a pipe of wine and a moio and a half of wheat.
The earliest known record of the Madalena chapel dates from this year, when a quit-rent was donated to it.
After a violent, extremely hot east wind blew over Madeira on 24 and 25 July, the 'Fogo do Céu' fire of 26 July 1593 destroyed about 150 houses, sugar stores and crops in the city.
Francisco de Betencourt built the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Vitória in São Martinho.
The São Sebastião chapel at Caniçal was enlarged or rebuilt.
Diogo de Azambuja de Melo was appointed governor-general of Madeira.
The curacy of Ribeira Brava parish was created.
A post of organist was created in Machico church.
English ships under Captain Amias Preston attacked and burned Porto Santo.
Diogo de Azambuja de Melo took office as governor-general of Madeira, bringing António Pereira de Barredo's governorship to an end.
A royal warrant appointed a fortificador (named Francisco Jorge or Jerónimo Jorge in different entries) to direct the fortification works of Madeira.
Dr António da Gama died in Lisbon.
Manuel Soares founded the chapel of Senhora da Boa Morte in São Pedro church.
João Fernandes Vieira was probably baptised in Faial parish.
The offices of provedor and corregedor in Madeira were united.
A municipal book recorded four seaward gates in Funchal.
Bishop Luís Figueiredo de Lemos held a diocesan synod in Funchal Cathedral producing the Constituições Extravagantes, which received episcopal approval on 15 August 1597.
Funchal council obtained a charter barring ships from loading foreign sugar in Madeira.
António do Carvalhal died in Ponta Delgada parish.
A royal charter raised the stipend of the vicar of Ponta do Sol to 29$000 réis.
Henrique de Bettencourt founded the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Glória.
Padre Manuel Constantino's Insulae Materiae, a Latin history of Madeira's discovery, was published in Rome.
A further 3,000 réis was added to the stipend of the vicar of Ribeira Brava.
Serious disturbances in Funchal prompted a punitive commission sent from Lisbon.
The Spanish garrison in Madeira mutinied over arrears of pay.
A document records the three-day route of the Litanies procession in Ponta do Sol.
The mill tithes commandery of Madeira and the Azores was valued at 140,000 réis.
The office of alcaide do mar already existed at the Santa Cruz customs house.
The first recorded lease of seafront land in Funchal for building a capstan was made.
Governor-general Diogo de Azambuja de Melo died in Funchal.
Padre Manuel de Lira died in Calheta.
Friar Damião das Chagas died in mainland Portugal.
Canon Jorge Furtado de Sousa founded the chapel of Nossa Senhora do Desterro.
The stipend of the Sé parish curates was raised to 20,000 réis.
Cristóvão Falcão e Sousa was appointed governor-general of the Madeira archipelago.
Manuel João Ferreira built the chapel of Nossa Senhora do Bom Sucesso at Garachico, Estreito de Câmara de Lobos.
A slow landslide pushed land into the sea in São Jorge parish.
The feast of the Menino Jesus Perdido was established at the Santa Clara convent.
Sebastião de Oliveira is said to have founded the Livramento chapel in Caniço.
The fortress of Nossa Senhora da Conceição do Ilhéu was built.
Francisco Rodrigues Jardim was hanged in effigy at the Funchal pillory for abducting D. Maria de Ornelas.
According to tradition the Forte de Loures was built by a private individual.
Inácio da Câmara Leme rebuilt the house and chapel of the Quinta do Leme.
The chapel of Santo Espírito at Lombada dos Esmeraldos, Ponta do Sol, was rebuilt on a larger scale.
The cut-leaved sweet potato was introduced to Madeira.
Brás Dias Aranha lived in Funchal.
Bartolomeu Telo Moniz de Meneses founded a chapel of Nossa Senhora da Conceição in Santa Cruz.
Bishop Luís de Figueiredo had the diocesan Constitutions reprinted in Lisbon by Pedro Craesbeeck together with the Constituições Extravagantes.
The chapel of Nossa Senhora dos Remédios was built in Quinta Grande.
Ambrósio Berenguer founded an entailed estate in Ponta do Sol parish.
The French traveller Moquet visited Madeira and recorded destructive floods.
António Favila died.
António Correia Herédia came to Madeira as captain of the Castilian garrison company.
Mateus Fernandes received a letter of appointment as fortificador.
Philip II created a curacy in the parish of Estreito da Calheta.
A curacy was created in the parish of Santo António.
Gaspar Berenguer de Andrade was born.
Disorders broke out in the Corpus Christi procession in Funchal when the vicar-general left his place to police it.
João Fogaça de Eça was appointed governor-general of Madeira.
A regulation fixed the powers of the alcaides-mores appointed by the Philippine government.
The captaincy of Machico was recovered by and passed to D. Luís de Portugal, Count of Vimioso.
Tristão Vaz da Veiga died in or shortly before 1604, aged about 67.
The curacy of Caniço was created.
The date 1606 was carved with the Ornelas arms on the gate of a surviving Gothic house in Funchal.
The curate's annual salary at Ribeira Brava was set at 20,000 réis.
A royal charter created the curacy of São Vicente.
Antónia Delgada died.
Fr. António da Visitação died.
The Ponta do Sol council reordered the route of the Litanies procession and excused the parishioners of Canhas and Madalena do Mar.
Francisco Dias built the Santana chapel in São Roque.
Belchior de Teive left teaching for royal service and was sent to Portugal as superintendent general of public finances.
The will of João Bettencourt de Vasconcelos, entailing his third to the Convent of São Bernardino, was approved.
The first consulate in Madeira, the Flemish one, was created.
Bishop D. Luís Figueiredo de Lemos died in Funchal and was buried in his São Luís chapel beside the Episcopal Palace.
A tower clock already existed at Machico parish church before 1609.
Francisco de Abreu founded the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Alegria in São Roque.
A final decree raised the Caniçal priest's stipend to 24,000 réis plus wheat and wine.
D. Lourenço de Távora was appointed bishop of Madeira.
D. Manuel Pereira Coutinho was appointed governor-general of Madeira.
João Gomes de Castro was administrator of the Prazeres chapel in Santa Maria Maior.
D. Lourenço de Távora received episcopal consecration.
D. Lourenço de Távora took charge of the diocese of Funchal.
Tristão Gomes de Castro founded the Prazeres chapel in Monte; he is also recorded as dying that year.
A great flood in Funchal largely destroyed the church of Nossa Senhora do Calhau (Santa Maria Maior) and its adjoining hospital.
The bishop requested restoration of the curacy of Achadas da Cruz for its 84 residents.
Desembargador Francisco Cardoso was sent to Funchal over hostility to Philippine rule.
Philip II granted the title of Count of Castelo-Melhor to Rui Mendes de Vasconcelos.
A royal charter set rules for corregedors conducting municipal elections and penalties for bribery.
The Madalena do Mar priest's stipend was increased by 3,000 réis.
Fr. João Pinto da Vitória's Vida del Fr. Juan Sanz was published in Valencia.
A stone dated 1612 commemorates foundlings murdered at the Achada.
Francisco Cardoso de Cernejo was commissioned as Inquisition visitor to Madeira.
A royal charter granted 70,000 réis for an altarpiece for the chapel at Santo António da Serra.
A provision regulated how the corregedor selected persons eligible for municipal office.
Philip II gave an organ to Funchal Cathedral.
Francisco da Madre de Deus professed in the Franciscan order.
Domingos Rodrigues Garcez founded the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Piedade in Funchal, at the Largo da Igrejinha.
Manuel de Vasconcelos sailed to India with his six sons.
Birth year of João Fernandes Vieira as given in the first edition.
The earliest recorded editions of several of Baltazar Dias's autos were printed.
Period covered by the loose manuscripts on Madeira and Porto Santo in the Arquivo da Marinha e Ultramar.
The Funchal council protested against Governor Manuel Pereira Coutinho's interference in the works on the stream walls.
The Fortress of São Tiago in Funchal was built under Philippine rule, its original portal bearing the date 1614.
Fr. Rafael de Jesus was born.
Francisco Morais de Aguiar founded the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Salvação at Moinhos, Caniço.
Jorge da Câmara was appointed governor-general of Madeira.
António Pimentel was appointed almoxarife of the Santa Cruz customs house.
A royal warrant named Bishop D. Lourenço de Távora interim governor and captain-general of Madeira.
Padre Manuel Constantino died in Rome.
Philip III commissioned Dr Gonçalo de Sousa to hold an alçada in Madeira to punish crimes.
Jorge da Câmara took office as governor-general of Madeira.
Manuel Afonso Cortez, founder of the Cortez family, died in Câmara de Lobos.
João Bettencourt de Vasconcelos died.
The statutes (compromisso) of the Calheta Misericórdia were dated.
Fr. João Pinto da Vitória's Gerarchia Carmelitana was published in Valencia.
António Veloso de Lira was born in Calheta.

North African corsairs sacked Porto Santo, killing or carrying off most of the population, burning the parish church and destroying the council and parish archives; the raid prompted fortification of Pico do Castelo.
Bartolomeu Arias was sent to fortify Madeira after corsair raids on coastal settlements.
Bishop D. Lourenço de Távora left Madeira on transfer to the see of Elvas, leaving the see of Funchal vacant.
Philip III funded the eastern walls of Funchal, completed in 1637.
Jordão de Freitas da Silva was living in Santa Cruz.
Padre Manuel de Almeida served as chapel master of Funchal cathedral.
Pedro da Silva was appointed governor-general of Madeira.
Pedro da Silva took office as governor-general of Madeira.
João Bartolomeu was appointed engineer director of the fortifications under construction in Madeira.
D. Jerónimo Fernando was nominated bishop of Funchal.
The date 1619 was inscribed over the door of the classroom courtyard of the Jesuit college of São João Evangelista.
Philip II wrote to João Fogaça summoning him to represent Madeira at the Cortes at Tomar.
A door of the customs house was moved, according to an inscription.
Luís Gonçalves Mercador built a chapel of Nossa Senhora da Penha de França at Monte.
The Conselho da Fazenda ordered the reconstruction of the parish church of Ponta do Pargo.
Bishop Jerónimo Fernando excommunicated treasury and customs officials; a royal order of 21 November lifted the excommunication.
D. Jerónimo Fernando took possession of the see of Funchal.
Fr. Gregório Batista published two Latin works cited in the Bibliotheca Lusitana.
The priest Jerónimo da Silva founded the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Paz.
Belchior de Teive was still a privy councillor of Philip II.
The Relação das Festas, containing a sermon by Padre Luís de Morais, was published.
António Dantas founded the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Penha de França in Funchal.
A religious play was staged in the church of São João Evangelista in Funchal for the canonisation of Francis Xavier.
Padre Luís de Morais died.
D. Francisco Henriques was appointed governor-general of Madeira.
D. Francisco Henriques took office as governor-general of Madeira on 28 October 1622 and began building the Castle of São João Baptista do Pico above Funchal, constructed between 1622 and 1640.
The ordenanças (militia) were restored after their abolition by Philip II.
Fr. Gregório Batista published his Completas da Vida de Cristo.
João Gonçalves da Câmara's possession of the captaincy of Funchal was confirmed.
The most advanced beatification process for Frei Pedro da Guarda was conducted.
Bishop Jerónimo Fernando governed Madeira, the period of events mentioned in the Arte de Furtar.
António de Carvalhal Esmeraldo owned the house held to be one of Zarco's dwellings.
João Fernandes Vieira left Madeira and changed his name.
Francisco de Sousa was appointed first master gunner of the Pico fortress.
Governor-general D. Francisco Henriques died in office in Madeira (another entry gives 23 July 1624).
Bishop D. Jerónimo Fernando was confirmed as governor-general of Madeira by royal letter.
D. Lourenço de Távora resigned the see of Elvas and retired to his convent in Lisbon.
Canon Jorge Furtado de Sousa founded the chapel of Nossa Senhora do Desterro at Monte.
Pirates, described as Algerian corsairs, raided Fajã dos Padres in Campanário and destroyed the Jesuit chapel there.
Fernão Saldanha was appointed Governor General of Madeira.
Fernão Saldanha took office as Governor General of Madeira.
The office of judge of orphans was created in Machico.
The present chapel of Santo Amaro was rebuilt.

mentions.as_written: segundo ou terceiro quartel do século XVII

summary: Canon Manuel Afonso founded a chapel of Jesus, Maria, José in the Sé parish.
A Portuguese fleet was lost on the French coast; Félix Ferreira helped save most of the men.
The French consulate in Madeira was created.
Unpaid soldiers rioted in Funchal and besieged the customs house.
A royal decree set the Calheta parish priest's stipend at 18,000 réis plus wheat and wine.
An alvará noted that tithes did not cover the stipends of the cathedral clergy.
Governor Fernão Saldanha died in Madeira and Bishop D. Jerónimo Fernando assumed the government.
Martim Vaz founded the Nazaré chapel at São Martinho.
D. Francisco de Sousa was appointed governor-general of Madeira.
Dr Estêvão Leitão (or Coelho) de Meireles was named judge of an alçada to punish crimes in Madeira and enforce earlier sentences.
The fort of São Filipe da Praça in Funchal was built by order of the bishop-governor D. Jerónimo Fernando.
D. Francisco de Sousa took office as governor-general of Madeira.
D. Lourenço de Távora died in Lisbon with a reputation for sanctity.
By tradition, the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Incarnação at Ribeira da Janela was founded by two residents.
The Dutch invaded Pernambuco while the Madeiran João Fernandes Vieira was a clerk there.
Work began on completing the chancel of Funchal Cathedral with its panelling and choir stalls.
Fr. João Pinto da Vitória died in Valencia.
