summary: The Provedor da Fazenda reported that the walls of Funchal's streams needed rebuilding.
Mateus de Abreu Pereira, later a bishop, was reportedly born in Madeira.
A great storm endangered ships and damaged the Funchal harbour works.
D. Maria do Rosário Henriques built the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Nazaré at Câmara de Lobos.
According to the Elucidário, Ricardo Smith founded an acclimatisation garden in Funchal.
Walls were built joining the inner Pontinha islet to the Funchal coast, the first stage of the Pontinha mole.
D. Gaspar Afonso da Costa Brandão governed the diocese of Funchal as its 17th bishop.
Governor Manuel Saldanha da Gama Albuquerque was recalled to Lisbon and replaced by Bishop Gaspar Afonso da Costa Brandão.
Bishop Brandão arrived in Funchal.
A famine caused by a shortage of bread struck Madeira until cereal supplies arrived in November.
A gale damaged the newly begun Pontinha wall in Funchal.
The chapel of Nossa Senhora de Belém was rebuilt by Francisco Inácio Telo de Meneses.
João de Morais Perestrelo was captain of the Caniçal fort.
The palace that now houses Funchal's town hall was built.
Bishop Brandão served as governor and captain-general of Madeira.
José Correia de Sá was appointed governor and captain-general of Madeira.
A decree required passports for those leaving Madeira.
The Misericórdia building of Santa Cruz underwent major repairs paid for by public charity.
The Jesuits' property in Madeira, including Quinta Grande, was confiscated.
José Correia de Sá took office as governor of Madeira.
On Pombal's orders the Jesuit college in Funchal was surrounded and the Jesuits confined, ending their teaching; the eighteen Madeiran Jesuits were shipped under arrest to Lisbon on 16 July 1760.
João Pedro de Freitas Pereira Drumond was born in Câmara de Lobos.
António Rodrigues Ciebra published his Narração cirúrgica on a malignant carbuncle in Lisbon.
Potato cultivation began in Madeira.
The School of Geometry and Trigonometry was founded in Funchal at the end of 1760.
The deed of the chapel of St Francis Borgia at Cruz da Guarda, Porto da Cruz, was executed.
The chapel of Santo António at Terra do Baptista was founded by the Nunes Caldeira family.
The repaired Mosteiro Novo building became the seminary again.
Francisco José Rodrigues de Andrade was born.
The Carta critica by Julião Fernandes da Silva was printed.
A Council of War provision added a pipe of wine to the annual pay of the Paul do Mar fort's master gunner.
An order licensed British subjects to build a cemetery in Funchal.
João Francisco de Oliveira was born in Funchal.
Funchal council consulted the government on the treasurer's collection of the wine levy for foundlings.
A royal decree prohibited transporting slaves to mainland Portugal and freed those arriving there.
Funchal council resolved to hold festivities for the birth of Prince José.
The Conselho de Fazenda was confirmed by law.
Bishop Gaspar Afonso da Costa Brandão founded a confraternity of St John the Baptist at the chapel.
The chapel of Nossa Senhora do Bom Despacho in Campanário was rebuilt by Padre Francisco Nicolau de Brito.
Francisco João Róscio was appointed infantry adjutant.
At the Corpus Christi procession Governor José Correia de Sá walked behind the canopy with the Knights of Christ despite council objections.
Governor José Correia de Sá reported emigration from Madeira to Lisbon due to overpopulation.
Dr Thomas Heberden observed Jupiter's first satellite at Funchal.
The Count of Lippe's military regulations were introduced under D. José I, affecting the Madeiran militia.
The church of the Convent of São Bernardino was enlarged and rebuilt.
Pedro Jorge Monteiro settled in Funchal as tobacco administrator.
The Blessed Sacrament chapel was built in the parish of Porto da Cruz.
The district magistrate complained to the governor about abuses in the court of the Juiz dos Resíduos e Capelas.
A royal decree confirmed the Funchal council's right to walk behind the canopy in the Corpus Christi procession.
Commodore John Byron's ships Dolphin and Tamar called at Madeira and were well received by the governor.
Manuel Caetano Pimenta de Aguiar was born in Funchal.
António José de Jesus Lamedo was appointed doorkeeper and bookkeeper of the Funchal council.
The São Sebastião chapel at São Jorge, rebuilt by the parish priest, was blessed.
Joaquim de Menezes e Ataíde was born in Porto.
Funchal's streams flooded, destroying the Ponte da Praça.
João António de Sá Pereira was appointed captain-general of Madeira in 1766 and took office on 9 December 1767.
An oil bequest for the church of Arco de São Jorge was ratified by deed.
The bishop ordered a copy to be made of Faial's decayed first baptismal book.
A decree created the offices of corregedor and juiz de fora for the Azores, later extended to Madeira.
A royal warrant confirmed Lamedo's appointment to the Funchal council.
Philip Carteret's ship Swallow stayed at Madeira on its way to the Pacific.
The last donatary of Funchal, the Count of Castelo Melhor, ceded the captaincy's jurisdictional rights to the Crown, abolishing the donatary captaincy and leaving him a mere alcaide-mor.
The Fortress of São Tiago in Funchal was rebuilt and enlarged under governor José Correia de Sá and armed with fifty cannon brought from London.
João António de Sá Pereira governed Madeira during the Pombaline period (the text misprints 1677 to 1766).
Captain João Francisco de Freitas Esmeraldo had a chapel built at Cruz do Carvalho.
The Mother of God chapel at Corujeira, Tabua, destroyed by flood, was rebuilt on the opposite bank and inspected for divine service on 9 December 1767.
Manuel Joaquim Gonçalves de Andrade was born in Campanário.
A royal charter approved the statutes of the Misericórdia of Porto Santo.
Land for the first British cemetery in Funchal was acquired.
José Correia de Sá's governorship of Madeira ended.
The 1766 decree was applied to Madeira, and the first permanent, separate corregedor and juiz de fora took office, regularising justice on the island.
The Conselho de Fazenda ordered the Provedor to take the Machico captaincy for the Crown, apparently without effect.
A slave ship arrived in Madeira, but the corregedor forbade the sale of its slaves.
Date sometimes given for the completion of the new church associated with the Voto a São Tiago.
António Francisco de Caires founded the hermitage of Sant'Ana at Fajã do Penedo, Boaventura, endowing it by deed of 20 April 1768.
The chapel of Nossa Senhora das Preces at Santo António was built.
A petition shows the Santa Cruz customs house was already extinct.
The posts of Juiz de Fora and Presidente dos Resíduos were created, and Governor Sá Pereira banned mixing north and south coast wines.
Heberden recorded the magnetic declination at Funchal as 15°30' W.
An epidemic caused many deaths in the parish of Arco de São Jorge.
The Funchal council ordered execution of a royal provision allowing a Tuesday public fair in the Terreiro da Sé.
Birth in Madeira of the 1st Viscount of Torre Bela.
Birth of Sebastião Xavier Botelho.
Governor Sá Pereira questioned the annual payment made by the British to the governors.
The Funchal council contracted the building of the Ponte Nova over the Ribeira de Santa Luzia for 890$000 réis.
The corregedor reported that the old prison house in Funchal was badly ruined.
A letter applying the 1761 decree to Madeira was proclaimed in Funchal, beginning the gradual end of slavery on the island.
Diogo Luiz Drumond was appointed almoxarife of Porto Santo, the last known such appointment.
Cook left England on his first circumnavigation in the Endeavour.
Cook's Endeavour expedition lay at Funchal before sailing for Rio de Janeiro; Banks and Solander collected plants and the astronomer Green visited Madeira.
The Barão de Alverca ordered engineers to survey the Rabaçal springs and then sent the minister a report on the benefits of using their waters.
Francisco de Paula Medina e Vasconcelos was born in Funchal.
A royal charter founded Nova Aldeia, or Aldeia da Rainha, at Santo António da Serra for families from Porto Santo.
Inácio Correia Drumond was born in Funchal.
Câmara de Lobos fishermen founded a mutual fund dedicated to São Pedro Gonçalves Telmo.
On Governor Sá Pereira's orders, Francisco de Alincourt surveyed and drew the general map of Madeira and visited Porto Santo.
Governor Sá Pereira reported the good results of the School of Geometry and Trigonometry to Lisbon.
An order allowed anyone to land and sell salt, in practice ending the donatary monopoly.
João António Monteiro was born in Funchal.
Pombal's law suppressed many small entails.
Jerónimo Álvares da Silva Pinheiro was born in Calheta.
Members of a masonic lodge in Madeira were arrested on the governor's orders, among them Francisco de Alincourt, who was soon released.
The former Jesuit house, chapel and lands at Santo António were sold at public auction for seven contos de réis.
João Francisco Lopes Rocha graduated in canon law at Coimbra and was ordained priest.
Captain Rodrigo da Costa was administrator of the chapel of Nossa Senhora das Preces.
The Quinta Grande estate was sold at auction to João Francisco de Freitas Esmeraldo.
Vagrant boys from Porto Santo were sent to learn trades in the workshops of the Fortaleza do Pico.
The people of Machico built the chapel of Nossa Senhora do Terço.
João Nepomuceno de Freitas Leal founded the chapel of São João Nepomuceno at Lombo dos Leais.
A royal charter of José I on irrigation water confirmed old concessions, reaffirmed distribution according to cultivated land and declared water sales abusive.
A law reorganised existing entails and restricted the creation of new ones.
Licence was granted to bless the rebuilt chapel of São João Baptista at Calheta.
The royal charter known as the Law of Quintos e Oitavos reformed land tenure on Porto Santo, letting lands pay fifths and eighths instead of half the produce, to address the island's decline.
The chapel of Nossa Senhora da Conceição in Rua da Carreira, founded by Luís Bettencourt de Albuquerque e Freitas, was blessed.
Governor Sá Pereira stayed on Porto Santo to put the 1770 charter into effect.
The council granted two sums of 100,000 réis to build a house for the standard-bearer next to the Casa de Saúde.
Death of Manuel Saldanha da Gama Albuquerque.
Inácio Pedro Quintela leased the Madeira customs revenues for six years.
The Academy volume dated 1772, published in 1776, contained De Bory's account of his voyage to Madeira.
Public classes in philosophy, Latin, mathematics and rhetoric were created in Funchal, with Francisco Manuel de Oliveira appointed to the chair of philosophy.
The Marquês de Pombal reformed the University of Coimbra.
Engineer Domingos Rodrigues Martins was called to estimate the rebuilding of the walls of Funchal's streams.
Captain James Cook arrived at Funchal in the Resolution on his second voyage, accompanied by the botanists Forster; he recorded large numbers of Black and mulatto people in Madeira.
A royal law established secondary classes of Latin, Greek, rhetoric and philosophy in Funchal and the first six public primary schools in Madeira; the Greek class never opened.
A law created the subsídio literário tax to fund schools.
The poet Francisco Álvares de Nóbrega was born in Machico.
A second edition of Francisco de Vasconcelos Coutinho's works was published in one volume in Lisbon.
A further decree completed the slavery abolition measures of 1768.
Luís Monteiro was born in Funchal.
Padre João Manuel de Freitas Branco was born in Funchal.
The English botanist Robins carried out afforestation in Madeira.
The date 1774 was carved on the doorway of the chapel of Santo André Avelino at Carvalhal, Canhas.
Funchal's municipal council read a letter on the advantages of creating a wine company in Madeira.
Padre António João de Lessa was born in Madalena do Mar.
Morgado Agostinho António de Ornelas, exiled by the governor, died at his manor in Caniço.
The 9th Count of Vimioso died.
Captain Skinner drew a plan of Funchal, published by William Johnston with his map of Madeira.
Governor João António de Sá Pereira had a clock made and installed in the tower of Funchal Cathedral.
End date of the list of donataries of the captaincy of Machico.
Dr Fothergill published observations on consumption recommending Madeira's climate for lung patients.
A royal letter abolished the Provedoria da Real Fazenda attached to the Funchal customs house and created the Junta da Real Fazenda da Ilha da Madeira.
Luís José Baiardo was born, according to the dictionary Portugal.
The chapel of Nossa Senhora do Monte at Ponta do Sol was enlarged and blessed again.
A royal letter appointed João Francisco Lopes Rocha parish priest of Santa Maria Maior.
The last provedor da Fazenda became judge of the customs house.
João Batista Pelle was executed for plotting against the Marquis of Pombal.
Maritime pine and Italian ryegrass were apparently introduced to Madeira in the last quarter of the 18th century.
Padre Matias Jorge Jardim built a chapel of Nossa Senhora da Piedade at Ilha, São Jorge.
Carlos Nunes de Freitas da Silva built the chapel of Santo André Avelino at Carvalhal e Carreira, Canhas.
The São José chapel at Calheta was rebuilt on a safer site and inspected on 3 June.
José Júlio de França e Vasconcelos was born in Boaventura.
Cook began his third voyage, without calling at Madeira.
Charles Murray bought the fountain's surplus water from morgado Henrique Felix de Freitas.
The English botanist Downe collected plants on Madeira.

The Real Junta da Fazenda held thanksgiving ceremonies in the Colégio church, Funchal, for Pombal's escape from an assassination plot; Fr. Inácio José de Varona's sermon was published in Lisbon that year.
Padre Paulo Vieira Jardim, founder of the São Paulo chapel at Porto Moniz, died.
A lease was signed for the land on which Funchal's opera house was built.
The botanist Francis Masson arrived in Madeira in May 1776 and explored the island botanically into 1777, recording Guinea grass.
The council appointed the first keeper of the Cathedral clock.
The chapel of São João Nepomuceno at Folhadal, Porto da Cruz, was built and its endowment deed signed.
Joaquim de Oliveira Álvares was born in Madeira.
The chapel of Nossa Senhora da Piedade at Jangão, Ponta do Sol, was restored and enlarged by Francisco de Ornelas de Vasconcelos, and authorisation to rebless it was given on 3 August 1777.
João José de Freitas Aragão was born in Funchal.
João Agostinho Pereira de Agrela was born in Funchal.
Governor João António de Sá Pereira left Madeira for Lisbon, his enemies celebrating with illuminations and fireworks.
Funeral rites for King José I were held in Funchal.
Maria I was acclaimed queen in Funchal.
João Gonçalves da Câmara Coutinho was appointed governor and captain-general of Madeira on 19 August 1777 and took office on 15 September.
Vitúrio Lopes Rocha received the doctoral hood in mathematics at Coimbra.
José Anselmo Correia Henriques was born in Ribeira Brava.
Maria I granted the Duke of Lafões the Order of Christ commandery of Terceira, Madeira and São Miguel.
João de Carvalhal Esmeraldo e Câmara rebuilt the Reis Magos chapel at Ponta Delgada.
In Caniço the church of Espírito Santo was completely destroyed and that of Santo Antão badly ruined.
Manuel Caetano Pimenta de Aguiar left for Lisbon to enter the Colégio dos Nobres.
Manuel António de Azevedo Henriques published his 'Panegyrico Funchalense' in Lisbon.
Carlos Murray had the fountain at the Quinta do Belo Monte repaired and an aqueduct and roadside fountain built.
António de Gamboa e Liz was born.
João do Carvalhal Esmeraldo Albuquerque e Câmara, 1st Count of Carvalhal, was born in Funchal.
The botanist Francisco Masson stayed in the Azores.
The governor of Madeira ordered an inquiry into emigrant recruiters and ships.
A cemetery for patients of the São Lázaro hospital was completed.
The foundation stone of the new parish church of Caniço was blessed on 2 August 1779, and the church was solemnly blessed on 28 October 1783.
The old church of the Convent of São Francisco in Funchal was demolished and a larger one begun.
Machico council declared it held the same privileges as the council of Lisbon.
António de Carvalhal Esmeraldo e Alencastre built the chapel of São Caetano at Lombo das Terças, Ponta do Sol.
The pilgrims' house at Monte already existed in this period.
The deed of endowment was made for the Santana chapel at Ribeiro Seco, São Martinho, built that year.
Date of an inscription on a stone later found in the convent grounds of the Jardim Municipal.
The Teatro Grande was built and apparently completed in Funchal.
Luiz António Jardim was born in Funchal.
Roque José de Araujo had the Almas Pobres chapel built in Funchal; it was endowed with a perpetual pension of 5,000 réis in August 1781 and blessed by the vicar of São Pedro in December 1783.
Joaquim de Meneses e Ataíde took vows in the Order of Saint Augustine.
António José de Jesus Lamedo was appointed reweigher of wheat and flour.
Pina Manique ordered the inspection of prostitutes in Portugal.
A papal brief granted plenary indulgence to visitors of the Madre de Deus chapel at Tabua on the first Sunday of May.
A papal brief granted a special privilege to the altar of Senhor Jesus in Porto da Cruz.
D. Diogo Pereira Forjaz Coutinho was appointed governor and captain-general of Madeira by royal letter and took office on 15 November 1781.
The botanist Daniel Carlos Solander died in London.
The parish churches of Santo António, Caniço and Estreito da Calheta were built, bearing dated inscriptions of 1783, 1789 and 1791.
João Nepomuceno de Oliveira was born in Funchal.
The Porto Santo settlers finally abandoned the Aldeia at Santo António da Serra.
The Republic of Venice already had a consulate in Funchal.
The chapel of São Pedro de Alcântara at Lombo do Atouguia, Calheta, was built and endowed by deed on 9 February 1783, with licence for its blessing granted on 13 October.
The foundation stone of the present parish church of Camacha was laid.
Funchal council left the dilapidated Campo do Duque building and moved into the Casa da Saúde, which served as the town hall until about 1800.
The Paço chapel in São Vicente was erected.
Bishop D. Gaspar Afonso da Costa Brandão died in Funchal.
Funchal council resolved to build a sea wall to stop the sea silting up the João Diniz springs.
Funchal municipal council registered the royal grant to the Duke of Lafões.
Naturalist António de Carvalho e Almeida arrived in Madeira to organise a collection of natural products.
The rebuilt chapel of Nossa Senhora do Livramento at Monte was inspected for worship.
Santa Clara convent donated six alqueires of land at Curral das Freiras to the diocese for a new church and chaplain's residence.
Papal briefs granted a privileged altar and plenary indulgence to the church of Arco de São Jorge.
Botanist Francis Masson finally left Madeira.
Manuel Caetano Pimenta de Aguiar went to Paris to study arts and sciences.
Francisco Manuel Jardim Telo de Meneses was captain of the São Jorge redoubt.
Manuel da Câmara Perestrelo de Noronha became governor of Porto Santo.
João Francisco de Oliveira received his doctorate in medicine at Coimbra.
La Pérouse's expedition aboard the Boussole called at Funchal, where he lunched with consul Murray and dined with Monteiro, before leaving for the Canaries on 16 August.
A papal brief granted a plenary indulgence for the patronal feast of Faial parish.
Botanist Chetien Smith was born.
The Misericórdia building of Santa Cruz underwent major repairs paid for by public charity.
Francisco Manuel de Oliveira gave an opening address at the Diocesan Seminary.
The Teatro Grande reopened after repairs with a prologue by Francisco Manuel de Oliveira.
Licence was granted to bless the chapel of São João Nepomuceno, which received a privileged altar by papal brief that year.
A new proclamation imposed severe penalties against wine fraud in Madeira.
Pope Pius VI confirmed D. José da Costa Torres as bishop of Madeira; he took possession of the diocese of Funchal on 18 September 1787.
Permission was granted to bless the rebuilt chapel of Nossa Senhora do Rosário at Jardim do Mar.
João Francisco de Oliveira was appointed substitute in one of the Coimbra university chairs.
Georg Forster published Plantae Atlanticae, treating some Madeiran plants.
Gregório Nazianzeno Medina e Vasconcelos was born in Funchal.
Governor Diogo Forjaz Coutinho had the masonry arch bridge at Torreão built.
By royal charter D. Maria I ceded the former Jesuit College buildings to Bishop José da Costa Torres for a diocesan seminary.
D. Manuel de Portugal e Castro was born.
William Johnston made a geo-hydrographic survey of Madeira, the Desertas and Porto Santo.
Francisco de Paula Medina e Vasconcelos enrolled at Coimbra University.
The firm Phelps & C.ª existed in Madeira.
A pamphlet on reviving the drowned, paid for by Carlos Murray, was printed in Lisbon.
Governor Diogo Pereira Forjaz Coutinho ordered black cherry trees destroyed and their cultivation banned, as the fruit was used to colour wine fraudulently.
The diocesan seminary moved to and was solemnly opened in the former Jesuit College in Funchal.
A new entrance was built for the Misericórdia hospital in Funchal.
João Gualberto de Oliveira, future Count of Tojal, was born in Funchal.
Nicolau Caetano de Bettencourt Pita was born in Funchal.
The Magdalene chapel at Porto Moniz was enlarged.
João José de Orquigny arrived in Madeira to study its flora and set up a masonic lodge in Funchal.
The image of São Tiago was solemnly moved from the cathedral to the new church.
João Maria de Abreu Castelo Branco Cardoso e Melo, future 1st Count of Fornos de Algodres, was born.
D. Álvaro José Xavier Botelho de Távora died.
Lourenço José Moniz was born in Funchal.
The ruinous old parish church (chapel of São Roque) of São Roque collapsed and could no longer be used for worship.
The Sociedade Patriótica, Económica, de Comércio, Agricultura, Ciências e Artes was founded in Funchal.
Baptisms began to be performed at Boaventura.
A chapel of Santana was built at Cruz do Carvalho, São Pedro, Funchal.
Arabic documents in the Torre do Tombo were copied, including a Moorish chief's complaint about slave raids.
João Pedro de Freitas Drumond promoted an early attempt to found an agricultural association in Madeira.
A royal charter created the parish of Curral das Freiras, separated from Santo António, with its seat in the chapel of Saint Anthony.
Father Caetano Alberto Soares was born in Porto da Cruz.
A minister was appointed to supervise the theatre in Funchal.
João José de Orquigny delivered a farewell speech to the general assembly of the Sociedade Patriótica in Funchal.
Dr António Rodrigues de Oliveira took office as corregedor of Madeira.
Manuel Caetano Pimenta de Aguiar took part in France's internal revolts, reaching the rank of captain.
Francisco de Paula Medina e Vasconcelos was imprisoned at Coimbra and expelled from the university.
J. H. Castera's French translation of James Bruce's travels to the Nile was published.
João António Monteiro received his doctorate in philosophy at Coimbra.
The British consul denounced the fraud of blending Tenerife wine sold as Madeira.
The present parish church of Estreito da Calheta was built in 1791 and blessed in 1793.
The United States consulate in Madeira was established.
Patrício Malheiro de Melo was born in Funchal.
The Funchal council resolved to budget for a slaughterhouse by the Almotaceria.
José da Fonseca e Gouveia, Baron of Lordelo, was born.
An Inquisition edict launched a persecution of Madeiran freemasons, leading many families to emigrate to the United States.
Maria Riddell's book of voyages was published in Edinburgh.
John Barrow visited Madeira and described the dress of the middle classes.
The musician José Fradesso Belo was born.
Francisco de Paula Medina e Vasconcelos returned to Madeira after his release.
Dr William Gourlay arrived in Madeira.
Januário Vicente Camacho was born in Funchal.
Arsénio Pompílio Pompeu do Carpo was born in Funchal.
A pardon for members of secret societies reached Madeira.
Several persecuted members of secret societies and their families embarked clandestinely from Madeira.
Corregedor Veloso de Oliveira left tree-planting instructions to the Calheta council.
A royal charter licensed Tomás Watts and partners to set up fisheries and salt works in Madeira, the first of unsuccessful attempts to found fishing companies (another followed in 1802).
João Francisco de Freitas Esmeraldo issued the first known Madeiran tokens.
Dr William Gourlay made meteorological observations in Madeira.
A primary school was created in Campanário.
Francisco Manuel de Oliveira published Escolha de Poesias Orientaes in Lisbon.
A Moroccan brig carrying the family of Prince Muley Abdessalam arrived at Funchal; the princesses later left Lisbon for Morocco aboard three Portuguese government ships.
Francisco Correia Herédia was born in Madeira.
Dean João Francisco Lopes Rocha wrote to minister José de Seabra da Silva complaining of his persecution and continued suspension as a former freemason.
D. Manuel Martins Manso, later bishop, was born in Mogadouro.
Francisco Manuel de Oliveira's Colecção Poética was published, mentioning the Arcadia Funchalense.
António José de Jesus Lamedo's index of Funchal council records ends in this year.
Estufas for ageing wine were first used on Madeira.
D. Mateus de Abreu Pereira was presented as bishop of São Paulo.
The 2nd Viscount of Torre Bela was born.
Curral das Freiras had only 110 inhabitants.
José Maria Martiniano da Fonseca was born in the Sé parish of Funchal.
José Manuel da Veiga was born in Funchal.
Jerónimo Álvares da Silva Pinheiro was ordained priest.
The Funchal council asked the Royal Treasury for a loan of 400$000 réis for the slaughterhouse.
José Ferreira Pestana was born at Ribeira Brava.
A papal brief granted a plenary indulgence to visitors of the church of Porto da Cruz.
Pius VI confirmed D. Mateus de Abreu Pereira by bull as bishop of São Paulo.
António Joaquim Gonçalves de Andrade, later dean, was born in Funchal.
José António Monteiro Teixeira was born in Funchal.
The Funchal council rented Fernando José Correia Brandão's building until it could no longer afford the rent.
The Swedish consulate in Madeira was established.
A forest decree was issued for Madeira.
Bishop José da Costa Torres of Funchal was transferred to the see of Elvas.
Bishop José da Costa Torres, surrounded by troops at Penha, was forced to embark by night and left Madeira hastily without farewells.
The council ordered quadrilheiros to wear an identifying badge.
Johann Reinhold Forster's Herbarium Australe, treating some Madeiran plants, was published.
The council, nobility and people of Funchal resolved to ask the government for a subsidy for a new town hall; no answer came.
António José de Jesus Lamedo died suddenly in the Sé parish of Funchal.
D. Mateus de Abreu Pereira took possession of the see of São Paulo.
António Aluísio Jervis de Atouguia, later Visconde de Atouguia, was born in Funchal in the house beside the chapel of São Francisco das Furnas.
Pius VI confirmed Luís Rodrigues de Vilares as bishop of Madeira.
Queen Maria I created the curacy of Porto da Cruz at the chapel of São João Nepomuceno.
A treaty was negotiated in France with António de Araújo e Azevedo, later Conde da Barca, as Portuguese plenipotentiary.
José Xavier de Cerveira e Sousa, later bishop, was born at Mogofores.
Bishop Luís Rodrigues de Vilares took possession of the diocese of Funchal early in the year.
Funchal's arms still showed two sugar canes, as seen on a silver inkstand of that year.
Joaquim de Oliveira Álvares was appointed second lieutenant in the navy.
Construction of the Pilar de Banger in Funchal was completed at a cost of 1,350 pounds sterling.
Governor Diogo Pereira Forjaz Coutinho left the governorship because of illness.
Captain-general Diogo Pereira Forjaz Coutinho died in Funchal and was buried in the Carmo church.
The Madeira post office was created under an administrator.
The sea brought down one of the two pillars of the bell-shaped islet that gave Campanário its name.

A government tree nursery was established at the Lombada, Monte, its site chosen by José Maria de Afonseca and designated on 9 August 1799; it distributed over twenty thousand trees for replanting by 1823–24.
The people owed 162,000 cruzados of finto arrears, which the government ordered collected.
Francisco Manuel de Oliveira was retired from his chair by ministerial order.
A convoy of 96 ships loaded 3,041 pipes of wine at Funchal.
The curacy of Porto da Cruz was created, its curate being obliged to serve the chapel of São João Nepomuceno.
The government recommended the creation of a credit fund in Madeira.
Joaquim de Oliveira Álvares commanded a Portuguese caique against a French privateer off the Algarve.
The clerk of the court of bequests and chapels was found to have embezzled bequest money by forgery.
Padre Manuel Gonçalves Henriques built and endowed the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Piedade at Caldeira.
D. José Manuel da Câmara was appointed governor and captain-general of Madeira.
José Maria Baldy was born in Lisbon.
The English traveller Turnbull visited Madeira.
Hemlock and false acacia were introduced to Madeira from seeds sent by the government.
The Funchal council expelled two ships lacking bills of health and quarantined their guards for 40 days.
D. José Manuel da Câmara took office as governor of Madeira.
A decree regulated cask marks to prevent the adulteration of wine.
The firm Paulo Malheiro de Melo & Filhos traded in Funchal in the first quarter of the 19th century.
Captain Sebastião António Drumond rebuilt the Espírito Santo chapel at Campo de Baixo, Porto Santo.
The Conde do Carvalhal introduced the frog Rana temporaria to Madeira.
Giraldes published in Paris his Estatística Historico-Geographica of Madeira and Porto Santo.
Gorse was introduced to Madeira at the Quinta do Palheiro.
Tea was first grown in Madeira at Jardim da Serra, introduced by consul Henry Veitch.
Madeiran ladies used palanquins for outings and social visits.
Rebuilding of the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Graça on Porto Santo on a larger scale was begun but never completed.
The present parish church of São Roque was built, work finishing around the middle of the century.
Robert Page had two refuge huts built, at Paul da Serra and Ribeira das Cales.
José Maria de Afonseca planned and built a road network across Madeira.
The chayote was already present in Madeira, known as 'pepinos nelas'.
The Caminho do Monte was opened to the public on its present route.
A plant nursery known as the Jardim Botânico existed in Monte.
Cats were brought to Deserta Grande to kill rodents damaging crops.
Freemasonry in Madeira was reorganised during the British occupations of 1801–1802 and 1807–1814.
D. Antónia Basília Herédia de Bettencourt married António Saldanha da Gama.
A curacy was created in Camacha.
The municipal council granted John Light Banger a privilege to use a kiln for purifying grain.
Governor D. José Manuel da Câmara visited the Palheiro property and attended the laying of the doorsteps.
José de Freitas Teixeira Spinola de Castelo Branco was born in Funchal.
Anastácio Moniz de Bettencourt was appointed substitute professor of rhetoric and philosophy in Funchal.
A decree banned the import of Azorean wines into Madeira.

A British squadron arrived at Funchal, beginning the first British occupation of Madeira; troops under Clinton were quartered in the Jesuit college, the Penha de França fort and the theatre, forcing the seminary back to the Mosteiro Novo.
The allowance at the Hospital de S. Lázaro was raised to 100 réis.
The preliminaries of the Peace of Amiens were signed, prompting renewed Portuguese demands for the British evacuation of Madeira.
José Gerardo Ferreira Passos was born in Elvas.
Lieutenant-colonel Roberts published a plan of Porto Santo.
Miguel Fitzgerald brought the first English cattle and long-wool sheep to Madeira.
Bernardo Francisco Lobato Machado was born in Madeira.

Dr J. Adams was licensed by the governor and captain-general to vaccinate foundlings against smallpox, apparently the first vaccination in Madeira; the Funchal town council received his request for foundlings on 27 October 1802.
The workshops of the Fortaleza do Pico expanded greatly.
A famine on Porto Santo required relief supplies.
British troops embarked from Madeira, ending the first British occupation of the island.
Minister Rodrigo de Sousa Coutinho informed the captain-general of Madeira of the Prince Regent's satisfaction with the progress of cotton growing on the island.
The botanist Robert Brown stayed in Madeira.
An edict of the governor and captain-general prohibited estufas (wine-heating stoves) in Madeira.
An explosion aboard a Portuguese ship at Funchal killed 32 people.
António da Luz Pita was born at Ponta do Sol.
Augusto Frederico de Castilho, later Visconde de Castilho, was born in Lisbon.
The Funchal council held its first session in its house on the Largo da Sé.
Richard Thomas Lowe, clergyman and naturalist, was born.
The Senate of Funchal fixed the seating order at its sessions, ruling that the juiz do povo should sit on a low chair above the eldest of the mesteres.
Sérvulo Drumond de Meneses was born in Funchal.
After the flood destroyed the Calhau church, the seat of Santa Maria Maior parish was transferred to the church of São Tiago Menor.
The oak was introduced to Madeira by the 1st Count of Carvalhal.
The juiz de fora allowed the mesteres to sit at the Funchal council table, prompting noble protest and a stormy session.
An electoral provision almost identical to that of 1613 was issued.
Dr João António Monteiro's translation of Jenner's work on vaccination was published in Lisbon.
William Penfold was living in Funchal.
The morgado João de Freitas da Silva was imprisoned in the fortress of São Tiago.
Funchal held illuminations for the birth of an infante.
On the governor's orders the São Sebastião chapel in Funchal was emptied, its images carried to São Tiago, and razed overnight.
Anastácio Moniz de Bettencourt was appointed professor of rational philosophy in Funchal.
The Prince Regent granted Dr João Francisco de Oliveira lands in São Jorge and the Quinta de Sant'Ana in Monte.
A royal notice granted the Misericórdia of Funchal a lottery of thirty contos, apparently never drawn.
A serious conflict between Governor José Manuel da Câmara and Bishop D. Luís Rodrigues de Vilares over the Jesuit college led the governor to force the bishop out of Funchal to Santo da Serra.
The São Sebastião market in Funchal was inaugurated.

The Senado da Câmara of Funchal took possession of the house on the Largo da Sé.
Luís Vicente de Afonseca was born in Estreito de Câmara de Lobos.

A royal charter created the Junta da Justiça in Madeira.
A further governor's edict prohibited wine estufas in Madeira.
The nobility and people of Funchal agreed to the bishop's proposed vow to the Virgin after the flood.
The Funchal town council, and then Bishop D. Luís Rodrigues de Vilares and the cathedral chapter, vowed an annual votive procession and feast every 9 October in honour of Our Lady's patronage.
Judge Joaquim António de Araújo and the new governor Ascenso de Sequeira Freire arrived in Funchal on the frigate Carlota.
Ascenso de Sequeira Freire took office as governor of Madeira in Funchal.
Bishop D. Luís Rodrigues de Vilares and the dismissed governor sailed separately from Madeira to Lisbon under government orders.
José Caetano de Paiva Pereira was appointed provedor dos defuntos e ausentes.
Roberto Page was established in Madeira, where the firm Phelps, Page & C.ª existed.
Dr João António Monteiro left Portugal on a scientific journey through Europe, never to return.
A great landslide from the Lombada enlarged Lugar de Baixo and drove the sea into Ponta do Sol.
Francisco Álvares de Nóbrega's Rimas were published in Lisbon.
Joaquim de Oliveira Álvares served in Brazil as artillery captain of the São Paulo volunteer legion.

A royal order allowed wine estufas in Madeira to operate again.
João António Monteiro was appointed professor at the new chemical laboratory of Lisbon.
A royal letter on forests ordered hilltop planting on Madeira and Porto Santo and the punishment of forest arsonists.
A rescript of Pius VII confirmed Our Lady of Monte as protector of Funchal and instituted the feast of the Patrocínio.
The Funchal council instituted compulsory rota labour on stream repairs for men aged 16 to 60.
Justino António de Freitas was born.
Governor Avelar Brotero had the Pico fortress's roof tiles removed to repair the town barracks and his residence.
The auxiliary artillery corps of Madeira, including a Porto Santo corps, was instituted.
A royal order directed that the ruins of the Calhau church be preserved as a memorial of the flood.
The Viscondessa das Nogueiras was born in Funchal.
The ruins of Funchal's old council house were auctioned to Dr António José Monteiro.
A decree annexed the Madeira and Azores posts to the General Postal Administration.
Marceliano Ribeiro de Mendonça was born in Funchal.
The painter Vieira Portuense died suddenly in Funchal and was buried in the cathedral.
A papal brief granted a plenary indulgence for the feast of Nossa Senhora da Luz at Ponta do Sol.
Oudinot sent a detailed map of Funchal and its bay to the Visconde de Anadia.
Francisco João Róscio died in Brazil.
The British warship Favorita, with surgeon F. B. Spilsbury aboard, called at Madeira on its way to West Africa.
Benjamim de Oliveira was born in England.
Francisco de Paula Medina e Vasconcelos's epic poem Zargueida was published in Lisbon.
D. José da Costa Torres was appointed archbishop of Braga.
Madeira's tax revenues included 180 contos from customs.
Cândido Joaquim da Silva was born in Funchal.
The poet Francisco Álvares de Nóbrega took his own life, and the Inquisition destroyed his writings.
The fourth reform of the Madeiran militia took place.
Famine on Porto Santo required relief supplies from Madeira.
Francisco de Andrade was born in Funchal.
Bartolomeu dos Mártires Dias e Sousa was born.
António da Costa Paiva, later Barão de Castelo de Paiva, was born in Porto.
The alcaidarias of Funchal and Machico yielded 23:110$000 réis.
After the Portuguese court fled to Brazil, much of the São Carlos theatre company came to perform in Funchal.
Diogo Vieira de Tóvar e Albuquerque wrote his political and economic description of Madeira.
Governor Beresford abolished the capstan Patronado and handed it to the merchants.
For fear of an enemy landing, the Funchal council archive was moved to Santa Luzia and then to Monte.
Dr António Caetano de Freitas wrote his second report on vaccination in Madeira.
The painter Joaquim Leonardo da Rocha came to Madeira fleeing the first French invasion of Portugal.
The Funchal Câmara resolved to punish those absent without cause from the Crusade Bull procession.
Funchal was illuminated for three nights to celebrate a royal birth.
The engineer Reinaldo Oudinot died in Funchal.
Pedro Fagundes Bacelar de Antas e Meneses was appointed governor and captain-general of Madeira.
D. Jorge da Câmara Leme was born in Funchal.
António Rogério Gromicho Couceiro was born in Elvas.
Pedro Fagundes Bacelar de Antas e Meneses took office as governor of Madeira, succeeding Ascenso de Sequeira Freire.
The Funchal council reported receiving pine seed from America.

During the second British occupation John Blandy already had his trading house established in Madeira.
Padre António João de Lessa left Madeira for Brazil.

English residents paid for a pilgrims' house at Santo António da Serra, opposite the parish residence.
José António Monteiro Teixeira studied at a college in Pau, France.

Silvano Sátiro de Silva was born in Funchal, according to the Elucidário.

summary: A convention restored the civil administration of Madeira to Portugal during the British occupation.

A royal letter created the Junta de Melhoramentos da Agricultura for Madeira and Porto Santo, supplemented by a royal charter in September 1811.
Bishop D. Luís Rodrigues de Vilares died in Funchal.
A royal charter created the Junta da Justiça Criminal in the Azores.
Vice-rectors of Coimbra University were granted the treatment of senhoria for services during the French invasions.
Napoleon's troops left Portugal and the family of the Count of Ega went to France.
Padre João Crisóstomo Espínola de Macedo was imprisoned by order of the cathedral chapter after a complaint by the Santa Cruz judge.

The Junta do Desembargo do Paço was created in Madeira.
A charter on forests was issued for Madeira.
The corregedor urged the transfer of the Funchal prison to a safer house.
Corregedor Veloso de Oliveira reported to the government on the levada judges.
Madeira customs revenue reached 228 and 230 contos.
The Academia Real das Ciências published the first Portuguese translation of Cadamosto's Navegações.

Bishop Athaide brought many musicians to Madeira.

Wickerwork reportedly began in Camacha.
Manuel Celestino Emídio was born.
Joaquim Coelho de Meireles was treasurer of the Funchal council.

A royal letter ordered the Funchal council to let the Casa dos Vinte e Quatro use its council chamber.
The Funchal council heard that 9,233 trees had been planted in Ribeira Brava.
The Funchal council asked the captain-general for nightly military patrols against theft.
The Funchal council ordered a register of pregnant prostitutes so that they would rear their own children.
Nicolau Caetano de Bettencourt Pita received his doctorate in medicine at Edinburgh.
Major-General Gordon replaced Colonel Mead in command of the British troops occupying Madeira.
Diogo d'Ornelas Frazão, later Count of Calçada, was born.
The Funchal council resolved to import four moios of pine seed from Portugal.
Bishop D. Joaquim de Meneses e Ataíde created an archpriesthood seated at São Vicente.
A decree created Fernando José Correia Brandão Bettencourt de Noronha Henriques Viscount of Torre Bela.
The governor reported that some Madeiran levadas had cost their owners up to thirty thousand cruzados.
The captain-general sent Lisbon a description of the Santa Luzia levada.
Madeira wine production stood at 25,440 pipes.

The firm Penfold & Veitch was operating in Funchal.
The curacy of Santo da Serra was created as a dependency of Machico.
Luís Beltrão de Gouveia e Almeida was appointed governor and captain-general of Madeira.

José António de Almada was born in Machico.

A sermon was preached on the anniversary of the consecration of D. Mateus de Abreu Pereira, bishop of São Paulo.
Former governor Pedro Fagundes Bacelar de Antas e Meneses died in Lisbon.
Governor Luís Beltrão de Gouveia e Almeida convened the first meeting of the Junta de Melhoramentos da Agricultura of Madeira and Porto Santo.
An English soldier was hanged in Funchal for murdering a sergeant, despite the governor's protest.
The Funchal council resolved to build a new prison from the sale of the old one, but the alcaide-mor refused to contribute.
The chapel of Santa Quitéria at Pico do Cardo was found desecrated and long disused.

Alleged relics of Machim's cross were reportedly found in the Senhor dos Milagres chapel at Machico.
Bishop D. Joaquim de Meneses e Ataíde consecrated the parish church of Estreito de Câmara de Lobos.
A street (now Rua Hermenegildo Capelo) was opened through the Franciscan convent grounds in Funchal despite the friars' opposition.
The ruined chapel of Nossa Senhora da Piedade at Porto da Cruz was closed.
Rafael Coelho Machado was born in Madeira.
Funchal council minutes mention a lottery held for the benefit of lepers.
The Funchal council requested 80 militiamen nightly to restore the quadrilha policing system.
The jurisdiction of the archpriest of São Vicente was extended to Porto Moniz, Ribeira da Janela and Seixal.
António Pedro de Azevedo was born in Caminha.
A royal letter granted Nicolau Caetano Bettencourt Pita the privileges of Coimbra medical graduates.
Governor Luís Beltrão de Gouveia e Almeida died suddenly in Funchal and an interim government took over.
The last British troops left Funchal, ending the second British occupation of Madeira.
Florêncio José Correia de Melo was appointed governor and captain-general of Madeira.
The interim government ordered the sowing of pines in São Martinho and Santo António.
A report noted that protective works were still lacking on Funchal's streams.
The Funchal Misericórdia tried, unsuccessfully, to take over the property of the four rural Misericórdias.
A smallpox epidemic, brought by a ship from Cape Verde, killed about 2,000 people in Madeira.
The Câmara complained to the bishop because a chaplain rather than a canon had incensed it at the church of São Tiago.
Councillors were summoned to a beija-mão at the Palácio de São Lourenço for Queen Maria I's birthday.
Manuel de Pontes Câmara was born.
The Funchal council ordered a silk standard from Lisbon costing 524$000 réis.
Famine on Porto Santo required relief supplies.
Januário Vicente Camacho was ordained priest.
The municipal council greatly improved the Caminho do Paiol.
The council ordered the monthly vaccination of foundlings by the físico-mor.
Jacinto Augusto Camacho was born in Funchal.
Florêncio José Correia de Melo arrived in Funchal on 16 April 1815 and took office as governor and captain-general of the archipelago on 22 April.
The Funchal municipal council accompanied the procession of Saint Anthony.
Illuminations were held for a religious solemnity in honour of St James the Less.
Napoleon boarded HMS Bellerophon at Rochefort and was later transferred to the Northumberland under Sir George Cockburn, which sailed south.
Lourenço José Moniz defended his Latin thesis De Ictero at Edinburgh.
The squadron carrying Napoleon aboard the Northumberland to exile on Saint Helena arrived off Funchal, where consul Henry Veitch visited him, and left for Saint Helena.
An exceptionally hot leste wind and storm damaged crops and houses in Madeira, popularly blamed on Napoleon.
Princess Leopoldina called at Madeira en route to Brazil.
The squadron carrying Napoleon anchored at Saint Helena.
A major flood damaged Funchal, especially along the São João stream.
José Joaquim de Abreu Rego was born in Madeira.
Vicente Nery da Silva was ordained priest.
Joaquim José da Costa de Macedo's memoirs on the Canaries were published.
José Manuel da Veiga enrolled in the faculty of canon law at Coimbra.
Robert Page upheld Madeira wine prices against a monopoly and was thanked by the Funchal council.
Manuel Caetano Pimenta de Aguiar published his first tragedy, Virgínia.
Famine on Porto Santo again required relief supplies.
The French frigate Medusa passed within sight of Madeira without landing and was wrecked days later on the Arguin bank.
The Funchal council read the governor's order to build a lazaretto and petitioned the Prince Regent for a loan to build it.
The Misericórdia approved regulations for the Hospital Real de Santa Isabel, creating a medical-surgical class; they were printed in 1820.
Chetien Smith died in the Congo.
Joaquim de Oliveira Alvares defeated Artigas's forces at Carumbé.
Funchal's council held the breaking-of-shields ceremony and royal funeral rites for Queen Maria I.
The Count of Lambert was born.
The Austrian and Bavarian governments organised a scientific expedition to Brazil, which included the naturalist Martius.
The Fundoa reservoir and aqueduct supplying central Funchal were built.
Paulo Dias de Almeida wrote his manuscript description of Madeira, recording details such as carapuças, the Pontinha landing stair and a view of the São Lourenço palace.

The squadron carrying Archduchess Leopoldina to Rio de Janeiro anchored at Funchal.

After Funchal council minutes denounced Padre João Crisóstomo Espinola de Macedo as a public insulter, artillery officers dragged him from his home and flogged him at the Funchal pillory.
The Anglican church in Rua da Bela Vista, Funchal, was completed at a cost of 40,000 dollars.
Bishop Francisco José Rodrigues de Andrade took possession of the see of Funchal by proxy on 1 March and assumed direction of the diocese on 1 May.
António Correia Herédia was born.
The council announced the distribution of maritime pine seed to farmers.
A royal letter dismissed D. Rodrigo António de Melo as governor of Madeira at his own request.
A royal letter appointed António Manuel de Noronha governor and captain-general of Madeira.
António Manuel de Noronha took office as governor of Madeira, succeeding D. Rodrigo António de Melo.
The municipal council declared the pilgrims' house at Monte municipal property.
João da Câmara Carvalhal Esmeraldo married Teresa Xavier Botelho.
João Maria Moniz was born in Funchal.
The future Visconde de Atouguia graduated in mathematics at Coimbra.
The Sociedade Funchalense dos Amigos das Ciências e Artes held its first public session, of which the Patriota Funchalense published an account on 7 September.
Dr António Alves da Silva was born in Funchal.
A constitutional municipal council was elected without the mesteres (guild representatives).
A fishing company was founded in Funchal, run by fishermen brought from Sesimbra; it dissolved two years later after losses.
The Associação Funchalense acquired land for the Lancasterian school building.
The Franciscan friars leased the market land to the Funchal council.
The Sociedade Funchalense dos Amigos das Ciências e Artes came to an end with the restoration of absolute government in 1823.
A foundling wheel was installed at Câmara de Lobos beside the Espírito Santo chapel.
A new lottery was granted to the Misericórdia to pay debts and repair the Recolhimento das Órfãs.
João António Pedroso was deported from Madeira to Porto Santo for political reasons.
Morgado Luís Correia was administrator of the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Glória.
The naturalist Bowdich studied Madeira, identifying Porto Santo's fossil beds as Tertiary, measuring Pico Ruivo and noting the Paul da Serra's productive potential.
The Count of Ega was absolved of the crimes imputed to him.
José Pedro Pereira carried out a major repair of the Cathedral clock.
Francisco Vicente Espinosa da Câmara requested a 30-year monopoly on salt-making in Madeira.
Francisco João de Freitas Ferraz was born in Funchal.
The corregedor reported to Lisbon on the immense fortune and income of the Count of Carvalhal.
The Funchal council took custody of the St George image of the Corpus Christi procession and gave it a cloak.
A mole for Funchal harbour was first considered and the council consulted.
Potatoes, tobacco and vines were tried unsuccessfully on Deserta Grande.
António Manuel de Noronha requested his resignation on grounds of ill health.
In parliament, Dr João Francisco de Oliveira proposed a bank, a wine-export company and a quay for Funchal.
A report on the progress of the Lancasterian school was published.
O Pregador Imparcial, Madeira's second newspaper, edited by João Crisóstomo Espínola de Macedo, first appeared in Funchal.
A Atalaia da Liberdade, Funchal's third periodical, was published, its sixth issue appearing on 29 May.
The weekly newspaper O Regedor was published in Funchal, its first series running to nine issues.
Macedo was deported for political crimes, leaving Funchal for Gibraltar on the brig Fanny.
The zoologist José Vicente Barbosa du Bocage was born in Funchal.

mentions.as_written: 2 do mês de Maio do ano de 1823

summary: The Vila-Francada revolution of 27 May 1823 led João VI to dissolve the Cortes and restore absolute government in Portugal on 3 June.
Dr João Francisco de Oliveira served in the short-lived ministry formed after the Vila-Francada.

mentions.as_written: 31 de Maio a 3 de Julho de 1823

summary: The council invited parents to have children vaccinated free at the Misericórdia hospital.
News of the absolutist restoration reached Madeira on 16 June and absolute government was proclaimed and celebrated there the next day.
The municipal Mercado de São João was inaugurated in Funchal.
D. Manuel de Portugal e Castro, appointed in July 1823, took office as governor and captain-general of Madeira on 28 August and governed until 1825.
Frei José Cupertino preached a thanksgiving sermon in Funchal Cathedral for the King's restoration to absolute power (sources give 6 or 8 July).
A law restored the ordenanças and militias.
By this date the Monte nursery had distributed over 20,000 trees.
O Patriota Funchalense ceased publication with issue no. 214.

An absolutist royal tribunal (alçada) came to Funchal to investigate the 1821 constitutional events, holding its inquiry at the town hall until early November 1823; it dispersed the freemasons and sentenced many liberals to exile, including Joaquim Melchior Gonçalves to Cape Verde and others to Angola.

mentions.as_written: 30 de Agosto até os primeiros dias do mês de Novembro de 1823

summary: The frigate Amazonas arrived at Funchal with the new governor D. Manuel de Portugal e Castro, infantry regiment no. 7, artillery and the judicial alçada.
The absolutist authorities destroyed the foundations of the liberal constitutional monument in Funchal and had its medal crushed and sold.
The foundations of the unfinished Constitution monument in Funchal were demolished by order of the governor, and its foundation deposit was recorded.
Notices announced the arrival of pine seed for farmers in Madeira.
Illuminations were held to celebrate the restoration of the King of Spain's full powers.
The naturalist Bowdich stayed in Madeira.
The alçada of 1823 sentenced 24 people, mostly of the upper classes, including Pita to four years' exile on Terceira and a fine and Medina to eight years' exile in Angola.
António Saldanha da Gama was created Count of Porto Santo by decree.
The Lancasterian association's mutual-teaching class opened in Funchal.
The corregedor Manuel José Soares de Lobão e Albergaria sent the Conde de Subserra a memorandum on the state of Madeira and its needed improvements.
António Marcelino Gomes wrote a draft regulation for the Madeira customs house.
Filipe José Nunes was born at Monte.

By royal letter of 13 September 1824, Brigadier Francisco António Raposo was sent to study a mole in Funchal; with Major Sant'Ana he chose the Baixas de São Tiago, and the letter was read to the council on 26 November, but although 37 contos were spent on materials the works never began.
The old tower clock of the Machico parish church stopped working.
The future Visconde das Nogueiras was born in Funchal.
Afonso de Castro was born in Lamego.
Dr Carlos Heineken published an article recommending Funchal's climate for lung diseases.
The old prison house in Funchal was sold to José António Monteiro.
Francisco de Paula Medina e Vasconcelos died in exile in Cape Verde.
António José de Sousa Almada was born in Madeira.
Dr Lourenço José Moniz was appointed professor of humanities in Funchal.
The governor reported that Porto Santo and rural Madeira had no operating surgeon and urged Lisbon to create a class in operative surgery.
The governor complained of the Junta da Justiça's excesses and proposed adopting the Azores model.
Heineken made weather observations in Madeira.
D. Manuel Martins Manso was appointed vicar general of Bragança.
Death of the naturalist T. E. Bowdich.
Januário Justiniano de Nóbrega was born in Funchal.
D. Mateus de Abreu Pereira died in São Paulo.
Ricardo Júlio Ferraz was born in Funchal.
Governor D. Manuel de Portugal e Castro requested the creation of a bank in Funchal.
The 61st and last issue of the Funchal periodical O Pregador Imparcial appeared.
Daniel Ferreira Pestana was born in Funchal.
The Funchal municipal council resolved to have iron chains made for convicts sentenced to forced labour.
The chapel of Nossa Senhora da Piedade at Jardim do Mar was rebuilt and enlarged by Francisco João de Vasconcelos de Couto Cardoso.
Henry Nelson Coleridge published Six Months in the West Indies, which includes an account of Madeira.
Joaquim da Trindade e Vasconcelos was born in Machico.
João Crisóstomo Espínola de Macedo's anonymous pamphlet O Tramista Descoberto was printed in London.
Leopold von Buch published his work on the Canaries, including Robert Brown's list of Madeiran plants.
Bowdich's Excursions in Madeira, citing Kirwan's data, was published in London.
Serious political disturbances in Campanário required the intervention of armed forces.
Dr João Francisco de Oliveira founded a surgery class at the Funchal hospital, a forerunner of the Medical-Surgical School.
The military powder magazine was built.
Public classes in French and English were created in Funchal.
João Jacinto Gonçalves de Andrade was born in Campanário.
Luís António Jardim died in Funchal.
João Pedro de Freitas Pereira Drumond died without issue.
Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo was born in Vila Franca de Xira.
An association of co-owners of the Levada de D. Isabel was formed by public deed.
Governor D. Manuel de Portugal e Castro reported favourably on the petition to create a municipality of Porto Moniz.
The Funchal council returned to its premises in the Largo da Sé after works to install the jail there.
The Funchal slaughterhouse was moved near the Santa Luzia stream.
A decree required oil lanterns instead of wax for public illuminations.
Carlos Stuart was granted the title of Count of Machico by decree.
The endowment deed of the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Fé at Porto da Cruz was executed.
João da Câmara de Carvalhal founded the Montepio home for poor widows in Funchal.
The long-deconsecrated church of São Bartolomeu was demolished.
Roberto Page had the Meio Paul shelter built on the Paul da Serra plateau.

mentions.as_written: fins do primeiro quartel do século XIX

summary: Maria Clementina professed as a nun at the Convent of Santa Clara to satisfy her father's wishes.

mentions.as_written: fins do primeiro quartel do seculo XIX

summary: Lourenço José Moniz and Manuel Caetano Pimenta de Aguiar sat as deputies for Madeira in the first constitutional Cortes; Aguiar proposed free export of Madeira wine.
Disturbances accompanied the change of institutions in Madeira.
Festivities in Funchal marked João VI taking the title of emperor of Brazil, with oil lanterns used for the first time at the town hall.
The chapel of Nossa Senhora da Fé at Porto da Cruz was founded by Diogo Dias de Orneias e Vasconcelos and licensed for worship on 11 August.
José Marciano da Silveira was born in Camacha.
Padre João Manuel de Freitas Branco was appointed professor of Latin grammar in Funchal.
The naturalist Ricardo Tomás Lowe resided in Madeira.
Joaquim Melchior Gonçalves returned from exile.
Sérvulo Drumond de Meneses was appointed judicial clerk.
Dr Joaquim de Menezes e Ataíde was made a peer of the realm.
Renton and Heineken made meteorological observations in Funchal; in 1826 Heineken measured Pico Ruivo at 1,850 m.
João da Silveira Caldeira published his annotated translation of Vauquelin's assayer's manual.
A French translation of Bowdich's work on Madeira was published in Paris.
Much more rain fell in Funchal than in other years.
Only one sugar mill remained on Madeira.
António de Gouveia Osório, later Visconde de Vila Mendo, was born at Vila Mendo.
The author of 'Rambles in Madeira' travelled in Madeira and Portugal and saw Maria Clementina, describing her fair hair and captivating expression.
The poet Monteiro Teixeira stayed a fortnight in São Vicente and wrote a satirical verse letter.
A brotherhood of Saint Barbara existed in Funchal to distribute alms to the needy.
An English visitor toured and described the Palheiro estate near Funchal.
The Funchal Câmara asked the governor to remove the ruined chapel of São Sebastião.
King João VI died.
D. Pedro IV granted the Constitutional Charter to the Portuguese monarchy.
Carlos Stuart was made Marquis of Angra by decree.
Francisco António de Freitas e Abreu was born in Ponta Delgada.
Funeral rites for João VI were held in Funchal.
News of the Constitutional Charter reached Madeira.
Soldiers of the absolutist 7th Infantry attacked constitutionalists celebrating the Charter at Manuel José da Silveira's house in Funchal.
The Constitutional Charter was solemnly proclaimed and sworn in Funchal under governor D. Manuel de Portugal e Castro, with festivities and illuminations.

mentions.as_written: 6, 7 e 8 de Agôsto do mesmo ano

summary: Funchal council sought the suspension of patrols by the absolutist 7th Infantry and its transfer, thanking the Regent D. Isabel Maria in November for ordering its departure.
Madeira elected its deputies to the Cortes under the Charter, including Lourenço José Moniz and Padre Caetano Alberto Soares.
Manuel Joaquim Gonçalves de Andrade was confirmed as bishop of São Paulo.
Carlos Stuart was created Count of Machico.
D. Jorge da Câmara Leme enlisted as a volunteer in infantry regiment no. 4.
Archduchess Leopoldina died in Rio de Janeiro.
The Sardinian consulate in Madeira was established.
An Azorean branch of the Vieira family arrived in Madeira.
The Rev. James Bulwer published twenty-six engravings of Madeira.
Dr Renton published a paper on Madeira's climate and pulmonary disease in the Edinburgh Medical and Surgical Journal.
A foreign author described the life-sized images of the Ash Wednesday procession (Procissão da Cinza).
The book Rambles in Madeira and in Portugal was published in London.
Nicolau Anastácio de Bettencourt joined the liberal academic battalion.
By this year the Chapel of São Sebastião had been demolished and a fountain built in the square.
Governor D. Manuel de Portugal e Castro was appointed viceroy of India.
Birth of the historian João Agostinho de Freitas, linked to Ponta do Sol parish.
Governor José Lúcio Travassos Valdez began building the Porto Novo fort.
The Conde de Bonfim (José Lúcio Travassos Valdez) served as governor and captain-general of Madeira.
A Brazilian vice-consulate was created in Madeira.
The newspaper O Funchalense Liberal first appeared on 3 February 1827, running to its seventeenth issue on 26 May 1827.
José Lúcio Travassos Valdez was appointed governor and captain-general of Madeira.
Vicente Gomes da Silva was born in Funchal.
The new governor José Lúcio Travassos Valdez arrived in Funchal to succeed D. Manuel de Portugal e Castro.
José Lúcio Travassos Valdez took office as governor in Funchal.
Governor Travassos Valdez wrote on the drawbacks of sending convicts to Madeira.
The botanist Frederico Holl collected plants in Madeira from June to August.
The newspaper A Flor do Oceano first appeared.
The newspaper O Defensor da Liberdade was published from 2 June 1827 to 26 April 1828.
Nicolau Caetano Bettencourt Pita was granted the rank of major as a military doctor.
The director of the Lancasterian School reported 275 pupils taught and 78 enrolled.
O Defensor da Liberdade denounced the conditions of the prison at the Largo da Sé in Funchal.
Father João Manuel de Freitas Branco became a member of the censorship board.
António João de França Bettencourt was born in Calheta.
D. Manuel Joaquim Gonçalves de Andrade was consecrated bishop.
The theft of the vessel containing the Eucharist from Prazeres church caused a sensation across Madeira.
António Gonçalves de Freitas was born in Ponta Delgada.
Under Governor José Maria Monteiro, Madeira's liberals suffered violent persecution.
Francisco Ferreira de Abreu was orphans' judge of the Machico captaincy.
D. Miguel's judicial commission (alçada) came to Madeira, indicting 216 liberals and freemasons and imprisoning 101; some, like Nery and Agrela, were sent to Lisbon, while others fled or hid.
Richard Thomas Lowe married Catarina Maria.

A Miguelist expedition under Colonel José António de Azevedo Lemos landed at Machico and occupied Madeira, proclaiming absolutism; Governor Valdez and liberal leaders took refuge aboard the British frigate Alligator.
Philip Barker Webb spent several months in Madeira studying its flora and forming botanical collections.
Captain-general José Maria Monteiro created the Voluntários Realistas Urbanos da Madeira.
Father João Crisóstomo Espínola de Macedo died at an advanced age.
Fleeing Miguelist persecution, liberals such as the Moniz family, Caetano Alberto Soares and António Gil Gomes left for Brazil, while Bettencourt went to England.
The political upheavals of 1828–1834 dispersed many Madeiran families and their genealogical records.
The Lancasterian school method was probably abandoned when its teacher left for America.
The Miguelist government abolished the Monte nursery.
A vice-consulate of the Two Sicilies was created in Madeira.
Four further issues of O Regedor were published.
Luiz Figueiroa de Albuquerque was born in Funchal.
O Regedor Filho ran for 24 issues from 14 February to 24 May 1828.
Alexandre Luiz da Cunha was sentenced to thirty days' prison for abuse of press freedom.
Severiano Alberto de Freitas Ferraz founded in Funchal the first sugar mill in Madeira since the collapse of the industry.
Illuminations were held to celebrate D. Miguel's arrival in Lisbon.
João Fortunato de Oliveira was born in Funchal.
The Duke of York, the first steamship to visit Funchal, arrived with many passengers and on 15 May landed over 400 at Porto Santo.

mentions.as_written: primeira quinzena do mês de Maio de 1828

summary: D. Miguel dissolved the Cortes, convened the three estates and was proclaimed absolute king, restoring absolutism.
D. Manuel de Portugal e Castro left Madeira, according to one statement.
News of D. Miguel's proclamation as absolute king reached Madeira.
José Maria Monteiro was appointed Miguelist governor of Madeira.
A Flor do Oceano, edited by Sérvulo Drumond de Meneses among others, was published from 22 June to 22 August 1828.
Governor Valdez solemnly proclaimed in Madeira the rights of D. Pedro IV and D. Maria.
Nicolau Caetano Bettencourt Pita signed the acclamation of D. Pedro IV and D. Maria at Angra.
The frigate Príncipe Real arrived at Funchal with the Miguelist governor José Maria Monteiro, whose landing Governor Travassos Valdez refused.
Enlistment began in Funchal for the liberal battalion of Voluntários Reais de D. Pedro.
The Bishop of Funchal, D. Francisco José Rodrigues de Andrade, issued a pastoral praising representative government and D. Pedro.
Fearing the political turmoil, the bishop left Madeira with many clergy.
The British corvette Alligator arrived at Madeira to protect British residents.
The future Visconde de Atouguia sailed to Madeira to help Governor Travassos Valdez resist the absolutists.
A royal letter appointed Francisco António Maciel Monteiro to hold an inquiry (alçada) in Madeira.
The Miguelist squadron under Henrique da Fonseca Prego appeared off Funchal.
Francisco Xavier Pereira da Silva arrived at Funchal from England to aid the liberal defence.
The Miguelist squadron bombarded Machico, landed troops there and occupied Madeira, entering Funchal unopposed on 23 August; the Forte de S. João Baptista fired on the brig Infante D. Sebastião.
After capitulating, Governor Travassos Valdez took refuge with his family aboard HMS Alligator, as did the Conde de Carvalhal.
D. Miguel was proclaimed in Madeira and José Maria Monteiro landed in Funchal and took office as Miguelist governor.
The two judges of the alçada landed in Funchal with the Miguelist fleet.
The alçada began its inquiry into Madeiran liberals.
The Alligator left Funchal and transferred Valdez and other liberal émigrés at sea to the brig Jane, bound for England.
By this date the alçada had imprisoned some 167 people, including 21 clergy.
In Lisbon the Bishop of Funchal issued a pastoral defending absolutism and D. Miguel.
The brig Jane reached Saint Ives with the Madeiran refugees.
Commander W. P. Canning of the Alligator drowned in the tank of an English merchant's quinta near Funchal.
A decree granted privileges to the Voluntários do Reino (royalist volunteers).
Dr Joaquim de Menezes e Ataíde died of plague in Gibraltar after fleeing Miguelist persecution.
João da Silveira Caldeira apparently took his own life.
Frei João José da Purificação was appointed preacher to the Funchal Municipal Council.
The yacht Bang Up called at Madeira and Porto Santo.
Famine struck Porto Santo, requiring relief supplies.
The court of the Juiz dos Resíduos e Capelas was still functioning in Madeira.
Illuminations were held for D. Miguel's recovery.
The old playhouse of the Comédia Velha in Funchal collapsed, leaving only its façade.
The Porto tribunal sentenced ten liberal defendants, including José Maria Martiniano da Fonseca, to death, and José Ferreira Pestana to perpetual exile.
Funchal Câmara ordered fines for those who failed their duties at the 1 May Bula da Santa Cruzada procession.
Madeiran liberal José Maria Martiniano da Fonseca and nine others were hanged in Praça Nova, Porto (one entry gives 9 May).
The Misericórdia buried Fonseca's head in its chapel.
João da Câmara Leme Homem de Vasconcelos, later Count of Canavial, was born in Funchal.
Francisco Joaquim de Sá Camelo Lampreia was born in Funchal.
Fonseca left Funchal on an American ship as emissary to the Porto junta, arriving in Porto on 13 July (dates as given, apparently inconsistent).
The 13th Infantry Regiment in Madeira mutinied after an outside officer was appointed acting commander.
Nicolau Anastácio de Bettencourt fought in the liberal victory at Praia, Terceira.
Soldiers rioted in Funchal after poisonings in the 13th regiment.
Two more liberals were executed in Porto, later counted among the Twelve Martyrs.
The church of Estreito de Câmara de Lobos was broken into and robbed of sacred vessels and silver and gold objects, a sacrilege later punished by seven executions.

mentions.as_written: Na noite de 6 para 7 de Novembro de 1829

summary: Dr João Francisco de Oliveira died in Lisbon.
Captain António Jacinto de Faria Andrade de Bettencourt asked the government for ownership of the Rabaçal waters.
The Sociedade da Nova Levada do Furado was organised as a joint-stock company.
The first volume of Joaquim José Ferreira de Freitas's Bibliotheca Histórica, Política e Diplomatica appeared in London.
Inácio Correia Drumond died.
Ayrshire dairy cows were introduced to Madeira between 1830 and 1840.
The ruined chapel of Nossa Senhora da Nazaré at Paredes, Arco da Calheta, was entirely rebuilt by António João Barbosa de Matos e Câmara.
Frederico Holl's list of Madeiran plants appeared in Flora oder Botanische Zeitung.
A Madeiran physician (cited in the entries on António de Luz Pita and Cândido Joaquim da Silva) received his doctorate in medicine at Montpellier.
The tower of the parish church of Arco da Calheta was built.
Joaquim de Oliveira Alvares lived in London.
The Junta da Justiça was still functioning in Madeira.
The first Azorean periodical appeared on Terceira, by which time eight had already been published in Funchal.
D. João Henriques Moniz was deported from Lisbon to Cape Verde.
The Reading Rooms library was established at the English Club in Funchal.
The second edition of James Clarke's book on climate and chronic disease was published in London.
Sir W. Jardin published his article on the birds of Madeira.
Dr Carlos Heineken died in Funchal.
The council treasurer was authorised to import two moios of pine seed.
The Relação of Lisbon sentenced the robbers of the Estreito de Câmara de Lobos church, six to death by garrotte and two to perpetual exile in Africa.
D. Álvaro da Costa de Sousa Macedo took office as the last listed governor and captain-general of Madeira, ending José Maria Monteiro's governorship; Monteiro left the island at the end of April.
Francisco Ferreira de Abreu was sentenced to three years' banishment from Madeira for liberalism.
Antero Drumond de Meneses was born in Funchal.
Outdoor Way of the Cross processions in Ponta do Sol ceased around this time.
Padre João Manuel de Freitas Branco died in Rio de Janeiro.
António Augusto Larica was born in Funchal.
Frei José de Jesus was appointed preacher to the Funchal Municipal Council.
José Anselmo Correia Henriques died in Lisbon.
A diocesan minor seminary operated in the São Bernardino convent buildings at Câmara de Lobos.
Dr António de Luz Pita received the doctorate in surgery in Paris.
Liberal constitutional principles were officially proclaimed in Funchal, according to the Elucidário's date.
João de Nóbrega Soares was born in Funchal.
Joaquim José Ferreira de Freitas died in London.
Governor D. Álvaro da Costa de Sousa Macedo wrote to the Count of Basto reporting that the Royalist Volunteers corps in Madeira had only one company.
The 2nd Count of Carvalhal was born in Funchal.
José Gonçalves de Aguiar was born in Câmara de Lobos.
Princess D. Maria Amélia, daughter of D. Pedro IV, was born in Paris.
José Luiz Brandão was appointed the last alcaide of Funchal.
The municipalities of Santana, Câmara de Lobos and Porto Moniz were created; Câmara de Lobos was not installed at the time.
Jacinto Augusto Camacho was promoted to ensign.
Robert Reid Kalley completed his medical degree.
Domingos António de Sousa Coutinho, Marquis of Funchal, died in London.
Governor Álvaro de Sousa de Macedo ordered the demolition of Funchal's Teatro Grande, which was pulled down in 1833.
F. de Assis Sousa Vaz's treatise on Madeira's climate and phthisis was published in Paris.
D. Júlia da Cunha died of cholera in Lisbon.
English committees ceased administering the pilgrims' house at Santo António da Serra.
Manuel Caetano Pimenta de Aguiar died of apoplexy in Lisbon.
A liberal expedition sent by D. Pedro IV under Mousinho de Albuquerque to take Madeira from the Miguelists failed to attack and turned to Porto Santo instead.

A constitutional force of 60 artillerymen from Terceira occupied Porto Santo and proclaimed D. Maria II, joined on 7 April by Admiral Sartorius and Mousinho de Albuquerque; it left for the Azores with 104 Madeiran volunteers in May.
During the blockade of Madeira, José António de Almada fled to the Queen's naval division.
A decree created the prefecture council.
Mouzinho de Albuquerque was named prefect, the first constitutional administrative authority of the archipelago.
A national judicial reform abolishing the corregedores was decreed, applied in Madeira only in 1835.
A decree created provincial general councils, which never functioned in Madeira.
A Miguelist party from Madeira proclaimed D. Miguel on Porto Santo and returned the same night.
D. Pedro's liberal army of 7,500 men, including Madeirans such as D. Jorge da Câmara Leme, landed at Mindelo.
Decrees definitively abolished the militias and ordenanças, ending the office of capitão-mor in Madeira.
A decree abolished the alcaidarias-mores of Funchal and Machico.
João Joaquim de Freitas was born in Machico.
The section of Rua da Ponte Nova towards Rua dos Ferreiros was opened in Funchal.
José António de Almada was promoted to sergeant.
The Fortaleza do Pico was renamed Forte de S. Miguel under the Miguelist government.
Dr António de Luz Pita tried to return home but stopped at Gibraltar because of the civil war.
António J. de Santa Marta Andaluz was born.
João Augusto de Ornelas was born in Estreito de Câmara de Lobos.
Henrique João Fernandes, one of the Madeiran Bravos do Mindelo, died in action at the Porto lines.
Cristovão Lomelino de Carvalho died at the Lisbon lines.
At the request of the juiz do povo, Funchal council had all Constitutional government documents publicly burned in the Largo da Sé on 4 October.
Constitutional (liberal) government was established in Madeira, bringing the island under mainland law, ending the old council arrangements, the militia and the white city flag.
Madeira became an administrative district like those of the mainland, no longer an overseas province, with civil and military government separated and Mousinho de Albuquerque as first prefect.
The prefect created police commissioners, parish commissioners and constables under the new liberal administration.
João António Pedroso introduced the tamarisk to Porto Santo.
The bálsamo (Mesembrianthemum edule) was introduced to Porto Santo.
Canon Jerónimo Álvares da Silva Pinheiro's exile in Brazil ended.
Juvenal Honório de Ornelas published his Paris medical thesis on post-partum haemorrhage.
Richard Thomas Lowe served as chaplain of the British church in Funchal.
J. A. Mason visited Madeira to treat a lung disease.
District heads began addressing councils and officials as senhoria.
Acúrsio Garcia Ramos was born on Terceira.
The Conde de Tojal served as deputy for Madeira.
Metal founding probably began in Madeira.
John Driver wrote his letters from Madeira.
A Flor do Oceano mentioned Manuel Carlos de Vasconcelos's lost manuscript.
The office of juiz do povo came to an end.
M. Raynold Brucker's article on the Chapel of Skulls appeared in the Musée des Familles.
Luís Monteiro was entrusted with a mission to the Portuguese legation in London.
The Sociedade Patriótica Madeirense existed in Funchal and published a pamphlet with a member's motion.
Ernst Haeckel was born.
The winter of 1834–35 in Funchal had more rainy days than usual, with fine persistent rain.
With the end of the civil wars, A Flor do Oceano, organ of the Madeiran Cartists, appeared.
Dr João António Monteiro died in Paris aged 65.
Lourenço José Moniz represented Madeira in parliament through successive legislatures, except 1842–45.
A popular uprising in Calheta spread to Arco da Calheta.
The Visconde de Atouguia was elected deputy for Madeira.
The Aljube prison in Funchal was still in existence.
All nine collegiate chapters of the diocese had been abolished shortly before 1834.
The Fortaleza do Pico regained its old name after the fall of the Miguelists.
At the end of 1834 the first Count of Carvalhal returned from exile to Madeira and ordered major repairs to the theatre.
Mousinho de Albuquerque served as deputy for Madeira.
The Bocage family returned to Madeira from Brazil.
João Agostinho Pereira de Agrela returned to Madeira.
The future Visconde de Atouguia was made full lecturer of the Naval Academy.
A decree set out who was to serve in the National Guard.
Bishop Francisco José Rodrigues de Andrade left Madeira for exile in Italy, accompanied by António Joaquim Gonçalves de Andrade and António Alexandrino de Vasconcelos.
A decree abolished the Casa dos Vinte e Quatro and the guild representation.
José António de Almada was wounded at the battle of Asseiceira.
The Convention of Évora Monte ended the Portuguese civil war.
A decree abolished the religious orders and convents; the Franciscan convent in Funchal was abandoned.
The liberal frigate D. Pedro began blockading Madeira, and the Miguelist governor refused to receive its envoy.
With the establishment of constitutional government in Madeira, Marceliano Ribeiro de Mendonça ended six years in hiding.
The schooner Amélia arrived at Madeira with news of the Convention of Évora-Monte.

The constitutional (liberal) government and Constitutional Charter were proclaimed in Funchal, peacefully in the town though with violence in some parishes, establishing liberal institutions in Madeira.
The Charter was sworn and D. Maria II acclaimed queen at the town hall of Funchal.
D. Maria II was again proclaimed queen on Porto Santo.
Bishop D. Francisco José Rodrigues de Andrade entrusted the diocese to the cathedral chapter and left for Italy the next day.
The last juiz de fora of Funchal, Manuel Cirilo Esperança Freire, ceased to serve, ending the office.
Januário Cardoso de Melo was appointed by decree provedor do concelho of Funchal.
