Legislation of 23 June 1834 placed the Funchal customs on the mainland footing, imposed taxes criticised as harmful to Madeira, blamed estufas for discrediting Madeira wine, and abolished the Junta da Real Fazenda in favour of an interim treasury commission.
Luiz da Silva Mousinho de Albuquerque was appointed prefect of Madeira by decree.
The Constitutional Municipal Commission of Funchal was elected to replace councillors appointed under the usurpation.
A riot against the new constitutional government broke out in Calheta and was put down by troops and marines.
Governor D. Álvaro da Costa de Sousa Macedo left Madeira for Lisbon, replaced by an interim government.
José Ferreira Pestana was appointed professor of mathematics at Coimbra.
An administrative commission was appointed for the Machico council after the constitutional restoration.
Infantry Regiment no. 5 was organised by decree for the defence of Madeira.
António Gil Gomes returned to Madeira after representative government was established.
Mousinho de Albuquerque arrived and took office as prefect and military governor of Madeira on 6 August 1834, governing until September 1835.
The Junta da Real Fazenda of Madeira ceased functioning.
Porto Santo was made a provedoria, with João de Santana e Vasconcelos Moniz de Bettencourt as its first provedor.
Januário Cardoso de Melo took office as first provedor of the municipality of Funchal.
After the civil war Madeira elected four deputies to the Cortes, among them José Liberato Freire de Carvalho for the 1834–36 session.
The prefect and military governor appointed a commission to enrol men in the National Guard in Madeira.
Queen D. Maria II made José António de Almada a knight of the Order of the Tower and Sword.
Governor Mousinho de Albuquerque appointed a new juiz de fora and corregedor in Madeira.
The first constitutional council of Machico was elected.
The Constitutional Municipal Commission of Funchal ended its functions.
The council agreed to pay the Misericórdia once for treating prostitutes with venereal disease.
António Alfredo was appointed temporal governor of the diocese of Funchal.
Prefect Mousinho de Albuquerque placed the Santa Casa da Misericórdia under a municipal administrative commission and approved a new regulation for it.
The second A Flor do Oceano, the first Madeiran newspaper after the constitutional government, was published from 1834 to 1840.
Mousinho de Albuquerque gave the Auxiliary Artillery corps a regulation of fifteen companies.
The orphan asylum (Asilo da Infância) opened in the São Lourenço palace in mid-December 1834.
Illuminations were held in Madeira for the marriage of D. Maria II, with national mourning suspended.
Construction of the Rabaçal levada began under Luís Mousinho de Albuquerque.

A new administrative organisation gave Madeira ten municipalities, creating among others Câmara de Lobos, Santana (including Porto da Cruz, over Machico's protests), Porto Moniz, São Vicente, Calheta and a reorganised Ponta do Sol; Funchal's limits were fixed at the end of the year and the district head became Civil Governor.
Provedores do concelho were renamed administradores do concelho and the first municipal administrators were appointed.
Manuel de la Quadra was born in Spain.
Mousinho de Albuquerque conceived the monumental bridge and road as a memorial to D. Pedro IV.
After the Funchal council sought leave on 12 June to demolish the remains of the Calhau church, the União market was built on its ruins.
James Wild made a survey of Madeira.
Manuel Júlio Tôrres Mangas was born in Funchal.
The Conde de Vargas de Bédmar made geological observations in Madeira, Porto Santo and the Azores.
Starting year of the list of juízes de direito in the Funchal comarcas.
The council requisitioned a bell from the dissolved São Francisco convent for the town clock.
Joaquim de Oliveira Alvares died in Paris aged 59.
Marceliano Ribeiro de Mendonça published his elements of Latin grammar.
D. João Henriques Moniz was appointed governor of the bishopric of Cape Verde.
About 40,000 people emigrated from Madeira, only half with passports.
D. Ana Mascarenhas e Ataíde presented a flag to the Funchal National Guard.
By prefect's decree Funchal lost its share of Ponta do Sol parish.
A prefect's alvará incorporated the Lombada dos Esmeraldos into Ponta do Sol.
João Agostinho Pereira de Agrela died.
A decree substantially modified the 1834 doctrine on wine estufas.
A portaria ordered the formation of a National Guard caçadores battalion in Madeira.
O Liberal, co-edited by Nicolau Caetano Bettencourt Pita, began publication in Angra.
A law gave parish juntas the apportionment of the quinto tax.
The Câmara began supplying food directly to the São Lázaro hospital.
A law abolished the ordinary judges.
The prefect dissolved the liquidating commission of the Santa Casa da Misericórdia.
Diocesan governor António Alfredo de Santa Catarina Braga had the statue of Frei Pedro da Guarda publicly burnt at São Bernardino and next day published a provision forbidding his cult.
After the abolition of the Machico Misericórdia brotherhood, the civil governor appointed an administrative commission.
The Junta da Fazenda ceased handling Madeira's public funds, which passed to a receiver-general, first Francisco Correia Herédia.
Governor Mousinho de Albuquerque appointed a commission, including João Shortridge, to organise the Associação Comercial of Funchal.
A law established the district general councils (juntas gerais).
A decree replaced the prefect with a civil governor.
A decree created parish councils in the Madeira archipelago.
The Visconde de Atouguia became minister of the navy.
The prefect's order arranged municipal elections, including in the new councils.
João José Xavier de Carvalhal was created Count of Carvalhal.
The Count of Carvalhal was appointed civil governor of Madeira by royal letter.
Alexandre Luiz da Cunha was appointed professor of French and English in Funchal.
Mousinho de Albuquerque left the civil government of Madeira, remaining only military governor until 8 November 1835.
The first municipal elections under the liberal regime were held peacefully across the archipelago.
Municipal elections were held throughout the Madeiran archipelago.
Alberto de Oliveira was appointed the first administrator of the municipality of Machico.
The first thirteen members of the Junta Geral were elected in the town hall.
The 1832 judicial reform took effect in Madeira, ending the old regime of corregedores and installing two julgados with juízes de direito in Funchal.
The municipality of Câmara de Lobos was definitively installed.
The municipality of Porto Moniz, created in 1835, was formally installed.
Felisberto de Betencourt Miranda was appointed clerk of the municipal secretariat.
The Funchal council ordered the pillory demolished as an emblem of feudal times.
Luiz da Silva Mousinho de Albuquerque left Madeira for Lisbon to take up a ministerial post.
The office of district receiver replaced that of receiver-general.
Under the 1835 administrative reform Porto Santo became a concelho, with João José de Alencastre as its first administrator.
The Funchal council demolished the remaining ruins of the Calhau church and built the Mercado União on the site.
António de Gamboa e Liz was appointed civil governor of Funchal district by decree.
D. Manuel Agostinho Barreto was born.
José Carlos de Faria e Castro was born in Santa Maria Maior, Funchal.
The Funchal council asked the municipal administrator to watch for and remove prostitutes from the central streets.
The São Roque cemetery, Funchal's oldest Catholic cemetery, was built and work began on the Angústias cemetery.
The Administrative Code created the district council and abolished the prefecture council.
E. Maurice's article on the discovery of Madeira appeared in volume IV of the Musée des Familles.
The Administrator General ordered the Marquês de Castelo Melhor to be assessed for the redízima.
In early 1836 part of the churchyard of São João Evangelista was demolished to create the Largo do Colégio in Funchal.
Prisoners were returned from the São Francisco convent to the prison house in the Largo da Sé.
The Visconde de Atouguia was appointed civil governor of Porto.
The Liceu do Funchal was founded, with Marceliano Ribeiro de Mendonça on its teaching staff.
Justino António de Freitas completed his law degree at Coimbra.
The Funchal municipal council demolished the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Piedade in the Largo da Igrejinha.
D. Luís da Câmara Leme enlisted in the army.
The 9th Military Division was created in Madeira.
The Junta Geral apparently held its only extraordinary meeting.
Of the eleven city gates remaining in Funchal in 1836, several were demolished between 1836 and 1839.
The Calheta rioters were tried; seven were sentenced to perpetual exile in Angola and a priest to Mozambique.
The officers of the National Guard battalion were elected at a meeting in the Praça da Constituição, Funchal.
An order granted a house in the Campo da Barca to the Asilo da Infância.
The Funchal Commercial Association was formally installed and its first board elected.
António Policarpo dos Passos Sousa was born at Madalena do Mar.
Funchal council ordered the demolition of the chapel of Santo António in Rua da Laranjeira.
The victims' remains were exhumed and reburied in an urn in the Misericórdia church.
The government granted 1:000$000 réis to the Funchal Misericórdia for treating venereal disease.
The Clube União, one of Funchal's first recreational clubs, was founded.
A royal letter approved the first statutes of the Funchal Commercial Association.
Agostinho de Ornelas de Vasconcelos was born in Funchal.
Pedro Maria Gonçalves de Freitas, later Visconde de Gonçalves de Freitas, was born in Madeira.
António de Gamboa e Liz took office as civil governor in Funchal.
Father Armando Augusto de Pontes was born in Funchal.
The parish of Água de Pena was suppressed and annexed to Santo da Serra, forming the parish of Santo da Serra e Água de Pena.
João da Câmara de Carvalhal offered land to enlarge the Angústias cemetery.
Manuel José Vieira was born in Funchal.
The Câmara ordered the first bridge over the Ribeira de Santa Luzia near the fish market.
Following the political events of September 1836, the head of the archipelago's government took the title of Administrador Geral, held by Luís da Silva Mousinho de Albuquerque.

The September Revolution in Portugal overturned the Constitutional Charter and the queen swore the restored Constitution of 1820, so the newly elected Cortes never met; in Madeira it passed without notable hostilities.
The restored Constitution of 1820 was solemnly sworn in Madeira.
The governor of the bishopric separated Jardim do Mar from its dependence on Paul do Mar.
A decree established mortgage registers in municipal administrations.
A decree created a lyceum in each district capital.
Boaventura was raised to an independent parish, separated from Ponta Delgada.
Issue 108 ended the continuous numbering of the second A Flor do Oceano; later numbering was annual.
A decree created medical-surgical schools in overseas district capitals, including Funchal.
The boganga (Cucurbita melanosperma) was introduced to Madeira from Tenerife.
An administrative reform renamed district governors administradores gerais.
Period covered by the published minutes of the Funchal District General Council.
Dr José Manuel da Veiga published his Código Penal da Nação Portuguesa.
By this year one cane in Funchal's arms had been replaced by a vine branch.
João Joaquim Figueira graduated in medicine at Montpellier.
The Canary pine was introduced to Madeira from Tenerife.
A memoir on the geology of Madeira, Porto Santo and the Desertas was published in Lisbon.
Funchal council began a municipal fire service, buying a pump from London for 460$000 réis.
Funchal municipal revenue was estimated at 35.678$00.
The Judicial Reform of 1837 created elected parish judges and restored ordinary judges.
Funchal council left its Largo da Sé building because of the stench of the prisons, which held 180 prisoners.
The wooden building known as the Vapor was built over the Santa Luzia stream.
The Funchal academy staged a performance celebrating Queen Maria II's marriage, whose proceeds built the Praça Académica.
An edition of John Atkins's voyage was published in London.
The government ceded a house in Campo da Barca to the Sociedade das Escolas Infantis.
Gregório Nazianzeno Medina e Vasconcelos served as deputy for Madeira.
Funchal council supplied copies of Oudinot's Instructions to the parish councils.
The Gabinete Português de Leitura was founded in Rio de Janeiro by the Portuguese community.
The English botanist Carlos Lemann arrived in Madeira.
Queen Adelaide was widowed on the death of William IV.
A further decree regulated mortgage and other registers.
A decree assigned the São Francisco convent grounds in Funchal as a nursery, apparently without result.
The council again showed interest in afforesting the serras and commons.
António de Pádua da Costa commanded the 9th Military Division.
Jaime Moniz was born in Funchal.
César Augusto Mourão Pita was born in Lisbon.
Justino António de Freitas took his doctorate in law.
Pedro de Castelo Branco was born in Funchal.
The Medical-Surgical School of Funchal was installed on 2 May 1837 at the Santa Isabel hospital, replacing the former British Infirmary; it operated until 1910.
An ordinance barred north-coast wines of Madeira from passing to the southern parishes.
João Baptista de Freitas Leal was born in Funchal.
Januário Justiniano de Nóbrega was appointed amanuensis of the municipal administration.
The Junta Geral of the Funchal district held its first ordinary session, opening on 15 July and closing on 25 August 1837 after eighteen meetings.
Funchal council began building the Casa das Angústias, intended as a municipal beggars' asylum.
Aires de Ornelas de Vasconcelos was born in Funchal.
The Funchal lyceum was created and solemnly opened on 10 October 1837, installed in the former Jesuit college buildings (Aulas do Pátio); seminarians attended its classes.
The 1st Count of Carvalhal died at the Quinta do Palheiro.
José Dias Ferreira was born.
Alípio Augusto Ferreira was born in Santa Cruz.
The Angústias cemetery in Funchal and the Porto Santo cemetery were completed.
The Porto Santo cemetery beside the chapel of Santa Catarina was opened on Corpus Christi day.
Domingos Olavo Correia de Azevedo served as substitute deputy and senator for Madeira in the 1838–1840 legislative session.
The Marquis of Saldanha sat as senator for Madeira in the 1838–1840 legislative session.
Jacob Ruffy and Diogo Taylor established the first coal depot in Funchal.
The Funchal council petitioned the government against the poor administration of António de Gamboa e Liz.
Padre Drumond e Vasconcelos began spelling the parish name Tábua instead of Atabua.
John Driver's 'Letters from Madeira in 1834' was published in London.
José de Freitas Teixeira Spinola de Castelo Branco published Noções de calculo differencial.
The Barão de Lordelo, as civil governor, tried to continue the works on the monumental road and bridge.
The German botanist Dr Lippold botanised in Madeira, studying among others the plants of the Quinta do Vale.
Royal Mail steamers were already calling at Madeira.
William Hinton came to Madeira for health reasons.
The chapel of Nossa Senhora da Penha de França returned to the possession of the bishops.
Dr Patrício Moniz published the verse collection Meditações Nocturnas.
The Funchal council requested the old fountain's basins from the Administrador Geral for the fountain of the Largo de São Sebastião.
The Sociedade Harmonia existed in Funchal, promoting musical gatherings.
The last known performance took place at the Teatro de Bom Gosto.
Rafael Coelho Machado left Madeira for Brazil.
The office of parish regedor was introduced in Madeira.
A government order authorised the Funchal council to demolish the city gate at Saúde and widen the street.
The Funchal council resolved, on the initiative of Sérvulo Drumond de Meneses, to create the Municipal Library.
Júlio Augusto Henriques was born at Cabeceiras de Basto.
A law created municipal guards in district capitals, which A Chronica wanted extended to Madeira.
The first issue of the newspaper A Chronica appeared.
Félix de Brito Capelo was born in Peniche.
Francisco de Andrade was appointed interim teacher at the Funchal lyceum.
A Chronica stated that Madeirans had remained united and law-abiding.
João Gualberto de Oliveira was created Baron of Tojal.
A new decree enforced the 1805 annexation of the posts.
José da Fonseca e Gouveia was appointed Administrator General of the Funchal district by decree of 28 April 1838 and took office on 14 September.
Construction of the new municipal cemetery of the Angústias was completed.
D. Francisco José Rodrigues de Andrade died in exile at Promontorio, Genoa.
The Constitution of 1838 was solemnly sworn in Madeira.
The two julgados were converted into the eastern and western comarcas, both seated in Funchal.
Dr Carlos Lemann left Madeira for London.
The juízes ordinários of the newly created julgados were elected.
The central government praised the Funchal council's plan for a children's asylum.
Francisco Ferreira de Abreu was appointed mortgage-registry notary of the western comarca.
The Angústias cemetery in Funchal was solemnly blessed.
The American geologist J. D. Dana visited Madeira.
Francisco de Andrade was appointed permanent professor of Portuguese and Latin grammar at the Funchal lyceum.
Alexandre Luiz da Cunha was appointed by decree to a professorship at the Funchal lyceum.
A decree made the first staff appointments of the Funchal Medical-Surgical School definitive.
Wilkes's American Exploring Expedition visited Madeira and its officers measured Pico Ruivo at 1,901 m.
Lippold published a note on Dr Renton's Madeira gardens in Gardner's Magazine.
Robert Reid Kalley arrived in Funchal on 2 October 1838, beginning a Protestant proselytising campaign in Madeira that lasted until 1846.
José da Fonseca e Gouveia was created Baron of Lordelo.
The administrative commission of the Misericórdia was discharged and an interim one appointed.
The Funchal municipal council sent the municipal administrator its nominations for the parish regedores.
The Municipal Library of Funchal opened to the public.
The British Factory in Madeira was dissolved.
Several sections and gates of the Funchal city wall were demolished.
José Joaquim de Abreu Rego graduated in mathematics at Coimbra with the highest marks.
Paulo Perestrelo da Câmara published Descripção Geral de Lisboa.
A signalling telegraph operated at Garajau from 1839 to 1847.
The União market was enclosed with an iron gallery with three gates.
José Maria Smith Barruncho was born in Funchal.
William Hinton married Mary Wallas.
Dr Patrício Moniz published Composições poéticas, dedicated to his father.
Luís Alexandre Ribeiro Mendonça, later Baron of Úzel, was born in Funchal.
The Praça da Rainha was built on land formerly used by the Trem Militar for boats and anchors.
D. Filomena, later 1st Countess of Torre Bela, was born in Berlin.
José Vicente Barbosa du Bocage enrolled at the University of Coimbra.
Dr James Macaulay spent part of 1839 and 1840 in Madeira.
The parish cemetery of Santo António was built.
Francisco António Rodrigues da Silva was appointed keeper of the Angústias cemetery.
The Funchal council put the Entrada da Cidade works out to tender on 8 February 1839 and awarded the contract on 22 February; the Porto da Saúde gate was demolished to build the street.
The works for the Praça de São Pedro (fish market) were put out to tender on 8 February 1839, contracted on 22 February, and alterations contracted on 17 August.
Daniel de Ornelas was elected senator for Madeira to fill a vacancy.
Azevedo and Soulier de Sauve measured a magnetic inclination of 59° 30' in the Praça Académica, Funchal.
João Maneio Teixeira was born in Madeira.
The Funchal council resolved to establish annual and weekly fairs, a decision never carried out.
A law imposed a third on municipal levies, later waived for cereals during the famine.
The council again discussed afforestation of the serras and commons.
Sir James Clark Ross's expedition with HMS Erebus and Terror visited Madeira and its officers measured Pico Ruivo at 1,858 and 1,860 m.
The Junta Geral was ordered to draw up regulations for the levadas.
The Clube Funchalense was installed in Funchal.
João Gomes do Espírito Santo died in Porto aged about eighty.
The last issue (no. 96) of the newspaper A Chronica appeared.
The Santa Luzia cemetery was established in Funchal.
James Clark Ross led the Erebus and Terror expedition in Antarctic seas.
The Instituição Filosófica e Mecânica, a society for the scientific study of Madeira, was founded in Funchal.
A concert society directed by António Maria Frutuoso da Silva existed in Funchal.
William White Cooper's 'The Invalid's Guide to Madeira' was published in London.
Over twenty British commercial houses existed in Funchal.
Luís Vicente de Afonseca was first elected deputy for Madeira, beginning a 34-year parliamentary career.
James Smith's paper on Madeiran geology appeared in the Proceedings of the Geological Society.
Madeiran stamped paper began to carry a Funchal government overprint.
José Joaquim de Sena Freitas was born on São Miguel.
D. João Henriques Moniz was elected substitute senator for Madeira.
Justino António de Freitas joined the Coimbra law faculty as substitute lecturer.
The first doctors graduated from the Funchal Medical-Surgical School.
The only issue of The Stranger, an English-language newspaper, was published in Funchal.
The first issue of the newspaper O Defensor appeared in Funchal.
Michael Grabham was born.
A decree relieved António Alfredo of the government of the Funchal diocese.
Januário Vicente Camacho was appointed governor of the diocese of Funchal by decree.
Eduardo Ernesto de Castelo Branco was born in Funchal.
The statutes of the Sociedade da Nova Levada do Furado were approved.
Januário Vicente Camacho was elected capitular vicar of Funchal.
António Alfredo left Madeira for Lisbon.
The first newspaper O Imparcial was published in Funchal, issuing 300 numbers until June 1846.
Sebastião Xavier Botelho died.
Alfredo César de Oliveira was born in Santa Cruz.
The Praça de São Pedro fish market in Funchal was formally opened.
The French frigates La Belle Poule and La Favorite, carrying the Prince of Joinville's mission to recover Napoleon's remains from Saint Helena, stayed at Funchal.
James Macaulay's notes on Madeira appeared in the Edinburgh New Philosophical Journal.
Mary Jane Wilson was born in Madras.
The first issue of the newspaper Chronica appeared.
A Chronica Official was published, producing six issues.

mentions.as_written: 7 de Novembro a 12 de Dezembro de 1840

summary: José da Fonseca e Gouveia, barão de Lordelo, was dismissed at his own request by decree.
The poet António Feliciano de Castilho arrived in Funchal with his sick brother aboard the brig-schooner Funchal and lived in the Penha house until January 1841.

mentions.as_written: De 27 de Novembro de 1840 a 9 de Janeiro de 1841

summary: The Prazer Regenerado theatre opened in the former São Francisco convent in Funchal.
Joaquim Pestana was born in Câmara de Lobos.
Canon Augusto Frederico de Castilho, brother of the poet, died of tuberculosis in Funchal.
The hermitage of Sant'Ana at Fajã do Penedo, Boaventura, was demolished shortly after 1840.
The American Isabella vine was introduced to Madeira shortly after 1840.
The abundância (Eupatorium adenophorum) was introduced to Madeira as an ornamental plant shortly before 1840.
Henrique Félix Freitas Vale was born in Funchal.
The geologist James Smith visited Madeira.
Large-scale Madeiran emigration to Demerara and the British West Indies began.
The São Gonçalo cemetery was established.
Paulo Perestrelo da Câmara sailed for Brazil and published Breve Noticia sobre a Ilha da Madeira in Lisbon.
Manuel de Arriaga was born in Horta.
Diogo d'Ornelas Frazão issued tokens for his sugar mill at Calheta.
Arthur Bertrand published his book in Paris.
The present fountain at the Fontes de João Diniz was built.
Azurara's Crónica da Guiné was first published in Paris by the Visconde de Santarém.
The Santana municipal council printed its by-laws as a pamphlet.
William Hinton settled permanently in Madeira.
Dr. Lourenço José Moniz served as vice-president (later president) of the Chamber of Deputies.
Dr. Kampfer stayed in Madeira.
The Tribunal Secreto apparently first appeared.
Agostinho Martins was born.
D. João Henriques Moniz was nominated bishop of Cape Verde.
António Feliciano de Castilho left Madeira.
Domingos Olavo Correia de Azevedo was appointed Administrador Geral (civil governor) of Madeira by decree of 26 March 1841 and took office on 2 April.
Funchal council created boys' schools in São Roque, São Martinho and São Gonçalo.
Francisco Ferreira de Abreu was appointed clerk of the Funchal municipal administration.
Ships of a commercial expedition to West Africa, with Dr. George Tams, called at Porto Santo.
Served as Minister of the Navy.
Funchal council resolved to move the prison to the Angústias house, but the Government refused.
The British brig Savage entered Funchal bay demanding the return of the seized vessel Bernarda, which the authorities refused.
José Leite Monteiro was born in Porto.
A law declared Madeira's special legislation on levada waters and woodland to remain in force.
João Bettencourt Araújo Carvalhal Esmeraldo, future Count of Ribeiro Real, was born in Funchal.
Francisco Ferreira de Abreu died in Cabo Verde.
Bartolomeu dos Mártires Dias e Sousa served as deputy for Madeira.
João da Câmara Carvalhal Esmeraldo was elected deputy for Madeira.
Francisco Correia Herédia served as deputy for the Funchal district.
Indirect election of deputies was restored.
Captain A. T. E. Vidal aboard HMS Styx, with António Pedro de Azevedo, surveyed Madeira, Porto Santo and the Desertas.
The Calheta municipal council printed its by-laws as a pamphlet.
The American John A. Dix stayed in Madeira and described the palanquin.
The Madeiran copper coinage Pecunia Madeirensis, bearing two vine branches, was first issued in 1842, with further issues in 1850 and 1852.
The Scottish church opened in a house in Travessa do Surdo, Funchal.
The British government began paying emigrants' passages to its colonies.
João de Freitas da Silva was born in Lisbon.
Andrew Picken's 'Madeira illustrated' was published in London.
The Asilo dos Inválidos was established in the Misericórdia building in Funchal.
Rafael Coelho Machado published his music method and Diccionario musical in Rio de Janeiro.
The 1826 Constitutional Charter was restored, ending the Constitution of 1838; in Madeira the title of civil governor was reinstated.
The newspaper O Beija Flôr ran from its first to its last issue.
Patrício Malheiro de Melo died in Caniço.
A treaty abolished the British right to a conservator judge, providing mixed juries instead.
João José de Freitas Aragão died in Lisbon.

A terrible flood struck Funchal, damaging the council house on the Largo do Pelourinho, followed by a harbour storm wrecking boats; it led to the Central Relief Committee and to part of the Machico wall.
Magnetic variation on Porto Santo was recorded as 24°38'12".
The dwarf banana began to be cultivated in Madeira.
Maurício José de Castelo Branco was born in Funchal.
The Concórdia society built a small theatre in Rua do Monteiro, Funchal.
Manuel António Rodrigues Leitão, Visconde de Cacongo, was born at Ponte da Barca.
The Conde de Tojal took his seat as a peer of the realm.
José de Freitas Teixeira Spínola de Castelo Branco published Elementos de algebra superior.
Matias Figueira da Silva was born in Funchal.
The first instituted vicar of Boaventura parish was appointed.
Captain Vidal's charts were published, including a chart of Madeira, Porto Santo and the Desertas and 'Funchal Bay' with a plan of the city.
The course of the Funchal Medical-Surgical School was extended to four years.
Arsénio Pompílio Pompeu do Carpo published the poetry collection Dedo de Pigmeu in Lisbon.
Feliciano João Teixeira was born in Ponta do Sol.
A new regulation for the Misericórdias was provisionally approved.
A storm felled the largest recorded Madeiran dragon tree, at Pontinha de Cima in Machico.
Luís de Ornelas Pinto Coelho was born in São Pedro parish, Funchal.
José António de Almada was born in Machico.
Henrique de Lima e Cunha was born in Barreiro.
Funchal council resolved to build a stone quay at the Entrada da Cidade and the District Council authorised the expenditure; construction began but was never finished.
José Júlio Rodrigues was born in Funchal.
A law authorised the government to alter municipal boundaries, leading to parts of Água de Pena and Santo António da Serra passing to Santa Cruz.
D. José Xavier de Cerveira e Sousa was confirmed as bishop of Funchal.
João da Silveira Caldeira's Nova nomenclatura was printed in Rio de Janeiro.
Work on the Rabaçal levada was interrupted.
The frigate Diana, commanded by Francisco Maria Bordalo, brought several political deportees to Madeira.
According to Duncan Maclaren, 250 foreigners, including invalids with their companions and servants, visited Madeira in the 1844–45 season.
Dean António Joaquim Gonçalves de Andrade was recalled to Madeira by Bishop Cerveira e Sousa.
The second edition of John Osborne's guide was published in London.
The bell tower of the parish church of Machico was demolished as it threatened ruin.
The hospital regulation first provided secure rooms for the insane.
Captain Vidal and engineer António Pedro de Azevedo measured the height of Pico Ruivo.
The clandestine anti-Cabralist paper Tribunal Secreto appeared in Funchal; its twelve known issues date from this year.
Francisco de Andrade's Princípios de Gramática Portuguesa was published in Funchal.
The chapel of the Angústias cemetery in Funchal was built and was blessed by Bishop Cerveira e Sousa on 15 December 1844.
D. João Henriques Moniz received episcopal consecration in Lisbon.
Public disorder and arrests in Santo António da Serra were linked to Robert Reid Kalley's Protestant preaching.
Luís da Costa Pereira graduated in mathematics at Coimbra.
The Count de Montalembert stayed in Madeira for his wife's health.

mentions.as_written: desde 26 de Janeiro a 4 de Março de 1844

summary: A revolt broke out at Torres Vedras against the Costa Cabral government, leading to deportations to Madeira.
Funchal council rejected a proposed commission to direct the quay works.
The civil governor appointed a commission to propose an asylum for beggars in Funchal, which was never realised.
João da Câmara Carvalhal Esmeraldo died.
José Bettencourt da Câmara was born at the Quinta do Descanso.
Political prisoners from the Torres Vedras revolt reached Funchal aboard the brig Douro on 20 April and the cutter Andorinha on 28 April.
The Rev. J. M. Neale's paper on the ecclesiology and Gothic churches of Madeira was read before the Cambridge Camden Society.
Dr Manuel da Assunção was born in Vila Real.
D. José Xavier de Cerveira e Sousa received episcopal consecration.
The new bishop, D. José Xavier de Cerveira e Sousa, arrived in Madeira, ending a ten-year vacancy of the see.
Sérvulo de Paula Medina e Vasconcelos's drama Amor e Pátria was performed at the Teatro Concórdia in Funchal.
Platão de Vaksel was born near Petrograd.
João Gualberto de Oliveira was created Count of Tojal.
A plague of Decticus albifrons locusts devastated crops and foliage on Madeira and Porto Santo.
Duncan Maclaren stayed in Madeira from October 1844 until the summer of 1845.

mentions.as_written: de Outubro de 1844 até o verão de 1845

summary: João José Vieira was born in Funchal.
A military reorganisation made the Madeira archipelago an autonomous Command under a colonel.
A decree ceded the land and building of the São Francisco convent in Funchal to the council, for law courts; the site later became the Municipal Garden.
Nicolau Anastácio de Bettencourt became civil governor of Angra do Heroísmo.
The government approved Nathaniel Lister's donation condition for the Medical School library in Funchal.
William Reid arrived in Madeira and established a hotel in Funchal.
George Tams published his account of the expedition in Hamburg.
The English poet T. M. Hughes visited Madeira, and his poem The Ocean Flower was published in London.
Dr Schmeller published in Munich a memoir on the manuscripts collected by Valentim Fernandes.
Daniel Ferreira Pestana accompanied his uncle to India as aide-de-camp.
The post of municipal librarian was created in Funchal.
Father Júlio César Pereira da Silva was born in Madeira.
Jane Wallas Penfold's botanical book on Madeira was published in London.
A small landing stage was built on the rocky spit in Santa Cruz bay.
There were 293 British residents in Funchal.
British visitors to Madeira averaged 342 a year between 1845 and 1855.
M. Knowler visited Madeira and gave six lectures on dramatic poetry in Funchal.
Carlos Stuart, Count of Machico, died.
Powdery mildew of the vine was first recorded in a garden in England.
Sérvulo de Paula Medina e Vasconcelos published Amor e Pátria and left for Cape Verde as a civil servant.
Manuel José Júlio Guerra Júnior was born in Funchal.
The entire-leaved (cordifolia) sweet potato was first cultivated in Madeira, from Demerara stock.
A second resolution to move Funchal's prison to the Angústias house was passed but not carried out.
Ernesto João Schmitz was born in Rheydt.
Dr Robert Reid Kalley visited England and met leaders of Bible societies.
Father Carlos Acciaioly was born in Santana.
Maurício Augusto de Sequeira was born in Funchal.
Dr Luiz Henriques died by suicide in Funchal from an opium overdose.
João Augusto Teixeira was born at Ponta do Sol.
Daniel de Ornelas e Vasconcelos was created Baron of São Pedro.
Joaquim Pedro Cardoso Casado Giraldes died in Genoa, where he was Portuguese consul.
João da Silva Carvalho founded his first school in Funchal.
Bartolomeu dos Mártires Dias e Sousa again sat as deputy for Madeira.
Under civil governor José Silvestre Ribeiro the planting of maritime pine in Madeira greatly increased.
António Joaquim Gonçalves de Andrade was appointed vicar-general.
João Nepomuceno de Oliveira died.
Tito Omboni's Viaggi nell'Africa Occidentale was published in Milan.
The title of Governador Civil was restored.

The Maria da Fonte popular revolt broke out in the Minho, sparking a revolutionary movement in Portugal; Justino António de Freitas joined its provisional government and António Alves da Silva interrupted his Coimbra studies.
Civil governor José Silvestre Ribeiro visited Curral das Freiras and found only the priest and the regedor literate.
Luiz da Silva Mousinho de Albuquerque died of a wound received at Torres Vedras.
Arsénio Pompílio Pompeu do Carpo was brought prisoner to São Jorge castle in Lisbon on serious charges but freed himself.
Francisco Clementino de Sousa was born in Funchal.
The Funchal market was reopened.
Alexandre Alberto da Rocha Serpa Pinto was born.
Prince Frederick Charles Christian of Denmark stayed in Funchal and gave a gala dinner aboard his frigate.
The Funchal municipal council was dissolved following the Maria da Fonte revolution.
The newspaper O Echo da Revolução appeared in Funchal after the Patuleia insurrection, publishing 31 issues.

mentions.as_written: 27 de Junho de 1846 a 23 de Janeiro de 1847

summary: Popular riots against Robert Reid Kalley's Protestant propaganda culminated in a crowd sacking his house in Funchal, forcing his hurried flight from Madeira.
The first newspaper O Independente ran in Funchal, issuing 36 numbers.
António José de Ávila was appointed by decree royal commissioner with discretionary powers for Madeira.
Royal commissioner António José de Ávila left Lisbon with José Silvestre Ribeiro, the new civil governor, arriving in Madeira on 12 September.
A decree replaced the office of district receiver with that of contador de fazenda, taking effect in Madeira on 28 November.
Ávila suspended the interim civil governor and the administrator of Funchal municipality.

Madeira suffered the 'year of hunger', a famine caused by potato disease amid agricultural and commercial crisis, killing a large part of the population; João Howard March helped organise relief subscriptions.
José Silvestre Ribeiro ordered an inventory of the silver of the São Lourenço chapel, weighing 36 pounds.
José Silvestre Ribeiro took office as civil governor of the Funchal district on 7 October 1846, serving until 1852 and reviving projects such as the Ribeiro Seco bridge.
A law dissolved the national guards.
Ávila left Madeira for Lisbon.
A meeting of authorities approved advancing 1,500$000 réis for clearing ribeiras to employ the poor during the famine.
José Silvestre Ribeiro ordered the first public lamps placed in central Funchal.
The council resolved to build a shelter for travellers and beasts beside Monte church.
Luís Maria dos Reis was born.
A. P. de Azevedo and officers of the Rattermaker measured a magnetic inclination of 60° 40' at the Colégio in Funchal.
The loquat was introduced to Madeira.
Levada works advanced notably under the governorship of José Silvestre Ribeiro.

Madeira suffered a severe famine, peaking in February 1847, with high mortality from digestive illness; it also reached Porto Santo. The governor José Silvestre Ribeiro took relief measures, merchants raised funds for food and charity performances were held in Funchal.
Laureano da Câmara Falcão developed maize cultivation in Santana and São Jorge using Azorean farmers.
The Fonte Vermelha drinking fountain was built.
Maria Helena Jervis de Atouguia e Almeida was born in Funchal.
José de Freitas Teixeira Spinola de Castelo Branco published Applicação da algebra à geometria.
William Hooker's Notes on Madeira Plants appeared in the Journal of Botany.
The first cane-brandy distillery was set up in Câmara de Lobos.
Walls were built along the Santa Luzia and João Gomes streams in Funchal.
Dr Kampfer published notes on Madeira in the Zeitschrift für die gesammte Medizin.
A Portuguese warship was stationed off Madeira to curb clandestine emigration.
José Silvestre Ribeiro, as governor, had the ruined church of São João Evangelista restored to worship.
A government decree authorised ceding land from the former Jesuit college enclosure to widen Rua do Castanheiro.
The first issue of the newspaper O Madeirense appeared.

The Funchal Beggars' Asylum was founded in a state warehouse; about 400 inmates moved in procession to the former São Francisco convent on 27 March, and it was definitively installed in the Casa das Angústias on 8 December.
José Silvestre Ribeiro proposed moving the prison to the former São Francisco convent.

Linked to the Maria da Fonte movement, Infantry no. 11 and Artillery no. 4 with the Funchal council pronounced for the Junta do Porto and installed a Junta Governativa da Madeira, with António Correia Herédia as secretary, which ruled until 14 July 1847.
O Boletim Official was published, without issue numbers.

mentions.as_written: de 3 de Maio a 27 de Junho de 1847

summary: The last issue of O Defensor appeared.
Bishop D. Manuel Joaquim Gonçalves de Andrade died.

The British frigate Thetis arrived at Funchal demanding the junta's dissolution; the junta dissolved itself on 14 July and British and French commanders restored José Silvestre Ribeiro as civil governor on 26 July.
D. João Henriques Moniz died of fever in Cape Verde, months after arriving there in February 1847.
Only three issues of the first O Funchalense appeared.
Dr José Joaquim de Abreu Rego died in Funchal aged little over 30.
The warship D. Luiz brought the Caçadores no. 6 battalion to Funchal.
António de Pádua da Costa resumed command of the 9th Military Division.
The Duke of Palmela returned to Madeira with his wife, who was seriously ill with lung disease.
T. Vernon Wollaston made his first visit to the Madeira archipelago.
A. T. E. Vidal's survey of the islands was published in London.
Jacinto Pinto Coelho was born in Funchal.
HMS Howe brought Queen Adelaide of England to Funchal, where she resided at Quinta Lambert until 11 April 1848.

mentions.as_written: 3 de Novembro de 1847 a 11 de Abril de 1848

summary: Prince Alexander of the Netherlands arrived in Madeira on the frigate Príncipe de Orange.
A large theft of silver took place from the church of Ponta Delgada.
Dr Nuno Silvestre Teixeira was born at Ponta do Sol.
English treasure hunters searched the Selvagens in successive years, spending £2,500.
Frederico Carlos succeeded his father as King Frederick VII of Denmark.

Controversy over the Rev. T. K. Brown's Anglican chaplaincy in Madeira produced publications, including Lowe's protest, 'The Madeira Chaplaincy' in London and a pamphlet on the English Church in Funchal.
After religious disputes among British residents, a second Anglican church opened in Rua dos Aranhas, Funchal.
Frank Dillon made his views of Madeira.
Sérvulo Drumond de Meneses published document collections on the mendicity asylum, the famine and the building of the Ribeiro Seco bridge.
Padre Manuel Nunes was born at Paul do Mar.
Daniel Ferreira Pestana's grammar was published in Nova Goa.
A lazaretto was established at the Quinta do Gorgulho.
Joaquim Nunes de Aguiar completed his civil engineering course in Paris.
Vicente Gomes da Silva made the first photographic experiments in Portuguese territory, in Madeira.
João Maria Moniz assembled his herbarium.
José Caetano Peixoto was appointed the last governor of Porto Santo, the office ending that year.
Dr António da Luz Pita performed an excision of the cervix in Lisbon.
A memoir by Padre Caetano Alberto Soares read at the Instituto dos Advogados was published.
António Joaquim Gonçalves de Freitas graduated in law at Coimbra.
José Silvestre Ribeiro represented Madeira in parliament, doing so again in 1853–56 and 1857–58.
Januário Vicente Camacho represented Madeira in the Cortes.
João de Sant'Ana e Vasconcelos compiled the Porto Santo municipal annals.
José António Monteiro Teixeira published the two volumes of Obras Poéticas.
A letter describing the Arco de São Jorge landslide was found in Lisbon.
José Silvestre Ribeiro issued a circular on keeping municipal annals on 3 January 1848, followed by a decree of 8 November requiring councils to keep annual Anais do Município.
The Duke of Palmela was still in Madeira, shortly before leaving for Lisbon with his ailing wife.
The Correio da Madeira published an account of the Funchal capstan.
Prince Alexander of the Netherlands died at Tomaz Burnett's quinta in Santa Luzia on 20 February 1848; his body was taken aboard the Dutch steamer Phoenix on 3 April.

Paid for by the surplus of the famine relief fund and contracted on 27 February for 5.799$000 réis, construction of the Ribeiro Seco bridge began under José Silvestre Ribeiro on 6 March 1848, being nearly finished by year end.
Queen Adelaide left Madeira after a five-month stay.
A decree transferred Bishop D. José Xavier de Cerveira e Sousa to the diocese of Beja.
The Ponta do Sol municipal council ordered and built the town's landing quay, work beginning on 8 May 1848 and lasting to 1850.
Work began on the masonry bridge over the Ribeira dos Socorridos.
A royal letter raised Jardim do Mar to a full parish.
Sérvulo Drumond de Meneses served as interim civil governor of Funchal during José Silvestre Ribeiro's absence.

mentions.as_written: desde 17 de Julho de 1848 até 24 de Julho de 1849

summary: By royal letter of 24 July 1848 Quinta Grande was separated from Campanário as an autonomous parish of the Câmara de Lobos municipality, taking over the Vera Cruz chapel.
A law of 24 July 1848 separated São Roque do Faial from Faial as an autonomous parish with its own priest.
Achadas da Cruz became an independent parish by law.
A law restored the parish of Água de Pena and made Santo da Serra an autonomous parish.
Floods caused heavy losses in Santana.
Carlos Mac Euen made meteorological observations at Quinta Hollway.
Dr António Alves da Silva received his doctorate in Paris free of charge in recognition of his talent.
Francisco João Moniz died around this year, according to a family member.
José Silvestre Ribeiro obtained an annual subsidy of six contos for the levada works in Madeira.
A commission drew up a list of the weights and measures standards in use in Madeira.
The first volume of António Alfredo's posthumous Miscellanea was published.
The Conde de Tojal served as Portuguese minister of foreign affairs.
The three volumes of Uma Época Administrativa da Madeira e Porto Santo, recording José Silvestre Ribeiro's administration, were published in 1849, 1850 and 1852.
A regimento of eight articles was drawn up for the Recolhimento das Órfãs but never put into effect.
Joaquim Nunes de Aguiar served as engineer to the Funchal municipal council.
Francisco de Andrade's primary-school Portuguese grammar went through five editions.
João Maria Moniz entered the Funchal revenue office as a trainee.
Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo completed his law degree.
Gerardo José de Nóbrega published 'The Cultivation of Cochineal'.
Queen Adelaide of England sent José Silvestre Ribeiro an engraved silver piece in gratitude.
A diarrhoeal epidemic struck Arco de São Jorge, and the civil governor José Silvestre Ribeiro brought doctors.
The 87th and last issue of the first O Madeirense newspaper appeared.
The Ribeiro Seco bridge was completed, and engineer Tibério Augusto Blanc officially reported it finished to the civil governor on 5 December.
The first issue of the newspaper O Correio da Madeira appeared.
An order authorised moving the Military Hospital to a house in the Rua da Rochinha de Baixo, Funchal.
During a leste, Carlos Mac Euen measured a relative humidity of 18 per cent at Quinta Holloway.
The Barão de São Pedro presented a bill to abolish all Madeiran entails, which was not approved.
D. Manuel Martins Manso was presented as bishop of Funchal.
The government was authorised to complete the Levada do Rabaçal.
José Silvestre Ribeiro reported that Funchal was lit by 70 public lamps.

The Duke of Leuchtenberg arrived at Funchal aboard the Russian frigate Kamtchatka, landed after quarantine on 27 August, was received by José Silvestre Ribeiro, and resided at Quinta Lambert until April 1850.

mentions.as_written: 27 de Agosto de 1849 a 23 de Abril de 1850

summary: A decree abolished the municipality of Porto Moniz, whose parishes passed to Calheta; it was restored a few years later.
An official letter defined the manilha as an orifice one palm in circumference.
The Sociedade Agrícola Madeirense was solemnly inaugurated in the presence of the Duke of Leuchtenberg.
A decree abolished the 9th Military Division, leaving Madeira a simple Military Command.
Students held the first meeting to organise the Sociedade Filantrópica Académica in Coimbra.
The Monte toboggan cars appeared in their present form.
Dr J. A. Mason's work on Madeira's climate was published, with John Driver's guide appended.
Paulo Perestrelo da Câmara's Diccionario geographico, historico, politico was published in Rio de Janeiro.
Civil governor José Silvestre Ribeiro proposed a mutual-aid society for artisans.
Dr Osvaldo Heer stayed in Madeira from winter 1850 to spring 1851, making phenological observations.

mentions.as_written: desde o inverno de 1850 á primavera de 1851

summary: Civil governor José Silvestre Ribeiro intervened against Wilkinson's Protestant proselytising in Machico.
The boys' primary school of Ponta do Pargo was created.
Porto Santo's population was recorded as 1,799 people.
John A. Dix's 'A Winter in Madeira' was published in New York, and Harcourt's 'A Sketch of Madeira' in London.
Francisco Álvares de Nóbrega's Rimas were reprinted in Funchal by Januário Justiniano de Nóbrega.
Francisco Justino Gonçalves de Andrade graduated in juridical and social sciences at São Paulo.
Roberto White made meteorological observations in Funchal and Machico.
José Pereira Sanches de Castro published his observations on the colonia contract.
The Ponta do Sol quay was apparently completed.
The musician Cazella visited Madeira and gave concerts.
José Silvestre Ribeiro ordered the Poiso refuge house built, according to one account.
Famine struck Porto Santo; Governor José Silvestre Ribeiro funded 75 moios of cereals for the islanders.
The Lancasterian school building was repaired at State expense.
After 1850 the effectiveness of sulphur against the Oidium vine parasite became known.
The Duke of Leuchtenberg visited Porto Santo aboard the frigate Palas.
José Silvestre Ribeiro issued a further circular urging municipal annals.
The newspaper O Amigo do Povo was published, issuing 178 numbers.

mentions.as_written: 26 de Janeiro de 1850 a 27 de Abril de 1854

summary: Daniel de Ornelas de Vasconcelos presented a bill in parliament to abolish all morgados, vínculos and capelas in Madeira.
Maximiliano Eugénio de Azevedo was born in Funchal.
The Filarmónica dos Artistas Funchalenses was founded.
Roberto White recorded 25° in the shade during the leste wind.
Dr António Alves da Silva was appointed professor at the Escola Médico-Cirúrgica do Funchal by decree.
João Nunes Diabinho was born in Funchal.
An exhibition of Madeiran industry, including embroideries, was held in the Civil Government palace in Funchal, with 17 silver medals awarded.

mentions.as_written: quatro primeiros dias do mês de Abril de 1850

summary: Organisation of the natural history cabinet began in the Palácio de São Lourenço.
The Duke of Palmela died at his house at Rato, Lisbon.
The Duke of Leuchtenberg left Madeira for Russia.
Ramon Masferrer y Arquimbau was born in Vich.
The Holy See confirmed D. Manuel Martins Manso as bishop of Funchal.
A great fair organised by José Silvestre Ribeiro was held in the Praça Académica, Funchal, visited by some fifteen thousand people.
Civil Governor José Silvestre Ribeiro recommended building a viewpoint at Macelas, Machico, which was built soon after.
The poet Bulhão Pato stayed in Madeira.

mentions.as_written: de 7 de Agosto de 1850 a 6 de Março de 1851

summary: José Silvestre Ribeiro recommended that the municipal councils build cemeteries.

mentions.as_written: 19 de Agôsto e 26 de Outubro de 1850

summary: The statutes of the Sociedade Agrícola Madeirense were approved by royal charter.
Dr P. Garnier visited Madeira.
The German naturalist Albers stayed in Madeira.

mentions.as_written: de Outubro de 1850 a Junho de 1851

summary: D. Manuel Martins Manso received episcopal consecration.
The boring of the Estrebarias levada tunnel was completed.
D. Manuel Martins Manso governed the diocese of Funchal as its 24th bishop.

mentions.as_written: 16 de Novembro de 1850 a 13 de Junho de 1858

summary: A boat to Porto Santo was wrecked while landing, killing 15 of the 27 aboard and prompting regulation of the crossing.
The first issue of the newspaper O Archivista was published.
The wooden passenger stair at the Pontinha quay was replaced by one cut in the rock.
Around the mid-nineteenth century vine diseases wiped out Madeira's viticulture almost completely.
The orchil trade and export from Madeira ended around the mid-19th century.
João José Rodrigues Leitão settled in Funchal.
The Praça do Ribeiro Seco was built shortly after 1850.
The wickerwork industry apparently began in Camacha parish.
The Virtudes chapel in São Martinho was rebuilt.
James Yate Johnson came to Madeira seeking relief for lung disease.
The municipal butchers' stalls and slaughterhouse were built beside the fish market in Funchal.
The Jewish cemetery of Funchal received an entrance inscription dated 5611 of the Hebrew calendar, corresponding to 1851.
José Ferreira Pestana became Minister of the Kingdom.
Major repairs were made to the parish church of Ponta do Pargo.
Livestock censuses of Funchal district were taken in 1851, 1873 and 1893.
Funchal's lazaretto moved to houses at the mouth of the Ribeira de Gonçalo Aires.
Saldanha's revolt took place, supported at Coimbra by the future Viscount das Nogueiras.
No snow fell in Madeira's mountains in the winter of 1851–1852.
Under the Regeneration, which sought to reconcile parties, Madeira still elected two Cabralist deputies.
Francisco Justino Gonçalves de Andrade defended his theses and received his doctorate.
Dr Heer studied Madeiran phenology.
Robert White wrote 'Madeira, its climate and scenery'.
Dr António da Luz Pita represented Madeira in parliament.
The refuge house at Poiso was built.
José Silvestre Ribeiro tried unsuccessfully to establish a theatre in Funchal.
Entrance works at the Lancasterian School were carried out on Governor José Silvestre Ribeiro's orders.
Januário Vicente Camacho was raised to the peerage.
Rafael Coelho Machado published his Breve tratado de Harmonia.
The government rebuilt the chancel and part of the parish house of Santo António da Serra.
Luís da Costa Pereira was appointed teacher at the Funchal Lyceum.
Nuno Ferreira Jardim was born in Funchal.
A French visitor sold vine plants in Funchal, possibly introducing the vine fungus.
João Joaquim Pinto, later dean, was born in Porto Moniz.
The newspaper O Agricultor Madeirense was published in nine issues.

mentions.as_written: 26 de Março a 29 de Dezembro de 1851

summary: Frederico Pinto Coelho was born in Funchal.
The periodical O Estudo was published in Funchal.
Civil governor José Silvestre Ribeiro reported favourably on Dr Robert Kalley's claim.
The 132nd and last issue of O Correio da Madeira appeared.
O Progressista, organ of the liberal party, began publication in Funchal.
José Silvestre Ribeiro asked Funchal council to agree with Santana council on funding a resident keeper at Poiso.
António Manuel de Noronha was created Viscount of Santa Cruz.
The 56th and last issue of O Archivista was published.
Oidium appeared in Madeira and almost wholly destroyed the island's vineyards.
A District Public Works Directorate was created in Funchal to direct and administer public works, following the creation of the Ministry of Public Works.
The vine disease (oidium, or mangra) spread across Madeira and destroyed most of the vineyards, causing a severe economic crisis, misery and emigration.
Works for a new church at Ribeira da Janela were contracted for 6.100$000 réis but were never begun.
Correia de Azevedo Júnior defended his medical theses in Rio de Janeiro and published them there.
Luiz de Freitas Branco graduated in law at Coimbra.
António Jacinto de Freitas published the third volume of Uma Epocha Administrativa.
Pedro Júlio Vieira completed his medical course at Montpellier and published his thesis on Madeira's climate.
Dr Heer studied the plants of the Quinta do Vale.
Joaquim Nunes de Aguiar was called to work on the northern railway.
In the winter of 1852–1853 unusually heavy snow fell and night temperatures in Funchal dropped to 45°F.
António Manuel de Noronha was granted the title of Viscount of Santa Cruz.
The British cemetery in Funchal was enlarged.
Dr Carlos Mittermaier stayed in Funchal making meteorological observations.
Frederico Welwitsch proposed to the government the creation of acclimatisation gardens in Luanda and Funchal (dated variously 23 August or 23 September 1852).
The shelter house at Poiso was completed in early 1852.
Agostinho de Ornelas de Vasconcelos studied law at Coimbra.
António Joaquim Gonçalves de Freitas practised law, politics and journalism in Funchal.
The future Count of Canavial graduated bachelor of science at Montpellier.
The first issue of the newspaper A Ordem appeared.
The Count of Tojal died in Lisbon.
Father João Maurício Henriques was born in Funchal.
Francisco Correia Heredia, later Viscount of Ribeira Brava, was born at Ribeira Brava.
António Augusto Larica defended his medical thesis at Montpellier.
The government approved the statutes of the Sociedade Filantrópica Académica de Coimbra.
The Additional Act made the election of deputies permanently direct.
Prince Ferdinand Maximilian, later Emperor of Mexico, arrived in Madeira for the first time.
The newspaper O Baratíssimo published 13 issues before being suspended for abuse of press freedom.

mentions.as_written: desde 17 de Julho a 9 de Outubro de 1852

summary: On the night of 30 to 31 July 1852 soldiers of the 6th Caçadores Battalion mutinied at the Colégio barracks in Funchal and murdered Lieutenant Lapierre; the battalion was sent to Lisbon.

Empress Amélia of Brazil and Princess Maria Amélia, who travelled on medical advice, arrived in Funchal aboard the frigate D. Fernando, accompanied by Dr Barral; the council named a street after the princess.
Empress Amélia of Brazil took up residence at the Quinta Lambert in Funchal.
In September 1852 the shade temperature in Funchal reached 83°F, and 85°F in some places.
José de Azevedo Castelo Branco was born in Vila Real.
Alexandre Luiz da Cunha died at the Hospital Civil in Funchal, aged 49.
A decree transferred the parish of Porto da Cruz from Santana to the municipality of Machico and moved some Machico localities to Santa Cruz.
The postal service passed to direct state administration and postage stamps were introduced.
Dr Justino António de Freitas was promoted to full professor by decree.
The Viscount of Fornos de Algodres, João Maria de Abreu Castelo Branco Cardoso e Melo, was appointed civil governor of the Funchal district.
The civil governor appointed a commission to raise relief funds abroad for the victims of the vine disease crisis.
Civil governor José Silvestre Ribeiro left Madeira at the end of his governorship, after which the old natural history cabinet's collections were lost or stolen.

Dr José Júlio Rodrigues signed and promoted the Paris agreement on international exchanges.
A mausoleum for the Twelve Martyrs was erected in the Prado do Repouso cemetery.
E. A. Bettencourt published in Porto a pamphlet on the discovery of Porto Santo and Madeira.
William Longman published Impressions of Madeira, with a map.
Luciano Cordeiro's memoir recounting the Afonso Sanches tradition appeared in the proceedings of the International Congress of Americanists.
Maximiliano Eugénio de Azevedo completed the artillery course.
Serpa Pinto was in Funchal serving as a captain in the 12th Rifle Battalion.
The first Saint Vincent de Paul conference in Madeira was founded in São Pedro, Funchal.
The first issue of the Catholic Funchal newspaper A Verdade appeared.
Bishop D. Aires de Ornelas de Vasconcelos left Madeira amid an unprecedented farewell.
The Associação de Protecção e Instrução do Sexo Feminino Funchalense was established in Funchal; its statutes were approved by the district authority on 14 April.
A second Aurora Literária issued the first of its six numbers.
The statutes of the Sociedade Cooperativa de Consumo e Crédito do Funchal were approved.
António Policarpo dos Passos Sousa died at Ponta do Sol.
The Banco Commercial da Madeira was established in Funchal.
The title of 2nd Viscount of Nogueiras was conferred.
Conselheiro António Gonçalves de Freitas died in Lisbon.
José Bettencourt da Câmara died at Câmara de Lobos.
A decree reorganised Madeira's judicial administration into four comarcas: Funchal, Ponta do Sol, Santa Cruz and São Vicente, making São Vicente the seat of a judicial district.
The first number of A Aurora Liberal appeared.
The first issue of the Estrella Académica was published.
The first issue of the first newspaper titled O Liberal appeared.
João Blandy bought and restored the chapel of Nossa Senhora das Neves.
A new, more active Protestant proselytising campaign began in Madeira.
The Funchal customs house issued brass tokens.
The Associação de Protecção e Instrução do Sexo Feminino Funchalense opened a model school with classes and workshops.
Government works began on the landing quay at Câmara de Lobos.
Manuel José Vieira restored the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Ajuda, which was blessed on 16 August 1876.
The Cais da Pontinha was built in Funchal.
The Associação das Damas de Caridade was founded in Funchal.
Floods damaged Madalena do Mar.
Azevedo reported selling a manuscript copy of Saudades da Terra to a lord for Edinburgh.
A law exempted Madeiran sugar from duties in Portugal and the Azores for five years.
The eighth number of A Aurora Liberal appeared.
D. João Frederico da Câmara Leme left the governorship of Madeira.
The comarca of Ponta do Sol was installed.
Francisco Albuquerque de Mesquita e Castro was appointed civil governor of Madeira by decree and took office on 10 June.
Two great storms drove many ships ashore in Funchal bay.
José António Monteiro Teixeira died in Funchal.
Queen Josefina ordered by will that the Hospício da Princesa D. Maria Amélia become a perpetual foundation.
D. Manuel Agostinho Barreto was presented as bishop of Funchal, confirmed by the Holy See on 29 September and took possession of the diocese by proxy on 26 December.
The 84th issue of O Paquete was published.
The comarca of Santa Cruz was installed.
Construction of the Mercado de D. Pedro V in Funchal began.
A government order praised Dr Câmara Leme for founding the Associação de Protecção e Instrução do Sexo Feminino Funchalense.
The modern Progressive party was organised in Lisbon.
Canon Alfredo César de Oliveira founded the Diário de Notícias in Funchal, Madeira's first daily newspaper, whose first issue appeared on 11 October 1876.
The steamer Valente was driven ashore by a violent southerly storm below the Quinta Lambert, Funchal, and destroyed.
Judicial reorganisation: the comarca of São Vicente was installed and the single comarca of Funchal, divided into nine julgados, replaced the western and eastern comarcas.
The Sociedade Agrícola Madeirense was reorganised, though it did no effective work thereafter.
Birth of Marck Athias.
Francisco Joaquim de Sá Camelo Lampreia died in Lisbon while deputy for Moura.
The general assembly approved the statutes of the Clube Funchalense.
The Funchal police were reorganised.
Pedro de Alcântara Góis was appointed the first civil police commissioner of Funchal.
António Pedro de Azevedo published geo-hydrographic charts of Porto Santo (1877), Madeira and the Desertas, issued in 1877, 1879 and 1886.
Francisco de Sousa's treatise was first published in Ponta Delgada.
Richard Henry Major published The Discoveries of Prince Henry the Navigator and their results in London.
A Spanish friar's description relating to the discovery of the archipelago was published by the Madrid Geographical Society.
Between 1877 and 1882 tobacco was planted in Madeira, mainly in São Gonçalo and Santo António.
King Oscar of Sweden established the perpetual foundation of the Hospício da Princesa D. Maria Amélia, with a council and a fund of one million francs.
Canon António Aires Pacheco came to Madeira with Bishop D. Manuel Agostinho Barreto.
The astronomer Green observed Mars from Madeira.
Home delivery of mail began in Funchal.
The Associação Madeirense promotora do Bem Público e do Auxílio Mútuo was founded.
João Maurício Henriques was ordained priest.
A pamphlet, Companhia de Seguros Madeirense, recorded an unsuccessful attempt to found an insurance company in Madeira.
Nuno Silvestre Teixeira was a fifth-year medical student at Coimbra, regarded as the faculty's best student.

D. Manuel Agostinho Barreto was consecrated Bishop of Funchal at the Estrela basilica in Lisbon, arrived in Funchal on 22 February, entered the cathedral on 25 February and issued his first pastoral on 2 March.
The civil governor approved the statutes of the Clube Funchalense.

After a suicide in Funchal was refused church burial but buried in the Angústias cemetery, Bishop Barreto placed the cemetery under interdict; Cassiano das Neves published a pamphlet on the affair in Porto.
Funchal council granted the Praça da Rainha to the Conde do Canavial for a white-mulberry nursery and silkworm-rearing trials.
The periodical A Penumbra Literária published eight issues.
Jacinto Augusto Camacho was promoted brigadier general.
A contract signed in Paris entrusted the internal running of the Hospício da Princesa D. Maria Amélia to the Sisters of Charity.
A second newspaper titled O Districto do Funchal was published, running to 23 issues.
A permanent artillery battery was established in Madeira.
Vasco Gonçalves Marques was born in Funchal.
António da Cruz Rodrigues dos Santos was born in Funchal.
The first issue of Echo de Santa Cruz appeared, the first Madeiran newspaper published outside Funchal.
Under Bishop Barreto a full preparatory course was introduced at the reformed Funchal seminary.
The Visconde de Monte Belo founded a tobacco factory in Madeira.
The municipal drawing course in Funchal was inaugurated.
The statutes of the Levada do Pico do Arvoredo were published in the Diário do Governo.
Rodrigo José de Lima Felner died in Lisbon.
The Diário do Funchal began publication.
Joaquim Nunes de Aguiar died in Funchal from overwork.
The first issue of the Boletim Judicial was published.
Afonso de Castro was appointed civil governor of Funchal for a second time and took office on 24 December.
The first issue of O Athleta appeared.
D. Olímpia Pio Fernandes wrote the drama 'Aldo ou a Filha do Mar', staged in Funchal to great applause.
Charles Ridpath Blandy died.
The administrative code of 1878 raised the membership of the Junta Geral to 21 and replaced indirect election with direct election.
The Caixa Económica of the Associação de Socorros Mútuos 4 de Setembro de 1862, Madeira's first savings bank, began operating.
Father Ernesto João Schmitz settled in Madeira.
António da Costa published the pamphlet 'Instituição de Ouro' describing the Associação de Protecção e Instrução do Sexo Feminino Funchalense.
Tallow candle making in Madeira began to decline under cheap English stearin imports.
José de Azevedo Castelo Branco graduated in medicine.
Ernesto do Canto published the Archivo dos Açores, twelve volumes appearing between 1878 and 1894.
The administrative code of 1878 abolished municipal councils.

João José Rodrigues Leitão, agent of the Banco de Portugal, went bankrupt; director Henrique de Barros Gomes stayed in Funchal from 8 July to 2 September, and the agency passed to Tomás António Gomes on 15 July.

summary: In spring 1878 eight monk seals were killed on the Deserta Grande.
A better landing quay was completed at the Pontinha in Funchal.
Madeiran emigration to Hawaii began.
The Circo Funchalense was built within the market enclosure in Funchal.

Júlio Augusto Leiria died in Coimbra.

Daniel de Ornelas de Vasconcelos died in Lisbon.
Issue number 14 of the Echo de Santa Cruz appeared.
João Fortunato de Oliveira died in Funchal.
Francisco Jorge de Abreu was born in Funchal.
An orphanage opened beside the Hospício da Princesa D. Maria Amélia with twelve children.
The remains of the twelve martyrs of the homeland were moved to a cemetery, and a pamphlet describing the translation was published.
The Funchal council raised two loans of 10 contos each for the Pedro V market.

mentions.as_written: 15 de Julho a 18 de Novembro de 1878

summary: A fire at Payne's bakery in Rua da Alfândega, Funchal, caused less damage than the glass and crockery thrown during it.
The single 24-page issue of the monthly review Reflexos appeared, covering September to November 1878.
The Civil Police Commissariat of Funchal was installed.
The periodical Ilha da Madeira published its four issues.
Canon Alfredo César de Oliveira was elected opposition deputy for Ponta do Sol.
D. Ventura de Callejon's notice on Columbus's stay in Madeira and his house in Funchal was published in issue 38 of La Ilustración Española y Americana.
The Jornal do Funchal was published, ending with its 73rd issue.
The Maceta de Santa Cruz published its two issues, the first on 10 November and the last on 24 December 1878.
The second newspaper A Liberdade published 59 issues in Funchal.

summary: Dr Luís Vicente de Afonseca died in Lisbon.

Patrício Moniz left the Funchal seminary for mainland Portugal.
The Paul do Mar salt works passed to Filipe António Gonçalves.

Camilo Castelo Branco published 'A Lenda de Machim' in Historia e Sentimentalismo.

R. Fritze collected plants in Madeira.
Ricardo Júlio Ferraz represented Madeira in the Cortes.
The Clube Unido in Funchal was dissolved in early 1879.
The Conde de Canavial published in Funchal his study of the agricultural crisis.
Gaston Lemay's 'A bord de la «Junon»', touching on Madeira, was published in Paris.
João Joaquim Pinto graduated in theology at Coimbra and was ordained priest.
António Aurélio da Costa Ferreira was born in Funchal.
The civil governor approved the statutes of the Clube União in Funchal.
Dr Cândido Joaquim da Silva died of a stroke.
D. António Manuel Pereira Ribeiro was born at Friande.
The Prince Imperial, Eugène Louis Napoléon, landed at Funchal from the British steamer Danube on his way to the Cape of Good Hope.
The statutes of the São Paulo confraternity were approved by alvará of the district authority.
The Conde do Ribeiro Real took office as civil governor of Funchal.
Manuel José Vieira made his celebrated speech on Madeiran monetary unification in the Chamber of Deputies.
Félix de Brito Capelo died.
José Jorge Rodrigues dos Santos was born in Funchal.
The third newspaper A Lei began publication, reaching 97 issues.
O Ocidente published an engraving of the Gothic part of the house associated with Columbus.
The Clube Restauração was founded.
A law unified Madeira's monetary system with that of mainland Portugal, ending circulation of foreign money on the island except the pound sterling.
Agostinho de Ornelas de Vasconcelos returned ill to Madeira and was warmly received.
Afonso de Castro left the administration of the Funchal district.
António da Costa Paiva, Baron of Castelo de Paiva, died in Funchal.
The first issue of the first O Progresso appeared; it ran to 75 issues.
H. Grey made a voyage to Madeira and the Azores.
The Conde do Carvalhal wrote to João de Deus presenting teacher Teodoro João Henriques to learn his reading method.
The Government ordered a study for a new quay at Funchal.
Ernesto Venceslau de Sousa was born in Funchal.
Canon Alfredo César de Oliveira was re-elected deputy for Ponta do Sol.
The newspaper Religião e Progresso, founded by João Inocêncio Camacho, was published in Funchal, its first issue appearing on 15 November 1879.
The Clube Aliança came to an end.
A boys' state school was created in Estreito da Calheta.
Dennis Embleton spent the winter of 1880–81 in Madeira.
Canon Alfredo César de Oliveira was transferred to Évora Cathedral.
Acúrsio Garcia Ramos published 'Ilha da Madeira' in two volumes in Lisbon.
Madeiran embroidery exports fell to 12:937$000 réis as luxury embroidery went out of fashion in England.
Henry Vizetelly's 'Facts about Porto and Madeira' was published in London.
Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo published the Romanceiro do Archipelago da Madeira in Funchal.
Major repairs were made to the parish church of Santo António under civil governor Silvestre Ribeiro.
Luís António Gonçalves de Freitas completed his law degree at Coimbra.
An author writing in 1880 described penitent pilgrims carrying chains and crawling on their knees at Monte.
Father José Gonçalves de Aguiar published O Dogma da Imaculada Conceição de Maria Santíssima in Lisbon.
Julius Goldschmidt published Madère étudiée comme station d'hiver.
The cooperative's grocery closed after causing losses, reopening soon after under two merchants.
British visitors to Madeira averaged about 200 a year between 1880 and 1885.
Funchal municipal revenue was about 81 contos.
The Capela de Cristo was rebuilt for the second time and solemnly blessed in 1883.
Mary Jane Wilson settled in Madeira.
Manuel Celestino Emídio represented Madeira in the Cortes during the 1880–81 legislative session.
A project to extend the Ponta do Sol quay was drawn up but never carried out.
The Sociedade Agrícola Madeirense was definitively dissolved.
Vicente Cândido Machado graduated in medicine at the Paris faculty.
João Gouveia was born in Funchal.
José de Almada was born in Funchal.
Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo wrote to Teófilo Braga offering him his Cancioneiro Popular.
An earlier Sociedade Protectora dos Animais Domésticos was installed at the Hotel Miles in Funchal.
The first issue of the periodical A Grinalda Madeirense appeared.
João de Freitas da Silva was created Viscount of Monte Belo.
Empress Eugénie passed Madeira aboard the British steamer German.
Dr Spencer Wells's article on Madeira appeared in the British Medical Journal.
The statutes of the Associação Protectora dos Pobres were approved by permit, according to the Elucidário, though the date conflicts with its founding year.
Vasco Crispiniano da Silva was born in Funchal.
Carlos Olavo Correia de Azevedo was born in Funchal.
Posts, telegraphs and lighthouses were reorganised jointly.
João Augusto de Vasconcelos e Sá was born in Funchal.
Francisco Correia Herédia died in Lisbon; A Religião e Progresso reprinted a biographical article on him on 20 August.
Work began on the Funchal municipal garden in the enclosure of the Convento de São Francisco; in October an inscribed stone dated 1780 was found during the works.
Dr Jacinto António de Sousa died.
The feast of Nossa Senhora da Luz was held again in the Colégio church after 25 years, without the lyceum pupils.
The Funchal land registry office was installed.
Dr Vicente Cândido Machado successfully operated on Bishop D. Manuel Agostinho Barreto, earning great renown.
Jordão Maurício Henriques was born in Funchal.
The first Diário da Madeira was published, issuing 281 numbers.

summary: The last issue, no. 44, of Religião e Progresso was published.
D. Aires de Ornelas de Vasconcelos died in Lisbon.
The Mercado de D. Pedro V in Funchal opened to the public.
Ricardo Júlio Ferraz died in Funchal.
The rodas de caminho fell into disuse in Funchal.
The Junta Agrícola set up an experimental farm at Ribeira Brava.
Dennis Embleton's 'A visit to Madeira in the winter 1880-81' was published in London.
William and Alfred Reid published 'Madeira, a guide book of useful and varying information'.
Madeiran butter exports rose from 129 kg in 1881 to 48,124 kg in 1893.
J. M. Rendell's Concise Handbook of the Island of Madeira was published in London.
António Aires Pacheco and António Vicente Varela were ordained priests.
Pontes Câmara made his only return visit to Madeira.

Manuel Fernandes de Sant'Ana left the diocesan seminary to enter the Society of Jesus.
R. Fritze published his study of Madeira's fern vegetation.

Padre João António Marcial became the first collated vicar of Prazeres.
Frederico Pinto Coelho published the pamphlet Sudario Negro against Bishop Manuel Agostinho Barreto.
Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo retired from the Funchal lyceum and moved to Lisbon.
The Funchal lyceum moved to a former manor house in Rua dos Ferreiros.
Manuel Gomes Jardim was born in Porto Moniz.
Francisco de Andrade died in Funchal.

The newspaper A Luz published seventy-six issues.

A second newspaper O Independente published eight numbers.

summary: Dr Jaccoud stayed in Madeira to study its climate for treating lung disease.
Funchal council approved the design of the Municipal Garden.
Padre Ernesto João Schmitz became vice-rector of the Funchal Seminary.
A second newspaper As Novidades ran for twenty-six issues.
Américo Olavo Correia de Azevedo was born in Funchal.
The Diário da Tarde was published, issuing 305 numbers.
Eduardo Dias Grande died in Lisbon.
Phylloxera was still devastating Madeira's vineyards, with wine production at about 4,500 pipes.

Luís António Gonçalves de Freitas represented Madeira as a deputy in the Portuguese parliament.

Several Madeirans joined the Constituent party.

Madeiran processional crosses, including those of the Cathedral and Gaula's fifteenth-century silver cross, were shown at the Lisbon Retrospective Exhibition of Ornamental Art.

B. Stein published Lichenes Maderenses et Mindanoenses.

Captain Eurico Albertis collected algae on Madeira.

The newspaper Diário da Manhã ran from its first issue to its 129th and last.

Dr Manuel de Arriaga made his first visit to Madeira, receiving an enthusiastic reception.
Manuel da Costa Dias was born in Ponta do Pargo.
The first issue of the periodical O Palco was published.

Paul Langerhans published the Handbuch für Madeira in Berlin.

A second edition of a work by Francisco de Sousa appeared in Ponta Delgada.
The chapel of Santo António at the Quinta do Pombal was built.
Fidelio de Freitas Branco graduated in law at Coimbra.
