The Junta Geral substantially improved and enlarged the Câmara de Lobos quay.
Manuel Ribeiro published his verse booklet Flores Agrestes in Funchal.
José de Almada graduated in law at Coimbra.
Colonel Eduardo Agostinho Pereira measured Pico Ruivo at 1,950 m.
The Nationalist party was founded, gaining support among Madeiran clergy.
Manuel Gonçalves and Francisco de Araújo Figueira tried without success to install fixed fish traps.
An official school was created in São Roque do Faial.
The Junta Geral built the Faial quay at Pedra da Pescaria.
C. A. de Meneses carried out phenological observations in Madeira.
The Wilson Company quay near the Palace Hotel was built, in 1903 or shortly after.
The Junta Geral built the Seixal quay.
The Junta Geral built the Porto da Cruz quay.
Only a single juniper remained on Porto Santo, on Pico Branco.
António Feliciano Rodrigues published Versos da Mocidade in Funchal.
The Santo António parish cemetery was greatly enlarged.
The statutes of a women's mutual-aid association in Funchal were approved.
The tenth and last issue of the Revista Literária appeared.
A second series of O Democrata was published, with ten issues.

mentions.as_written: de 8 de Março a 10 de Maio de 1903

summary: The Funchal council ceded land on Campo da Barca to the Junta Geral for a disinfection station.
Canon Manuel Esteves Fazenda died in Lisbon aged 58.
João Augusto Pereira gave a speech on the anarchic state of the Funchal district, later published in Funchal.
The teacher Manuel de la Quadra (Cuadra) died in Funchal.
The last issue of O Debate appeared.
António Augusto Larica died in Funchal.
The Baron of Úzel died.
A ministerial order granted Prince Frederico Carlos de Hohenlohe a concession to establish tuberculosis sanatoria in Madeira.
Colonel Francisco Afonso de Chaves took magnetic measurements at Funchal, recording a declination of 20°31'30" W and an inclination of 54° 32' 5.
The botanist Júlio Augusto Henriques visited Madeira en route to São Tomé.
João da Silva Carvalho died in Funchal.
Dr Júlio Paulo de Freitas bought the Quinta das Angústias (Quinta Lambert) for 4,000 pounds.
A decree modified the 1895 sugar regime, raising minimum cane prices and reducing the duty on foreign molasses to 6 réis per kilogram.
Funchal Municipal Council approved the plan of the first houses of the Construção Predial do Funchal cooperative.
The Baron of Jardim do Mar died in Funchal.
Manuel José Varela enlisted in the army with the rank of ensign.
Lencastre signed his report on the Madeira sanatoria mission.
Father José Pereira da Silva preached a funeral oration for Leo XIII in Funchal Cathedral.
Manuel Alexandre de Sousa died in Lisbon.
Canon António Vicente Varela died in Funchal.
Alberto de Sousa Botelho died in Funchal.
The first motor car arrived in Madeira.
New salt pans owned by António Luís Pimenta were set up at Serra de Fora, Porto Santo.
Adolfo César de Noronha sent fossil corals of the archipelago to the palaeontologist Oppenheim.
An epidemic of cerebrospinal meningitis occurred in Madeira, with patients treated at the lazaretto.
Ernesto Venceslau de Sousa's Poema antipuniceo was published in Funchal.
Jubilee festivities for the 50th anniversary of the Immaculate Conception dogma were held in Madeira, with a procession from the cathedral to Monte.
The Junta Geral built the quay at Ribeira Brava between 1904 and 1908.
Carlos Azevedo de Menezes published 'Arvores e Arbustos Madeirenses' in Funchal.
João Frederico Júdice de Vasconcelos sat as deputy for Madeira in the parliamentary session.
Vasco Gonçalves Marques was appointed secretary of the emigration police in Funchal.
In 1904 and 1905 alone, registered factories fully bought the surplus brandy of unregistered ones as required.
Work began on the bridges of Faial.
The Selvagens were sold by the morgado's heirs to the banker Luís da Rocha Machado.
Manuel Gomes Jardim was ordained priest.
The Junta Geral built the present Machico quay.
The Junta Geral built the Porto Novo landing stage in 1904, 1905 and 1908.
The Junta Geral built the São Jorge quay at Ponta Gorda, linked by a footpath to the Santana–São Jorge road.
The disinfection station at Campo da Barca was built.
C. Gagel published Ein Ausflug nach Madeira in Berlin.
James Britten published 'R. Brown's List of Madeira Plants' in the Journal of Botany.
Martin Vahl published Madeiras Vegetation in Copenhagen.
The São Lázaro gate of Funchal was demolished.
J. Steiner published his study of lichens of Madeira.
D. Luís da Câmara Leme died in Lisbon aged 86.
An absolute minimum temperature of 4.5 °C was recorded in Funchal.
The committee bought the Quinta do Rochedo for the asylum.
The 'Monte-Pio Madeirense' mutual-aid society was founded by twenty-eight members of various social classes.
The Junta Geral resolved to pay the staff of the emigration police.
The government confirmed the donation of the asylum to the Junta Geral.
A decree created a police force for repressing clandestine emigration in Madeira.
A decree created the Laboratory of Bacteriology and Hygiene in Funchal, whose director became António Balbino do Rego.
A decree approved the staff establishment of the Campo da Barca disinfection station.
Bishop D. Manuel Agostinho Barreto blessed the repaired Santo Espírito chapel.
William Hinton died in Funchal.
The District Agricultural Council held its inaugural session.
The 'Reforma dos Operários Madeirenses' mutual-aid association was organised.
The Sanatoria Company received its first building materials from abroad for works at Monte.
The newspaper O Heraldo da Madeira began publication.
Pedro José Lomelino was appointed substitute civil governor of the district, taking office on 24 October.
The marquês do Funchal was appointed civil governor of the district for a second time on 22 October, taking office on 10 December.
Luís António Gonçalves de Freitas died of a cerebral congestion aged 46.
A law reinforced and altered Madeira's sugar regime, establishing a sugar and alcohol monopoly for Hinton & Sons and José Júlio de Lemos.
Luís Figueiroa de Albuquerque died at Caniço.
Regulations were issued for the 1903 sugar decree.
Colonel Joaquim Maria Alves obtained a three-conto subsidy from the Junta Geral for a rifle range.
Joaquim da Silva Tavares published his second contribution.
José Cabral Correia do Amaral sat as deputy for Madeira in the 1905–06 legislature.
Bubonic plague appeared in Funchal in late 1905 without becoming epidemic; patients were isolated at the Gonçalo Aires lazaretto, whose strict isolation fed popular fear and unrest.
Construction of the Marmeleiros sanatorium for the poor began.
Funchal council approved naming a street after Servulo Drumond de Meneses, but the decision was never recorded.
Meneses's earlier phenological observations appeared in the Bulletin de l'Académie Internationale de Géographie Botanique du Mans.
Canon António Homem de Gouveia represented Madeira in the Portuguese Cortes.
Manuel Ribeiro's Pyrilampos was published in Funchal.
The Junta Geral built or improved most of Madeira's quays.
Joaquim Maria Fragoso's description of Madeiran transport refers to this year.
A new beatification process for Frei Pedro da Guarda was opened in the episcopal curia of Funchal.
Father Luís Alves Martins came to Madeira as chaplain of Infantry Regiment no. 27.
K. Friderichsen published Rubi fra Madeira.
The Abra quay was built near Caniçal.
A new, larger quay was built at Machico.
Martin Vahl published Ueber die Vegetation Madeiras in Engler's Botanische Jahrbücher.
About 250 Madeirans emigrated to Argentina.
Marck Athias published Anatomia da celula nervosa in Lisbon.
Joana de Castelo Branco published As Minhas Flores in Lisbon.
According to a German guidebook, two Russians related to its author climbed the Pico do Gato.
The statutes of the Monte-Pio Madeirense mutual-aid society were approved.
Eduardo Ernesto de Castelo Branco died in Lisbon.
A general election was held in Madeira; Pereira's election was annulled and re-run on 7 May 1905.
The musician José Sarmento died in Funchal.
The Reforma dos Operários Madeirenses was legalised by alvará.
Dr José António de Almada died in Lisbon.
A young whale trapped between a sandbank and the shore at Porto Santo was captured by locals, its blubber yielding dozens of gallons of oil.
António Romão dos Passos delivered his eulogy of Ferreira Lapa at the Sociedade de Ciências Agronómicas de Portugal.
D. António Manuel Pereira Ribeiro took up a canonry at Funchal Cathedral.
The site of the Convento da Incarnação was granted to Bishop Manuel Agostinho Barreto for a seminary.
Water first ran along the Levada da Serra, formally inaugurated on 27 September 1905.
A telegraph station opened at Ponta Delgada.
António Batalha Reis lectured on oenology at the Associação Comercial.
The public land disinfection station at Campo da Barca, Funchal, opened.
The Duke of Connaught visited Madeira with his wife and daughter.
A Notícia of the descendants of Zarco was published in the Heraldo da Madeira.
Two oaks by the Ribeira de São João in Funchal began budding.
The reformed statutes of the women's mutual-aid association were approved by royal alvará.
The Portuguese translation of Paulo Mantegazza's book was published in Lisbon.
Roland Krohn published his 'Führer durch Madeira' in Berlin.
A very dry year, with only 488 mm of rain recorded in Funchal.
The Rabaçal levadas distributed 2,580 hours of water.
About 30,000 rural and 2,000 professional embroiderers worked in the district of Funchal.
Carlos Azevedo de Meneses published Madeira Ferns in Funchal.
The original Funchal fire company was dissolved and on 20 September a new company organised by Alfredo Jorge Ferraz was constituted.

The Chapel-Monument of Our Lady of the Conception was built at Babosas, Monte, commemorating the fiftieth anniversary of the dogma of the Immaculate Conception; the site thereafter became known as Conceição.
The raised bridge in Rua do Carmo by the Travessa do Rego in Funchal was lowered.
Publication of the Archivo dos Açores resumed.
Salvador Manuel Brum do Canto and Francisco Xavier Cabral Moncada sat as deputies for Madeira.
Johs. Sfenzel published a travel book on Madeira and the Canaries in Berlin, and Gustavo Manz published a Madeira travel article.
José da Cruz Batista Santos published Horas de inspiração.
William Mitten's herbarium was acquired by the New York Botanical Garden.
Death of the historian João Agostinho de Freitas.
The insurance company Garantia Funchalense was founded in Funchal.
João Franco appointed Aires de Ornelas de Vasconcelos minister of the navy and overseas.
The catalogue of the Gabinete compiled by Francisco Eduardo Alves Viana was published in two volumes.
João Soares Branco was appointed civil governor of Madeira by decree and took office on 30 January.
The Porto Santo municipal annals were published in full in the Heraldo da Madeira.
The Heraldo da Madeira transcribed Cadamosto's passages on Madeira and Porto Santo.

During the bubonic plague episode a popular riot sacked the Funchal Lazaretto at Gonçalo Aires and freed its patients; the disturbances forced the bacteriology laboratory director Balbino do Rego to leave his post.
The cruiser Dom Carlos arrived at Funchal to help keep order after the riots.
The Confraria da Misericórdia do Funchal was restored, ending 62 years of rule by commissions.
The periodical Alma Académica ran for fourteen issues.
Bishop Manuel Agostinho Barreto blessed the rebuilt chapel of Santo António at Lugar de Baixo.
José Leite Monteiro was again appointed substitute civil governor by decree.
The Nationalist newspaper O Jornal began publication in Funchal.
The Manicómio Câmara Pestana was founded and inaugurated in Funchal, and a bust of Câmara Pestana was erected.
Joaquim da Trindade e Vasconcelos died in Funchal.
A second newspaper A Pátria appeared, issuing thirty-seven numbers.

mentions.as_written: 25 de Abril de 1906 a 26 de Maio de 1907

summary: Demolition of the old chapel at Jardim do Mar began so a new church could be built.
César Augusto Mourão Pita died in Funchal.
José Ribeiro da Cunha was appointed civil governor for the third time, taking office on 29 May.
João Barbosa de Matos e Câmara died in Funchal.
João Vieira Caetano was ordained priest.
Colonel Francisco Afonso de Chaves measured magnetic declination (20°36'55" W) and inclination at Funchal.
Bernardo da Costa de Sousa Macedo was appointed civil governor of Madeira for a second time, taking office on 23 June.
Twelve issues of A Risota were published.

mentions.as_written: 6 de Agosto de 1906 a 21 de Outubro

summary: The first issue of the workers' weekly Trabalho e União was published in Funchal.
The Conde da Calçada, Diogo d'Ornelas Frazão, last holder of the França entail, died.
A clandestine paper 'O Garoto' ran for four issues until January 1907.
The statutes of the Stranger's Club (Casino Pavão) were dated.
Daniel Ferreira Pestana died in Nova Goa.
The Machico municipal annals were published in full in the Heraldo da Madeira.
The record of the acclamation at the Restoration of Portugal was first published in the Heraldo da Madeira.
The first issue of A Chacota appeared.
Vicente Gomes da Silva died in Funchal.
The first annual volume of the 'Ordens da Direcção da Alfândega do Funchal' covers this year.
The Duke of the Abruzzi visited Madeira in command of the cruiser Etna.
João da Câmara Pestana published a paper on wet root rot of the chestnut tree.
Tobacco cultivation was resumed in Madeira, though it did not become widespread.
Jaime Sanches Câmara published Poema Antigo in Lisbon.
D. Maria Helena Jervis de Atouguia e Almeida published Mosaicos.
Canon Henrique Modesto de Betencourt built and founded a chapel to the Sacred Heart of Jesus at Cardais, in Água de Pena parish.
A plague epidemic in Madeira caused intense public indignation; Dr António Balbino do Rego published two pamphlets on it.
João Franco's government took power and a Franquist political group formed in Madeira.
A short smallpox outbreak in Funchal was contained by isolating patients in the Gonçalo Aires lazaretto, where Miss Mary Jane Wilson directed the isolation hospital.
The new quay at Machico was modified and improved.
L. A. Dode published 'Un nouveau Sorbus', describing Sorbus maderensis, in the Bulletin de la Société Dendrologique de France.
Aires de Ornelas de Vasconcelos accompanied Prince Luís Filipe on a voyage to the African colonies.
The Faial bridge, about 130 metres long and the longest in Madeira, was built over the Ribeira do Faial.
Father Alphonse Luisier received a collection of Madeiran mosses and published his first note on them.
Eduardo de Castro e Almeida published volume I of the inventory of documents on Madeira and Porto Santo in the Arquivo da Marinha e Ultramar.
The Garantia Funchalense insurance company was founded in Funchal.
The second newspaper O Povo was published, issuing 1248 numbers until 30 September 1917.
A 40-réis Madeiran token was sold in Amsterdam for 6 florins.
Dr João Augusto Teixeira died in Funchal.
General Louis Botha passed through Funchal on his way to London.
Boaventura Mendes de Almeida was appointed civil governor of Funchal by decree of 13 June 1907 and took office on 3 August.
The autograph manuscript of Dr Julião Fernandes da Silva was discovered and bought by the Funchal Municipal Library.
A single-issue newspaper celebrating the anniversary of the Associação Protectora dos Estudantes Pobres was published.
A suspected disease in Santo António parish killed all 14 people it struck before being contained under Governor Boaventura Mendes de Almeida.
José Bettencourt de Abreu died, leaving his fortune to the works of São Martinho church.
An east wind (leste) brought an absolute maximum of 37.3 °C in the shade in Funchal.
The newspaper Revolucionário was published in six issues.

mentions.as_written: de 17 de Agosto a 7 de Outubro de 1907

summary: The last issue of A Chacota appeared.
A savings bank attached to the Monte-Pio Madeirense was approved.
José Dias Ferreira died at Vidago.
Helena M. J. Taylor died in England, aged about 65.
Bishop D. Manuel Agostinho Barreto blessed the new Gothic church of Jardim do Mar.
José Vicente Barbosa du Bocage died in Lisbon.
The first motor car began to circulate in Funchal.
The first issue of the seminary students' magazine Esperança appeared.
The newspaper Primeiro de Dezembro was published, issuing twenty numbers.

mentions.as_written: 1 Dezembro de 1907 a 3 de Maio de 1908

summary: Rui Barbosa visited Madeira and was given a luncheon before sailing for Brazil aboard the Araguaya.
Terceira commemorated the centenary of the birth of José Silvestre Ribeiro.
The building of the Misericórdia de Santa Cruz was repaired by order and at the expense of the State.
The Monte Medonho levada was diverted to irrigate Ribeira Brava and Tábua instead of São Vicente.
Eug. Simon published the description of Asphodelus madeirensis.
Carlos da Silva Carvalho's article Fichas Madeirenses appeared in the Almanach de lembranças Madeirense.
João da Câmara Pestana published a paper on destroying Lecanium hesperidum with a fungus.
The Companhia de Tabacos da Madeira was established in Funchal.
Football grew greatly in Madeira, promoted by Humberto de Passos Freitas.
Major repairs were made to the Espírito Santo chapel in Câmara de Lobos and its adjoining house.
The Resenha Cronológica do Jornalismo Madeirense was compiled under João Eleutério Martins and published by the Diário de Notícias.
The malacologist Ponsonby stayed in Madeira.
João Soares Branco served as deputy for Madeira.
José Ribeiro da Cunha represented Madeira in parliament.
Ernesto Jardim de Vilhena sat as deputy for Madeira in the 1908–1910 parliamentary session.
Funchal municipal council set terms for using the town hall tower as a telephone exchange.
Portugal banned the sweetening of Madeira wine with cane sugar.
The Junta Geral do Distrito built the larger present quay at Santa Cruz.
Alberto Artur Sarmento published a work on impressions of Funchal.
Th. Becker published his work on the Diptera of the Canaries and Madeira.
Funchal customs recorded imports of 2,012:000$00, exports of 750:000$00 and re-exports of 1,215:000$00.
Padre Luís Alves Martins was appointed royal preacher.
The Junta Geral built the landing stage at Campanário.
Alfred Merle Norman visited Madeira again.
'Notas sobre Portugal', containing João da Mota Prego's article, was shown at the national exhibition in Rio de Janeiro.
The landing stage at Porto Novo, Gaula, built by order of the Junta Geral, was completed.
The Grémio dos Empregados do Comércio Funchalense was founded.
King Carlos and Prince Luís Filipe were assassinated in Lisbon, ending João Franco's government; the Madeiran João Sabino da Costa was killed by Lisbon police in the aftermath.
João Rodrigues became the first Madeiran examined as a driver.
The statutes of the Novo Clube Restauração were dated.
João de Paiva was appointed civil governor of Funchal by decree on 22 February and took office on 9 March 1908.
Adolfo de Sousa Rodrigues died in Lisbon.
Funeral rites with a eulogy for King Carlos I and Prince Luís Filipe were held in Funchal Cathedral.
Carlos Azevedo de Meneses published his study of Porto Santo's vegetation in the Diario Popular of Funchal.
A general election was held for the deputies of Madeira.
Canon Alfredo César de Oliveira died in Évora.
The single issue of A Pena was published in honour of José Leite Monteiro.
Manuel II was acclaimed king in Funchal, without the customary procession.
Padre Ernesto Schmitz ceased directing the Seminary museum, was honoured by the single issue of Preito e Homenagem, and left Madeira on 7 July 1908 to direct the Hospice of St Paul in Jerusalem.
The first issue of A Voz da Madeira appeared.
Fire completely destroyed the parish church of Ponta Delgada.
The Santa Maria Maior conference of St Vincent de Paul was installed.
Negotiations for the buyback of the Hohenlohe sanatorium concession were concluded.
Funchal council signed a 400-conto loan with the Caixa Geral dos Depósitos for the city water supply works.
Parliament enacted a new sugar regime for Madeira that left the sugar monopoly largely unchanged.
Jean Charcot's Antarctic expedition aboard the Pourquoi-Pas? arrived at Funchal.
Article 31 of a law created the Viticulture Commission of Madeira.
A contract was signed for an Eastern Telegraph Company submarine cable.
A decree reformed the Viticulture Commission of Madeira.

mentions.as_written: Decreto de 1 de Outubro do mesmo ano

summary: The civil governor approved the statutes of Assistência a Crianças Fracas in Funchal.
The Rev. P. Murray died.
The last issue of Esperança appeared.
Aníbal Álvares da Silva died in Lisbon.
Dr Roland Krohn died of pulmonary tuberculosis in a Swiss sanatorium.
A short ramp was built giving access to the small beach at Ponta Delgada to ease the transport of goods.
Ella and Florence du Cane published The Flowers and Gardens of Madeira in London.
Johannes Richter published in Leipzig his study of the climatic basis of Madeiran agriculture.
A commission fixed the Várzea site for a rifle range, but local opposition halted progress.
Madeiran wine production recovered to 11,401 pipes after grafting and planting of Jacquez vines.
Alfredo Rodrigues Gaspar represented Portugal at the applied chemistry congress in London.
W. H. Koebel published 'Madeira old and new' in London.
Grupo Sportivo Internacional, Madeira's oldest sports club, was founded.
Padre Joaquim Plácido Pereira was ordained priest.
The second edition of Mosaicos by D. Maria Helena Jervis de Atouguia e Almeida appeared.
A tuna cannery was founded and inaugurated at Ponta da Cruz, Madeira.
A grey pearl the size of a pea was found in a fan shell in Madeira.
The Associação dos Industriais Madeirenses was founded.
Oak mildew (Oidium quercinum) was first observed in Madeira, on the oaks at Monte.
A small landing stage was built at the Campanário port.
The Junta Geral built the quay and landing stage at Ponta da Oliveira, Caniço.
Adaptation works began on the tower of the Funchal town hall.
Padre Manuel Fernandes de Sant'Ana published O Evangelho segundo S. Matheus.
The Junta Geral built an access stairway to the quay at Porto do Moniz.
João dos Reis Gomes published the novel A Filha de Tristão das Damas in Funchal.
H. N. Dixon published his contributions to the moss flora of Madeira.
Only one red cinchona tree survived in Madeira.
Padre João Maurício Henriques published a brief history of the extinct 12th Caçadores regiment.
Augusto José Vieira published the Historia do Partido Republicano.
Alfred Merle Norman published The Polyzoa of Madeira and Neighbouring Islands.
Eleonora Armitage botanised on Madeira in early 1909.
Volume II of Eduardo de Castro e Almeida's inventory of the Arquivo da Marinha e Ultramar was published.
Padre Camilo Torrend's three contributions on Madeiran fungi were published in Broteria.
A Portuguese translation of Avezac's study of Madeira appeared in nineteen issues of the Diario do Comercio.

mentions.as_written: dos meses de Janeiro a Abril de 1909

summary: Joaquim Pestana died in Câmara de Lobos.
António Aurélio da Costa Ferreira lectured on the Portuguese people from an anthropological viewpoint at the Lisbon Geographical Society.
The first wine regulation for Madeira was issued, limiting alcohol sales for winemaking to 50 litres per 500 litres of wine; Hinton & Sons contested it.
The council made its last annual subsidy payment to the Monte Railway company.
A German wine law regulated imports of Madeira wine.
Agostinho Martins died in Funchal.
Prince Albert of Belgium visited Madeira and was greeted by the district authorities.
Carlos de Meneses published an article on Madeiran lauraceae in the Diário da Madeira.
The first issue of the newspaper Brado d'Oeste appeared at Ponta do Sol.
A meeting discussed founding a Madeiran wine company, which was never established.
Princess Elisabeth of Belgium stayed in Madeira, arriving aboard the Araguaya and leaving for the Canaries aboard the Kamerun.
Anatole France called at Funchal on his South American voyage, leaving the same day.
The Viticulture Commission of Madeira held its inaugural session.
The bryologist A. Geheeb died.
The new diocesan seminary opened in its new building in the grounds of the Encarnação convent, under Bishop D. Manuel Agostinho Barreto.
The Pavilhão Paris was inaugurated in Funchal.
A decree modified Madeira's cereal regime.
A law authorised the government to rescind Prince Hohenlohe's sanatorium concession in Madeira, buying back its properties with compensation.
The American yacht Varuna, which had left Bermuda on 7 November, was wrecked on the coast of Achadas da Cruz with the loss of one sailor.
An order empowered the Visconde de Geraz de Lima to accept the buyback of the Hohenlohe sanatorium properties.
The São Vicente land registry office was installed.
The Funchal newspaper Diário do Commercio published an article on the subject connected with Dr. Julião Fernandes da Silva.
A municipal ordinance defined the limits of the urban area of Funchal.
The expenses of the Recolhimento das Órfãs amounted to 631$42 in the financial year 1909–1910.
Work on the new parish church of São Martinho resumed around 1909 or 1910.
Henrique Franco de Sousa first exhibited at the Sociedade Nacional de Belas-Artes, winning second- and third-class medals.
The internal and nursing services of the Santa Cruz Misericórdia hospital were in the charge of the Franciscan hospitaller sisters.
The restored Misericórdia confraternity was extinguished; it was restored again in 1927.
A bill to sell Madeira's state levadas was presented in parliament but lapsed in committee.
The flow of the Ribeiro Frio levada was measured at 40 litres per second.
Madeiran wine production over this period peaked at nearly 12 million litres in 1930.
After the Republican revolution the Franciscan sisters were expelled from the Convento de Santa Clara and from the Asilo dos Velhinhos, whose funding passed to the Junta Geral.
A cholera epidemic struck Madeira, causing about 550 deaths; Dr Carlos França was sent to direct sanitary services, and the lazaretto and a makeshift hospital at the Machico fort treated patients.
The União dos Viticultores da Madeira was founded early in the year with a capital of 100 contos de réis.
Birch saplings donated by a foreigner were sent to Porto Santo for planting.
Padre Longinos Navás published his synopsis of Madeiran lichens in Brotéria.
Jaime Sanches Câmara published the satire O funeral do Cyriaco in Funchal.
The Ponta da Cruz cannery exported a record 557,085 kg of tuna.
Eugène Ackermann's book on Madeira, reporting iron ore at Câmara de Lobos, was published at Rixheim, Alsace.
The book 'Uma Tragédia na Madeira' was published.
A girls' primary school was created at Ponta do Pargo.
An edition of A. Samler Brown's guide with 20 maps and plans was published.
Manuel Ribeiro's Outomnaes was published in Funchal.
Rev. Schodduyn identified several Madeiran freshwater algae sent by the Elucidário's author.
The Republic was proclaimed while the Madeiran Republican party was weak; several civil governors succeeded one another and Rua da Princesa was renamed Rua 31 de Janeiro.
J. A. Júdice Fialho, with Algarve fishermen, set up an unsuccessful tuna trap in Porto Santo bay, introducing the mujona.
José Ramos Coelho's Obras Completas were published in Lisbon.
Reconstruction of the church of Ponta Delgada began.
A five-volume edition of Garcia de Resende's Cancioneiro Geral was published.
Francisco Franco won the Valmor Bequest scholarship and went to study in Paris.
Administration of the Recolhimento do Bom Jesus passed to a commission appointed by the civil governor.
Eleonora Armitage published papers on Madeiran hepatics and intensive cultivation in Madeira.
Padre Alphonse Luisier lost his collections during the 1910 revolution.
Joana de Castelo Branco published Fluctuações in Lisbon.
Jaime de Gouveia Barreto was ordained priest.
Dr Afonso de Melo Pinto Veloso was appointed civil governor of the Funchal district by decree of 27 January and took office on 24 February.
The new cemetery of Fajã da Ovelha was blessed and opened.
Club Sports da Madeira was founded.
The two issues of the newspaper O Rebelde appeared.

mentions.as_written: 30 de Março e 15 de Setembro de 1910

summary: José Carlos de Faria e Castro died at Raudamy castle.
João Joaquim de Freitas died in Funchal.
Padre Manuel Fernandes de Sant'Ana died in Lisbon.
The first issue of the monthly Commercio do Funchal appeared.
João de Freitas Branco died in Lisbon aged 55.
Meneses published phenology articles in the Diário da Madeira.
Scott's Antarctic expedition ship Terra Nova called at Funchal.
José Ribeiro da Cunha was appointed civil governor for the fourth time, taking office on 13 July.

Jacinto do Carmo Sá Penela published O Incendio da Escola Naval.
A compilation of press articles on three bills, including the colonia contract, was published.
The 'Pedro Álvares Cabral' mutual-aid association was established in Funchal.
Manuel de Sousa Brasão served in Mozambique.
The road from Câmara de Lobos via Ribeira Brava to the Encumeada de São Vicente opened, making it reachable by car.
The Assembleia dos Unicos do Funchal charity spent 1:090$220 réis in the financial year.
The first edition of Vitorino José dos Santos's verse book Lágrimas was published in Funchal.
Berlese and Paoli published their description of Prospaltella in Redia, vol. XI.
The last Manueline ruins of the Machico customs house were demolished.
Funchal council petitioned the government for Santa Clara convent's historic articles for the museum.
Frederico Pinto Coelho died in Funchal.
The last issue of Parochia de Santo Antonio do Funchal was published.
Madeiran deputies presented bills to sell the levadas and reform the colonia contract; debated in the Funchal press, they were defeated by opposition in Madeira.
A bill granting autonomy to the Junta Agrícola was presented to Parliament but not approved.
A decree authorised the seizure of enemy ships in Portuguese ports.
António Pereira Reis served as Minister of the Interior after Germany declared war on Portugal.
Portuguese authorities occupied four German steamers in Funchal bay.
The Funchal schooner Senhora da Conceição was sunk off France.
A law reduced municipal councils to 24, 16 and 12 councillors, leaving administrative tribunal powers unchanged.
Comendador Manuel Gonçalves died in Monte parish.
The only issue of the newspaper O Chicote was published.
The Brado d'Oeste published an extensive article on the Reis Magos chapel at Lombo dos Reis, Estreito da Calheta, and its entail.
The Diário da Madeira reprinted Mario de Almeida's account of Princess Maria Amélia's last days.
Antero Drumond de Meneses died in Lisbon.
Miss Mary Jane Wilson died in Câmara de Lobos.
Funchal council rescinded the water-supply works contract because war had raised material costs.

The German submarine U-38 torpedoed three ships in Funchal harbour, including the French gunboat Surprise (33 crew and 7 Portuguese killed), and shelled the city, causing widespread panic. The victims were later commemorated by a monument made by Francisco Franco.
A third newspaper called O Imparcial appeared, lasting only a few numbers.
Decree no. 2922 established official time.
A second newspaper called O Progresso began publication.
Madeira's wine production fell to about 2.8 million litres, the lowest of the period.
The Funchal district recorded 3,631 deaths, 890 of them from diarrhoea and enteritis.
The Club Naval Madeirense was founded, its statutes being dated 20 July 1917.
Table tennis was introduced to Madeira.
Poetisas Portuguesas, including poems by D. Maria Helena Jervis de Atouguia e Almeida, was published.
Seventeen students enrolled in the first academic year of the Funchal navigation school, four passing to the second year.
The Montanha battery was built to defend Funchal against submarines.
The São Jorge lignite, long buried by landslides, was exposed again.
Alfredo Vital Miguéis was transferred to the Escola Industrial do Funchal.
The road to Pico dos Barcelos was built.
Early in 1917 the Red Cross first-aid post opened in the Rua dos Netos, Funchal.
The interior of the parish church of Curral das Freiras was substantially repaired.
Augusto Elmano Vieira's A Ultima Bênção was published in Funchal.
Juvenal Henriques de Araújo published his pamphlet on the expropriation of the Montado do Barreiro.
The salient of the north bastion of the Fortaleza de São Lourenço was cut to align the Avenida Dr. Manuel de Arriaga.
Carlos Elói Mota Freitas completed the Naval School course.
The 'Pedro Álvares Cabral' mutual aid association was legalised by alvará.
The current statutes of the Montepio Madeirense were approved.
The Sé clock in Funchal was advanced one hour at the military authority's request.
Construction of the São Martinho rifle range began.
Manuel de Arriaga died in Lisbon.
Rua da Mouraria in Funchal was renamed Rua do Dr. Sequeira.
Clemente de Freitas da Silva died in Ponta do Sol.
Tomás Nunes de Serra e Moura died in Lisbon.
João Paulo da Veiga Pestana was posted as officer cadet to Infantry Regiment 30.
The funds of the Asilo de Artes e Ofícios reached 22,000$000 réis and their income was ceded to the Asilo da Mendicidade e Órfãos in Funchal.
A newspaper advertisement invited subscriptions for an electric tramway company in Funchal, but nobody responded.
The Regional Chamber of Agriculture held its last session.
Urbano Canuto Soares came to Funchal to research Padre Manuel Alvares for the Ministry of Public Instruction.

As acting head of the district, António Jardim de Oliveira ordered maize unloaded from a Portuguese ship to avert famine; the act was disapproved and he was replaced by Colonel Sousa Rosa, prompting large demonstrations of support in Funchal on 7 and 9 August.
José de Sousa Rosa was appointed civil governor of Funchal by decree on 3 August 1917, took office on the 7th and served until 28 September.
The periodical Trabalho e União published a long article on mutualism.
João Paulo da Veiga Pestana was promoted to second lieutenant.
João Paulo da Veiga Pestana left for France with the Portuguese Expeditionary Corps.
Jaime Constantino de Freitas Moniz died in Lisbon.
A further forestry and grazing decree was issued for Madeira, but it was judged ineffective and never fully enforced.
Daniel Telo Simões Soares took office as civil governor of Funchal for the first time.
Gabriel Rocha de Gouveia was killed by shell fragments in the trenches in France.
A decree created the navigation school in Funchal.
The monument to the victims of the 1916 German bombardment of Funchal was inaugurated in the Angústias cemetery.
A German submarine bombarded Funchal for the second time, killing five people in the city and badly damaging Santa Clara church.
The bombardment victims' monument in the Angústias cemetery was handed over to the Funchal municipal council.
Carlos José Baeta Pinto Feio was appointed civil governor of the Funchal district by decree.
The Sindicato Agrícola Estreitense was founded in Estreito de Câmara de Lobos.
The 1 May procession followed its old route for the only time after the Republic, accompanied by two council members.
Funchal had 34 embroidery export houses after the wartime crisis.
He published Junia in Lisbon.
The Junta Geral commissioned the maquette of Zargo's statue.
The Associação dos Industriais de Destilação da Madeira was founded.
He published the pamphlet Rosario de Lágrimas.
A position artillery company defended Funchal against German attack.
Only 113 vessels entered Funchal, the lowest figure of the First World War period.
Construction of the chapel at Fajã do Penedo began.
A mainland Portuguese cultivator successfully trialled rice growing in São Vicente parish.
He died in Portugal.
Four central schools were created in Funchal.
He served as deputy for Madeira.
He graduated in letters at the University of Lisbon.
Armitage published a paper on the habitats of Madeiran bryophytes in the Journal of Ecology.
Second edition of 'Lágrimas' published in Coimbra.
An inlaid table was offered to President Sidónio Pais.
Last issue, no. 858.
Funchal steamer Neptuno torpedoed en route from Lisbon.
First issue of the newspaper A União of Ponta do Sol.
Feio arrived and took office as civil governor.
A second newspaper named A Luz began publication.
Feio left for Lisbon, soon resigning.
He was taken prisoner by the Germans in the great battle of that day.
Battle of the Lys, in which many Madeirans were killed or captured.
Ensign Veiga Pestana died in combat in France.
The first issue of O Desporto was published.
Funchal Municipal Council sold its small property at Fajãzinha de Bento with government authorisation.
A decree created district general commissioners, probably not applied in Funchal.
The first issue of the second newspaper titled O Madeirense appeared.
Duarte de Melo Ponces de Carvalho was elected deputy for Madeira.
The Chamber was abolished when agricultural services were reorganised.
The office was installed in the new bishop's palace at Ribeiro Real.
A decree created eleven agricultural regions, making Madeira the ninth, with its seat in Funchal.
A decree established eight forestry districts and eighteen forestry regencies, with Funchal as regency no. 18.
The constitution of the Clube Naval Madeirense was notified to the authorities.
Barreto left for France as chaplain of the Portuguese Expeditionary Corps.
He was appointed civil governor of the district by decree.
Rosa ceased to be military commander of the archipelago.
The first issue of the newspaper O Seringa was published.
He took office as civil governor.
The new parish church of São Martinho was consecrated.
Decree no. 4560 created customs clearance posts in Porto Santo, Câmara de Lobos and Machico, though not yet implemented.
The twelfth issue of O Seringa appeared, believed to be the last.
The Junta Agrícola resolved to hand the street built for the cold store to the municipal council.
O Atlantico published its twelve issues.
D. João de Alarcão died.
Colonel Eduardo Agostinho Pereira died.
Founding date given for the Empresa Madeirense de Tabacos, Lda.
The minesweeper Augusto Castilho was sunk by a German submarine while escorting the steamer São Miguel, killing Mota Freitas and its commander.
The minesweeper Augusto de Castilho was sunk by a German submarine near the Azores; the San Miguel escaped with passengers from Madeira.
Minesweeper Augusto de Castilho fought a German submarine; Mota Freitas was killed.
The viscount was shot dead in Lisbon with six other political prisoners while being escorted to a fortress.
João Pestana Júnior died while studying law at Coimbra.
He died in Sintra.
The first issue of the periodical O Nacional appeared.
Brum do Canto died in Lisbon aged 33.
The transport Lake Forest arrived in Madeira with American Red Cross food aid and Harrison Dibblee.
A dinner at the Palácio de São Lourenço and popular demonstrations honoured Dibblee and the American consul.
Public street lighting was restored in Funchal on news of the Armistice ending the First World War.
Harrison Dibblee left Madeira for Norfolk, Virginia.
Hector Léveillé died at Le Mans.
A law reformed the industrial schools and the curriculum of the Funchal industrial school, creating an inlay workshop.
The first issue of the Funchal newspaper O Vigilante was published.
The statutes of the Sindicato Agrícola Estreitense were published in the Diário do Governo.
Augusto José Vieira died in Lisbon.
A Republican Guard force arrived in Madeira.
Spanish flu and pneumonic influenza struck Madeira.
The first three students of the Escola de Pilotagem completed the course and qualified for the pilot's certificate.
Madeira imported 4,511 tonnes of wheat and 690 tonnes of flour.
Maria dos Anjos Ribeiro had a chapel of the Immaculate Heart of Mary built at Fajã do Penedo, Boaventura.
Luís de Ornelas Nóbrega de Quintal was elected deputy for India and appointed head of a department of the Colonial Ministry.
During the monarchist uprising Jorge Perestrelo Velosa Camacho was arrested in Beja.
Carlos Olavo Correia de Azevedo's book on captivity in Germany was published in Lisbon.
The rebuilt church of Ponta Delgada was consecrated.
The Asilo da Mendicidade issued small-change notes.
Dr Pedro Góis Pita represented Madeira as deputy in Parliament.
António Jardim de Oliveira retired from the civil government.
Augusto Elmano Vieira was a leader of the academic strike.
Eduardo Antonino Pestana completed the course of the Escola Normal Superior.
Decree no. 5086 created the commemorative medal of the Portuguese Army's campaigns.
The typographers published the single issue of O Gráfico.
The first issue of the periodical O Germinal appeared.
The last issue, no. 77, of the second O Madeirense appeared.
The last issue, no. 23, of O Nacional appeared.
The last issue of the Boletim Eclesiástico da Madeira appeared.
Jorge Perestrelo Velosa Camacho was murdered by a civilian while crossing the Terreiro do Paço under escort.
A branch of the Banco Nacional Ultramarino opened in Funchal.
Dean João Joaquim Pinto died in Funchal.
Dr Manuel Augusto Martins was again appointed civil governor of Funchal, taking office on 19 February and leaving in May on election as deputy.
The newspaper Trabalho e União reported the formation of the Madeiran Labour party.
Raising of the chancel floor of Santa Clara church in Funchal uncovered the tombstones of the second, third and fifth captains-donatary, but not Zarco's.
The Sindicato Agrícola Estreitense elected its governing bodies.
Francisco Franco's maquette of the Zarco statue was exhibited in the municipal theatre of Funchal.
The statutes of the Cooperativa Popular were approved.
A radio-telegraph station was inaugurated on Porto Santo, ending the island's isolation.
Hinton's lease of the José Júlio de Lemos sugar factory ended.
The outgoing commission of the Recolhimento do Bom Jesus handed over 437$15 to its successor.
The British wartime wireless post at Quinta Santana ceased operating.
Funchal council renamed Rua das Hortas as Rua do Alferes Veiga Pestana.
Decrees, including Decree 5492 of 2 May, ended the sugar monopoly and declared sugar manufacture free from 1 January 1920.

mentions.as_written: 12 de Abril e 2 de Maio de 1919

summary: At the request of the Associação do Registo Civil, the Travessa do Surdo was renamed after Augusto José Vieira.
José Mendes dos Reis was elected deputy for Madeira.
A decree modifying the sugar regime abolished the Junta Agrícola; its Areeiro station passed to the Junta Geral and the Estação Agrária took over forestry matters.
Decree 5492 fixed at 55 litres the alcohol allowed to treat a 500-litre pipe of wine.
A decree authorised brandy and melado taxes and assigned them to the Junta Geral to fund the Ninth Agricultural Region's station.
Some 289 political prisoners from the monarchist revolt, among them Salema Vaz, landed in Funchal from the steamer Africa and were interned in the Gonçalo Aires lazaretto.
Funchal council renamed Rua do Aljube after Carvalho de Araújo.
Funchal council renamed the Travessa da Sacristia after cadet Carlos Elói Mota e Freitas.
A decree abolished most normal schools, transforming Funchal's Escola Normal into the Escola Primária Superior.
Decree-law 5.787 introduced a new water regime that endangered levada rights.
A decree created independent company no. 1 of the Republican Guard in Funchal.
In the parliamentary elections Américo Olavo Correia de Azevedo and José Miguel Lamartine Prazeres da Costa were elected deputies and Heitor Passos senator for Madeira.
Seven political deportees held in Madeira were freed by telegram from the minister of war.
The last known issue of the second newspaper O Progresso appeared.
Augusto José da Cunha died.
Alfredo Ernesto de Sá Cardoso became president of the ministry.
The remaining political deportees in Madeira were shipped to Lisbon between June and August.
Padre Jaime de Gouveia Barreto returned to Portugal from France.
The escape of eight political deportees, including the Conde de Sucena, from Madeira to Las Palmas was discovered.
A decree transferred the staff of the Junta Agrícola to the 9th agricultural region under the Junta Geral.
Daniel Telo Simões Soares took office as civil governor of Funchal for the second time.
The Treaty of Versailles was signed, including articles protecting wine designations such as Madeira.
A law created a municipal tax on tobacco cleared through customs.
The naturalist Ernst Haeckel, a visitor to Madeira, died.
The former Seminary of the Incarnation in Funchal was ceded to the Junta Geral (for 7,500 escudos, or 9 contos by another account).

During a long leste wind, which brought Funchal's highest recorded shade temperature (38.4°), fires set criminally, reportedly by angry herders, destroyed much of Madeira's forest, including pine woods at Monte and São Roque, until rain put them out, causing over 2,000 contos of damage.
The chapel of the Immaculate Heart of Mary at Boaventura was solemnly blessed by Bishop António Manuel Pereira Ribeiro.
The Diário da Madeira published two unpublished letters written by Júlio Dinis in Madeira.
The seat of the western school district moved from Ribeira Brava to Funchal.
A locomotive boiler explosion on the Monte railway killed four people and injured many.
The Junta Geral abolished the Escola de Utilidades e Belas Artes and installed its offices in the former Incarnation convent/seminary building.
The Escola Primária Superior of Funchal began operating.
Funchal council ordered the two current municipal flags.
The first issue of Gente Nova appeared.
A bill allowing Madeira wines the same alcohol quantities as port was sought in Parliament but not approved.
J. Cruz Baptista Santos became administrator of the Campo da Barca disinfection post, replacing the retiring Manuel Sardinha.
J. C. Berkeley Cotter died.
The first Republican Guard contingent arrived in Funchal aboard the Quelimane.
Professor Cockerell surveyed the archipelago's coccids, recording over thirty species.
The 1920 census gave Madeira 179,000 inhabitants.
Madeira had 22 dairy factories and over 30 skimming stations.
Jaime Sanches Câmara published the verse tragedy 'Galateia'; Alberto Figueira Jardim published 'Fructos'.
The yacht Gonçalves Zargo was built at Cabrestante.
José Nunes da Mata visited Madeira.
Dr Vasco Gonçalves Marques joined the Republican Party of National Reconstitution.
The brandy resale tax yielded 82:434$87, mostly shared among the municipal councils.
Only 50 to 60 British people lived permanently in Funchal.
Pestana Júnior published 'O Reconhecimento da Madeira', proposing a new date for the island's discovery.
Funchal municipal revenue included 101.700$00 from the deposit for the city's sanitation works.
The census recorded 1,093 inhabitants in Madalena do Mar parish.
The 1920 census recorded 6,190 inhabitants in Ponta do Sol parish and 24,284 in the city of Funchal.
Martin Vahl made his second stay in Madeira and also visited Porto Santo.
Augusto Elmano Vieira completed his law degree at Lisbon.
Eduardo Antonino Pestana graduated in law at the University of Lisbon.
At the height of the embroidery industry Funchal had 60 export houses and over 35,000 embroiderers worked in Madeira and Porto Santo.
Joana de Castelo Branco died in Lisbon.
The first issue of Ecos da Madeira appeared.
The first issue of O Operário appeared.
João Maria de Santiago Presado was proclaimed deputy for Madeira unopposed.
Three descendants of the female line of the Phelps family visited Funchal.
Service on the Monte railway resumed after the explosion.
The last issue, number 61, of O Vigilante was published.
A violent storm with great gales struck Madeira, leaving over 500 homeless and bringing down the Areeiro instrument tower.
Demolition began in Funchal for the Avenida António José de Almeida.
A man aged 101 died in Madeira.
Conselheiro José Leite Monteiro died.
Luís de Ornelas Pinto Coelho died in Funchal.
The tenth and last issue of the first series of Gente Nova appeared.
Law no. 960 freed trade in national wheat and set rules for imported wheat and bread prices.
Conselheiro João Baptista de Freitas Leal died in Funchal aged 82.
The Cooperativa Popular opened its establishments.
Decree 6521 modified the 1919 sugar decree.
A decree on the sugar question left unrepealed provisions considered harmful to cane growers; it remained in force when the Elucidário was written.
Vasco Crispiniano da Silva was appointed civil governor of the Funchal district and was relieved at his own request on 1 October 1920.
Os Novos published its first issue; its tenth and probably last appeared in November 1920.
Regulations for the brandy resale tax were issued.
Most Madeiran Democrats decided to join the Reconstituição Nacional party.
A plaque to Corporal João de Andrade was unveiled at the Colégio barracks.
The Banco da Madeira opened in Funchal.
The Madeiran Evolutionists resolved to stay united as a group.
A man aged 106 died in Madeira.
Leacock & C.ª admitted Diogo Martinho de Freitas as partner.
A meeting was held in Funchal to plan a monument to the Conde de Canavial.
A Esperança published an artistic description of the Capela do Santo Espírito.
António da Cruz Rodrigues dos Santos served as civil governor of the Funchal district.
Brito Pais and Sarmento Beires took off from Amadora to fly to Madeira but ditched in the sea.
The Ministry of the Interior classified Madeira's municipalities into three orders.
Father César Martinho Fernandes died at Jardim do Mar.
The first issue of the Revista de Direito appeared.
A woman aged 103 died in Madeira.
Luís Maria dos Reis died as a retired general.
Funchal municipal council voted 200 escudos to install an oceanographic museum and 50 escudos a month for its upkeep.
Alberto Artur Sarmento was a provisional teacher at the Funchal lyceum.
The Calheta Misericórdia building had recently been restored.
The portrait of D. Josefina de Castelo Branco Ribeiro da Cunha hung in the sessions room of the Misericórdia do Funchal's administrative commission.
Pterygium was reported still to occur widely in Madeira.
Madeira had about 30,000 hectares of uncultivated land, some 10,000 of which yielded only grazing.
England was the chief importer of Madeiran wickerwork and raw osiers.
Armando Eduardo Pinto Correia published the pamphlet Um Poeta em frangalhos.
José Maria Malheiro represented the Malheiro family in Funchal.
The 1921 census recorded parish populations across Madeira, including 4,083 in the Sé, 3,107 in Santana and 7,061 in São Pedro.
Madeiran maize output stood at about 6,000 hectolitres, most consumption being imported.
The first volume of the Elucidário Madeirense was published.
Dr José Varela was elected senator for Madeira.
Jaime Sanches Câmara published Carta em prosa.
Salema Vaz published Pão do Exílio in Lisbon.
Feliciano Soares and Emanuel Vitorino Ribeiro published the pamphlet 'Terra! Terra!' on the discovery of Madeira.
José Nunes da Mata published a pamphlet on air navigation between Portugal and Madeira.
There was much talk of establishing an oceanographic museum in Funchal.
The name tubarão for Carcharias microps was known only to Caniçal fishermen.
Emanuel Ribeiro was teacher and director of an industrial school in Porto.
Madeira had about 169,000 inhabitants, only about a hundred of them Protestants.
João Prim Garibaldi e Costa's lecture Conferencia was published in Funchal.
Sixteen women lived in the Recolhimento das Órfãs with a regente, porteira and servente, supported by Misericórdia subsidies.
Luís de Ornelas Nóbrega de Quintal left to govern the Cuanza Sul district.
Adolfo de Noronha was preparing a publication on the shells of Porto Santo's raised beach.
Membership dues of the Sociedade Protectora dos Animais Domésticos were 50 centavos.
The Ponta do Pargo lighthouse buildings were complete but awaited a lantern delayed by the European war.
An orfeão was formed in Funchal under Dr Manuel Passos de Freitas.
Angélique de Beer Lomelino ended her post as piano professor at the Lisbon Conservatory.
The author urged the Funchal municipality to acquire Zarco's sword.
Madeira produced about 25 million kg of potatoes a year, about 10,000 kg per hectare.
A sharp post-war rise in Madeira's cost of living drove some wages 20 to 30 times above pre-war levels and firewood prices up sixfold, hardening life for formerly comfortable classes.
Maritime pine covered at least about 2,000 hectares in Madeira, while stone pine was almost abandoned.
Jacinto do Carmo Sá Penela published a chronological note on the Academy of Midshipmen and Naval School.
Dr Manuel Gomes Jardim was appointed canon of Funchal Cathedral.
About 250 British people were in Funchal to spend the winter.
The Missão Marquês de Pombal school in Funchal had 40 pupils.
Dr António Balbino do Rego served as physician in Lisbon's civil hospitals and director of the police anthropometric post.
José de Barros e Sousa's Preceitos de Moral da Infância was published.
Manuel Pereira da Silva addressed recruits of infantry regiments 12 and 34 at a flag presentation.
The Madeiran wickerwork industry was reported to be in decline.
Francisco Franco made a bronze aviators' monument for the Funchal Municipal Garden.
Dr Pedro Góis Pita published 'Pratica d'Advocacia' in Coimbra.
Treasury revenue in the Funchal district reached 3,080,248$18 in 1921–1922, the highest in the series.
The chapel of São Cândido in Câmara de Lobos was recorded as in ruins.
Stables remained in Rua da Queimada de Cima despite press campaigns for their removal.
After Manuel de Arriaga's death the Funchal theatre was again named Teatro Dr. Manuel de Arriaga.
António Jardim de Oliveira returned to Funchal and resumed practising law.
Augusto César de Gouveia successfully grew tea at Fajã da Ovelha.
The Poiso refuge house came under Caminata's superintendence.
Augusto Elmano Vieira was a member of the Funchal municipal council.
The Fort of São José on Porto Santo was ceded to the fiscal guard.
João Cabral do Nascimento was an editor of the Coimbra newspaper Restauração.
The Madeiran partridge was considered rare.
Manuel Teixeira Gomes was Portugal's representative in England.
James Yate Johnson's herbarium was recorded as being in good condition at the Seminary Museum in Funchal.
The Fortress of São Tiago served as barracks for Mountain Artillery Battery no. 3.
The price of milk was fixed at 10 centavos for butter-making and 14 for cheese-making.
A decree authorised the definitive constitution of the Banco da Madeira.
General João Alfredo de Faria died shortly after his promotion to general.
Alfredo Bettencourt da Câmara died in Funchal.
The periodical Gente Nova resumed publication.
Law no. 1123 granted a campaign medal to soldiers who served in the defence of Funchal during the Great War.
Floods struck Machico and Ribeira Brava, killing four children.
Gago Coutinho and Sacadura Cabral made the first flight from Lisbon to Funchal in the seaplane F-3.
The programme of national honours to the Unknown Soldiers was published in the Diário do Governo.

The urn of the Unknown Soldier of Africa arrived at Funchal on the Briton, lay in state at the town hall and was embarked on the cruiser República for Lisbon; General Norton de Matos joined the procession.

summary: The aviators' seaplane caught fire at Porto Santo while taking off for Lisbon.
Funchal flew flags at half-mast and rang bells while the Unknown Soldiers lay in state in Lisbon.
Urbano Canuto Soares delivered a Latin oration when Porto conferred honorary doctorates on Joffre, Diaz and Smith-Dorrien.
Engineer Sá Viana arrived in Madeira to organise the Ninth Agricultural Region.
The monument to the aviators Gago Coutinho and Sacadura Cabral was inaugurated in the Jardim Municipal.
The last issue of the Revista de Direito appeared.
General Smuts called at Madeira on the Arundel Castle, was received by the authorities and left the same day for England.
António Augusto da Silva Pires was appointed civil governor of Funchal.
Silva Pires took office as civil governor of Funchal.
Dr Manuel Augusto Martins was elected senator for Madeira.
Captain Manuel da Costa Dias visited Madeira to reorganise the Democratic party.
The first issue of Vida Diocesana appeared.
The Orfeão Madeirense gave its first public performances at the Teatro Dr. Manuel de Arriaga.
Parliamentary elections were held in Madeira: Vasco Gonçalves Marques was re-elected senator, Manuel de Sousa Brasão elected deputy, and the Catholic party's candidate failed.
Election riots at Câmara de Lobos injured Américo Olavo and Manuel Augusto Martins.
Civil governor Silva Pires left for Lisbon.
The Countess of Ribeiro Real, benefactor of the Funchal Asylum, died in Funchal.
Shops closed and riots broke out in Funchal against a proposed rise in the price of bread.
Rodrigo Rodrigues's name first appeared on the payroll of the Funchal finance office.
Vergílio Saque was appointed civil governor of Funchal district but never took office.
The Montepio Madeirense had 1,134 members.
A committee was formed to raise a monument to Mota Freitas, whose War Cross insignia were exhibited.
The Diário da Madeira published an article advocating a silk industry in Madeira.
Shackleton's Quest, bound for the Antarctic, and Schmidt's Dana called at Funchal.
French minister Albert Sarraut visited Funchal aboard the cruiser Gueydon, which left for Brest the next day.
The new clock for Funchal Cathedral arrived aboard the Walmer Castle.
Acácio Augusto Correia Pinto was appointed civil governor of Funchal by decree and took office on 23 November.
Ex-Emperor Charles and ex-Empress Zita of Austria arrived in exile at Funchal aboard HMS Cardiff.
António da Cruz Rodrigues dos Santos was reappointed civil governor of Funchal but declined.
General Mangin visited Funchal aboard the cruiser Jules Michelet, which left for France with the remains of the Surprise sailors after a procession from the Angústias cemetery.
A decree amended the cereal regime so that Funchal flour and bread prices were fixed by central government.
Independent republicans and Liberals in Madeira joined the Democratic group.
The Government withdrew the licence of the Companhia Atlântica de Pescarias.
The foundation stone of the monument to the Conde de Canavial was laid in Funchal.
The Madeiran victims of the sinking of the Surprise were laid to rest in a tomb-monument at the Angústias cemetery.
The Diário de Notícias published a memoir on the Piornais levada.

An English translation, 'The Climate of Madeira', was published.
The first Regional Scout Camp was held in Madeira.
Terra Negra published a pamphlet on Madeira as the 'Island of Love', read by the Elucidário's author.
The Diário da Madeira published an article on Madeiran regional dress.
The official gazette listed 62 Funchal residents entitled to compensation for damage from the First World War submarine attacks.
A decree approved a 44,000-conto plan for Madeira's complementary road network, 75% state-funded.
Herculano Amorim Ferreira visited Madeira to study its weather service.
A decree adopted measures protecting the export of Madeiran fruit and horticultural produce.
Decrees regulated the dairy Junta; rural resistance led to riots, deaths and deportations.

mentions.as_written: 22 de Setembro e 24 de Novembro de 1938 e 24 de Novembro de 1939

summary: The Escola Industrial António Augusto de Aguiar moved into the former Asilo dos Velhinhos building.
The military hospital left the Rochinha building and its first patients entered the Hospital dos Marmeleiros.
Alfredo Rodrigues Gaspar died in Lisbon.
The Mercado dos Lavradores, Funchal's main market, was inaugurated.
Funchal council improved Barreirinha beach and its access path for bathing.
The Avenida do Mar in Funchal was inaugurated.
A shelter house was built near the summit of Pico Ruivo.
Book I of Saudades da Terra was published in Ponta Delgada.
Madeira's Casa dos Pescadores began operating.
The Delegação de Turismo built a rest house and shelter in Serra de Água near the Encumeada.
Vicente Henriques de Gouveia published the second edition of his book on the banana.
The Pilar de Banger in Funchal was demolished despite protests from the local press.
A scout leaders' congress was held at Camacha.
A municipal park for poor children named after D. Maria Lívia Nosolini was inaugurated at the Praça Académica.
The Junta Autónoma dos Portos began publishing an annual tide table for Funchal.
A ministerial order made the Junta Geral and the Câmara cover the Misericórdia hospital's deficits.
Mary Jane Wilson's remains were transferred to her congregation's chapel in Rua do Carmo.
The monument to Dr Alexandre da Cunha Teles was inaugurated.
A further decree adopted measures protecting fruit and horticultural exports.
Decree-law 29.718 created a technical mission to study Madeira's hydro-electric and irrigation potential and hydraulic works.
Decree 29.742 granted the Junta Geral a subsidy for repairs to the São Lourenço palace.
Civil governor José Nosolini issued a regulation on must purchase and wine export.
The João Diniz springs disappeared during repair works on the São Lourenço palace.
The Diário da Madeira published an article on Zarco's sword.
The Areeiro meteorological post was enlarged with further instruments.
The Central Council of the women's Conferences of St Vincent de Paul was constituted.
A decree reorganised the Laboratory of Bacteriology and Hygiene into bacteriological and chemical sections.
A flood of the Ribeira da Madalena destroyed dozens of homes and killed several people.
J. C. de Morais published a geological study of the Selvagens.
The 1940 census counted about 250,000 inhabitants in the Madeira archipelago (figures of 251,798 and 249,771 are given).
The 1940 census recorded 2,701 inhabitants on Porto Santo.
The Tourism Delegation built a pousada near the Lapa da Cadela for climbers of Pico Ruivo.
The Associação de Natação do Funchal was founded.
The Second World War cut ship arrivals at Funchal to 389, 234, 190 and 187 a year between 1940 and 1943.
The Associação dos Irmãos de São João de Deus ended as the Order gained legal personality under the Concordat.
At the end of 1940 a monument commemorating the first Madeiran settlers was unveiled at Sá da Bandeira, Angola.
Pires de Matos published a geodesy article on Madeira in the Anais do Club Militar Naval.
The chapel of Nossa Senhora dos Remédios e Amparo at the Quinta de São João, built by the Bettencourt da Câmara family, was blessed on 1 January 1940.
A decree reorganised the Madeira military command under a brigadier or colonel.
A decree extended the Junta Nacional do Vinho to Madeira.
Major improvements at the Marmeleiros hospital, including wards for 120 patients and three operating theatres, were inaugurated.
The Diário do Governo published a list of national monuments and properties of public interest including Madeiran buildings such as the Casa de Dona Mécia.
The Diocesan Museum of Sacred Art was solemnly inaugurated in the chapter house of Funchal Cathedral.
Vicente Henriques de Gouveia was permanently appointed director of the Bacteriology and Hygiene Laboratory.
The Junta Geral voted a surcharge on water rents to fund levada repairs.
Decree-law no. 30.896 governed the position of permanent staff serving on commissions.
A scout exhibition marked the centenaries of Portugal's foundation and restoration.
The new Municipal Slaughterhouse of Funchal was built.
Sperm-whaling began in Madeira, with catches at Porto Moniz and Porto da Cruz.
A cross raised by the Juventude Antoniana commemorating Portugal's centenaries was inaugurated on Pico dos Barcelos.
Gustavo Teixeira Dias was appointed civil governor of Funchal.
The Sanatório Doutor João Francisco de Almada was solemnly inaugurated.
The value of fish landed in Madeira rose from 2,725 to 4,800 contos.
The Diário de Notícias published an editorial on livestock development.
Weather stations were set up at Encumeada, Lugar de Baixo and the Monte Sanatorium.
The Porto Santo weather station was set up.
Padre Eduardo Pereira's lecture on Porto Santo was published in the Diário de Notícias of Funchal.
The technical mission on the levadas completed its reports at the end of 1941.
Funchal Council unveiled a bust of António Nobre in the Jardim do Ribeiro Seco.
João Abel de Freitas, president of the Junta Geral, described the rainwater channel under construction on Porto Santo.
Funchal council revived its traditional devotions to St James and moved its holiday to 21 August.
103 sperm whales were landed at Porto Moniz and Reis Magos, plus one at Porto da Cruz.
A historical monograph on the Desterro chapel was published.
The long-profaned chapel of the Quinta do Leme was restored to worship.
The Santana weather station was set up.
Dr João Francisco de Almada died in Funchal.
Classes began in the new lyceum building in Funchal.
An article on the Santa Catarina chapel was published in the Jornal.
The public works department measured the flows and lengths of the state levadas for the first time in many years; the Rabaçal levadas were measured at 65 and 86 l/s.
J. Brito Câmara's poem Auto da Lenda was published.
Câmara de Lobos led Madeira's fish landings, while Reis Magos landed 102 sperm whales.
Only 187 vessels entered the port of Funchal during the Second World War.
Imports and exports through the port of Funchal reached 222,258 tonnes.
A. Artur Sarmento published a pamphlet on Archduchess Leopoldina's visit to Madeira.
The Praça do Município in Funchal was enlarged, the town hall freed from adjoining buildings and a large fountain built.
Armando Eduardo Pinto Correia died at Quelimane, Mozambique.
A series of articles on the beginning of Madeiran settlement, 1425–1450, was published in O Jornal.
Alfredo Vital Miguéis died in Funchal.
João de Oliveira Sá Camelo Lampreia died in Rio de Janeiro.
The Casa dos Pescadores building in Machico was inaugurated.
A further list of classified national monuments in Madeira was published in the Diário do Governo.
José da Cruz Tavares published an article on Madeiran wine folklore.

Decrees nos. 33,158 and 33,159 on the hydraulic development of Madeira were promulgated, changing the administration of the levadas, regulating the use of springs, and ordering a network of new irrigation channels and hydro-electric works.
The Junta Autónoma dos Portos published a table of sunrise and sunset times for Funchal.
Common upland land was sold at public auction by a state office in a rural municipality.
An official report noted that the Malvasia Candia vine had almost entirely disappeared from Madeira.
Aníbal Augusto Trigo died.
The Junta Geral inaugurated a fishermen's housing block at Paul do Mar.
Engineer Henrique Schreck presented to the Junta Geral a report on works to be carried out in Madeira's ports.
Madeira's forest posts were increased from 14 to 19 and the number of forest guards raised to 42.
Publication date given by the Elucidário for Moritz Edenfeld's travel book, probably a misprint.
A rain-gauge post was set up at São Vicente.
José de Oliveira Duarte's commemorative article on João Francisco de Sousa appeared in the Diário de Notícias.
A bill was presented in parliament to cede the Quinta Vigia in Funchal as a house for journalists.
